statement: Skills let Claude package specialized expertise so it performs specific, specialized tasks more capably.

Claude accesses a skill only when that skill is relevant to the task at hand.
condition: the skill is relevant to the current task

statement: When a skill matches, Claude loads only the minimal information and files that skill needs, keeping Claude fast while it draws on the specialized expertise.
Skills are composable: multiple skills stack together, and Claude identifies which ones a task needs and coordinates their use.
Skills use one portable format across Claude apps, Claude Code, and the API, so a skill can be built once and reused everywhere.
Put executable code in a skill for subtasks where deterministic programming is more reliable than having the model produce the result through token generation.
condition: the subtask is more reliably done by deterministic code than by token generation

statement: Claude automatically invokes the relevant skills for a task, requiring no manual skill selection by the user.

Use the skill-creator skill to scaffold a new skill: it interviews you about the workflow, generates the folder structure, formats the SKILL.md file, and bundles the resources, avoiding manual file editing.

On Team and Enterprise plans, an administrator must enable Skills organization-wide before users can use them.
condition: the account is on a Team or Enterprise plan

condition: using Skills through the API

condition: using Skills through the API

Share skills with a team by distributing them through version control.
The Claude Agent SDK provides the same Agent Skills support for building custom agents.
condition: building a custom agent with the Claude Agent SDK

statement: Because Skills give Claude the ability to execute code, install skills only from trusted sources to keep your data safe.
Agent Skills is published as an open standard so skills are portable across platforms.
Organization-wide skill management lets administrators distribute and govern skills across an organization.
condition: managing skills at the organization level

statement: A Skill is a folder of instructions, scripts, and resources that Claude discovers and loads dynamically when it is relevant to the current task.

Skills use progressive disclosure: roughly 100 tokens of metadata load first, the full instructions (under ~5k tokens) load only when the Skill is needed, and any bundled files or scripts load only when actually required.
Claude selects a Skill by first scanning the metadata of available Skills for a match to the task, then loading that Skill's full instructions.
Use a Skill when Claude must perform a specialized task consistently and repeatedly, such as organizational workflows, domain expertise, or personal-preference procedures.
condition: when the same specialized task recurs across conversations

statement: When the same prompt is being retyped across multiple conversations, convert it into a Skill so the procedure is captured once and executes consistently without re-explanation.
condition: when the same prompt is retyped across multiple conversations

statement: Prompts are natural-language instructions given during a conversation; they are ephemeral, conversational, and reactive.
Prompts do not persist across conversations.
Use prompts for one-off requests, conversational refinement, immediate context, and ad-hoc instructions.
A Project is a self-contained workspace with its own chat history and knowledge base, available on all paid Claude plans.
condition: on paid Claude plans

statement: Each Project provides a 200K-token context window and supports uploaded documents plus custom instructions that apply to every conversation within that project.
Content uploaded to a Project's knowledge base becomes available across all chats in that project without re-uploading or re-explaining it.
When a Project's knowledge base approaches the context limit, Claude switches to Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mode, expanding effective capacity by up to roughly 10x.
condition: when the project's knowledge base approaches the context limit

statement: Use a Project when you need persistent background context, workspace separation between initiatives, shared team knowledge, or project-specific custom instructions.
Shared team knowledge and conversation history within a Project require a Team or Enterprise plan.
condition: on Team or Enterprise plans

statement: When the same instructions are being copied across multiple Projects, move that knowledge into a Skill instead.
condition: when the same instructions are copied across multiple projects

statement: A subagent is a specialized assistant with its own context window, custom system prompt, and specific tool permissions, available in Claude Code and the Claude Agent SDK.
condition: in Claude Code and the Claude Agent SDK

statement: A subagent handles a discrete task independently and returns its result to the main agent.
Claude delegates a task to an appropriate subagent automatically based on the subagent's description, or on explicit request.
Use subagents for task specialization, context management by offloading work to keep the main conversation focused, parallel processing, and tool restriction.
Restrict a subagent to safe, read-only tools (for example Read, Grep, and Glob but not Write or Edit) when it must not risk unintended changes, as with a code-review subagent.
condition: when the subagent must not risk unintended changes to code or state

statement: When multiple agents or conversations need the same expertise, put that expertise in a portable Skill rather than duplicating it inside individual subagents.
condition: when multiple agents or conversations need the same expertise

statement: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to external systems where data lives, such as content repositories, business tools, databases, and development environments.
With MCP you build against a single standardized protocol instead of a custom integration for each data source.
MCP servers expose data and capabilities, and MCP clients such as Claude connect to those servers.
Use MCP when Claude needs to access external data, use business tools, connect to development environments, or integrate custom or proprietary systems.
MCP provides connectivity to data while Skills provide the procedural knowledge for using it, so pair MCP for access with Skills for how-to.

The building blocks differ in persistence: Skills persist across conversations, prompts last a single conversation, Project context persists within the project, subagents persist across sessions, and MCP is a continuous connection.

The building blocks differ in load timing: Skills load dynamically as needed, prompts load each turn, Project context is always loaded within the project, subagents load when invoked, and MCP is always available.
Skills, subagents, and MCP can include executable code, whereas prompts and Projects cannot.

Compose the building blocks for advanced agentic workflows: a Project for persistent context, MCP for data connectivity, Skills for the analytical framework, subagents for specialized parallel execution, and prompts for in-the-moment refinement.
In Claude Code and the Agent SDK, a subagent can load and use Skills just like the main agent.
condition: in Claude Code and the Agent SDK

statement: Choose a Project for always-loaded background knowledge that should inform every conversation about an initiative, and a Skill for on-demand procedural capability that loads only when relevant.

Choose a Skill for portable, reusable expertise any Claude instance can load, and a subagent when you need a complete, self-contained agent that runs a workflow independently with its own context and tools.
Skills must be enabled before use: on Claude.ai via Settings then Features, and in Claude Code via plugin marketplaces.
Agent Skills are organized folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that an agent can discover and load dynamically to perform better at specific tasks.
A skill is a directory that contains a SKILL.md file, optionally alongside bundled instructions, scripts, and resources.
A SKILL.md file must begin with YAML frontmatter that contains the required metadata fields name and description.
At startup the agent pre-loads the name and description of every installed skill into its system prompt.

Skill metadata (name and description) is the first level of progressive disclosure: it gives the agent just enough information to know when a skill should be used without loading the whole skill into context.
The body of a SKILL.md file is the second level of detail and is loaded into context only when the agent judges the skill relevant to the current task.
When a skill carries too much context for a single SKILL.md, bundle additional files in the skill directory and reference them by name from SKILL.md so the agent loads them only as needed.
condition: the skill's context is too large for one SKILL.md or is relevant only in specific scenarios

statement: Keep the core SKILL.md lean by moving scenario-specific instructions into separate bundled files, so the agent reads them only when that scenario arises.
Progressive disclosure — loading skill information only as needed — is the core design principle that makes Agent Skills flexible and scalable.
Because an agent with a filesystem and code-execution tools need not read an entire skill into its context window, the amount of context that can be bundled into a skill is effectively unbounded.
condition: the agent has a filesystem and code-execution tools

statement: Skills can include code that the agent executes as tools at its own discretion.
Some operations are better handled by traditional code execution than by token generation; for example, sorting a list by generating tokens is far more expensive than running a sorting algorithm.
Prefer code for operations that require deterministic reliability, because code is deterministic and makes the workflow consistent and repeatable.
An agent can run a skill's bundled script without loading either the script or its input data into the context window.
When authoring skills, start with evaluation: run agents on representative tasks to identify specific capability gaps, then build skills incrementally to address those gaps.
Structure skills for scale: when a SKILL.md becomes unwieldy, split its content into separate files and reference them.
Keep mutually-exclusive or rarely co-used contexts in separate skill files to reduce token usage.
condition: certain contexts are mutually exclusive or rarely used together

statement: Make it explicit whether the agent should execute a skill's code directly or read it as reference, since code can serve as both an executable tool and as documentation.
Design and refine skills from the agent's perspective: monitor how the agent uses a skill in real scenarios and iterate, watching for unexpected trajectories or overreliance on certain contexts.
Pay special attention to a skill's name and description, because the agent relies on them to decide whether to trigger the skill for the current task.
Iterate with the agent: have it capture successful approaches and common mistakes into reusable context and code within the skill, and ask it to self-reflect when it goes off track.
Discovering what context an agent actually needs by observing its real work is more effective than trying to anticipate that context upfront.
Malicious skills may introduce vulnerabilities into the environment where they are used, or direct the agent to exfiltrate data and take unintended actions.
Install skills only from trusted sources.

When installing a skill from a less-trusted source, thoroughly audit it before use: read the bundled files and pay particular attention to code dependencies and bundled resources such as images or scripts.
condition: installing a skill from a less-trusted source

statement: When auditing a skill, watch for instructions or code that direct the agent to connect to potentially untrusted external network sources.
condition: auditing a skill before use

statement: Building a skill is like writing an onboarding guide for a new hire: it captures and shares procedural knowledge as composable capabilities that specialize a general-purpose agent.
Agent Skills are supported across Claude.ai, Claude Code, the Claude Agent SDK, and the Claude Developer Platform, and have been published as an open standard for cross-platform portability.
A skill is defined by three core components: a name, a description, and instructions for execution.
Only the skill's name and description influence triggering; the instructions body does not affect whether Claude invokes the skill.
The description is the most critical component of a skill because it determines when the skill activates.
Write the skill description from Claude's perspective, focused on triggers, capabilities, and use cases.
A strong description balances four elements: specific capabilities, clear triggers, relevant context, and explicit boundaries.
Give the description concrete signals: specific action verbs, concrete use cases, and statements of what the skill is not for.
Name a skill in lowercase-with-hyphens, keeping it short, clear, and descriptive.
Skill triggering works by semantic relevance rather than keyword matching: Claude interprets the meaning of the description against the request.
Vague or overly generic descriptions reduce triggering accuracy: generic descriptions cause inappropriate activation while missing use cases cause missed activations.
Multiple skills can activate simultaneously when they address different aspects of a task.
condition: the task spans multiple distinct aspects

statement: Before writing a skill, clarify the concrete problem it solves; strong skills target concrete needs with measurable outcomes.
Define what a skill does by specifying the input format, the operation, and the expected output.
Scope a skill to a single purpose at a granularity focused enough for specific instructions yet broad enough to be reusable.
Write instructions that are structured, scannable, and actionable, using markdown headers, bullet lists, and code blocks.
Structure instructions with a clear hierarchy (overview, prerequisites, steps, examples, error handling, limitations) and break complex workflows into discrete phases with clear inputs and outputs.
Include concrete examples of correct usage in the instructions.
State explicitly what the skill cannot do, to prevent misuse and set expectations.
Keep the SKILL.md lean: do not load content into context on every invocation when it is only conditionally needed.
Use a progressive-disclosure menu structure: the SKILL.md lists what is available and links to separate files by relative path so Claude loads only the file relevant to the task.
Test a skill against realistic scenarios before deploying it.
Build a test matrix covering three scenario classes: normal operations, edge cases, and out-of-scope requests.
For out-of-scope requests a well-scoped skill should stay dormant and let other skills or general Claude handle them.
Handle edge cases gracefully by producing degraded-but-useful output or explaining what is needed to proceed.
condition: inputs are incomplete or unusual

statement: Test triggering and execution separately, exercising triggering with both explicit and natural-language requests and confirming the skill stays inactive for similar-but-distinct requests.
Run functional tests for output consistency across similar inputs, usability by a non-domain user, and documentation accuracy.
Iterate skills from real usage: refine the description when triggering is inconsistent and clarify instructions when outputs vary.
Build skills for real, repeated tasks rather than speculatively.
Apply a usage threshold before building a skill: build one only if the task has been done at least five times and will recur at least ten more.
Define explicit success criteria and embed them in the skill so Claude can self-check its output.
Use the skill-creator skill or template to scaffold a well-structured skill; it asks clarifying questions and suggests description improvements.
Debug a skill by adjusting the failing dimension: broaden the description and add use cases when it fails to activate; add instruction specificity and validation steps when results are inconsistent.
For organization-wide skills, establish governance: per-domain owners, a central library, usage examples, versioning with a changelog, and periodic review to retire outdated skills.
Provide precise information Claude does not inherently have, such as exact colour codes, font names, and size thresholds.
Route a multi-workflow skill with a decision tree that selects the correct workflow by task type.
condition: the skill covers multiple distinct workflows

statement: Show complex patterns with paired good and bad examples so the correct implementation is unambiguous.
Group many changes into small batches of about three to ten and verify each batch before proceeding.
condition: applying many changes in a single large edit

statement: In Claude Code, skills are installed by placing skill folders containing a SKILL.md under a skills/ directory in the plugin or project root, where Claude discovers them automatically.
On Claude.ai, custom skills require a Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plan with code execution enabled, and uploaded skills are individual to each user rather than shared organization-wide.
condition: on the Claude.ai surface

statement: Skill-creator enhancements add authoring support for writing evals, running benchmarks, and maintaining skills as model behavior changes.
Skill authors are often subject matter experts rather than engineers, so evaluation tools should make skill quality, triggering, and improvement measurable without requiring coding expertise.
condition: When authoring support is intended for non-engineer domain experts.

statement: Capability uplift skills encode techniques and patterns for tasks the base model cannot do, or cannot do consistently, from prompting alone.
condition: When a skill is meant to improve a capability beyond base-model reliability.

statement: Encoded preference skills capture team workflows where the model can perform individual steps but must sequence and apply them according to a preferred process.
condition: When the base model can perform the component actions but needs workflow fidelity.

statement: Skill type should influence the evaluation strategy because capability uplift and encoded preference skills fail for different reasons.
condition: When designing or maintaining skill evals.

statement: Capability uplift skills may become less necessary as base models improve, and evals can signal when the base model has absorbed the needed behavior.
condition: When evaluating a skill whose purpose is to add or stabilize a model capability.

statement: Encoded preference skills tend to remain useful only if they continue to match the actual workflow they encode, so their evals should verify process fidelity.
condition: When maintaining a skill that represents a team-specific or organization-specific workflow.

statement: Testing changes a skill from something that merely appears to work into something whose behavior can be checked against explicit expectations.
A useful skill eval should specify prompts, any required files, and the criteria that define a good output for each prompt.
condition: When authoring tests for skill behavior.

statement: Evals can isolate concrete skill failure modes and guide targeted fixes instead of relying on broad prompt edits.
condition: When a skill fails on a reproducible task case.

statement: The PDF skill failure on non-fillable forms was addressed after evals exposed coordinate-placement problems and led to anchoring placement against extracted text coordinates.
Running evals against a new model provides an early warning for quality regressions before changed behavior affects team work.
condition: When models or surrounding infrastructure change.

statement: For capability uplift skills, authors should compare eval performance with and without the skill to detect when the base model no longer needs the skill.
condition: When evaluating whether a capability uplift skill remains necessary.

statement: Benchmark runs should be used after model updates or skill iterations to track pass rate, elapsed time, and token usage over a standardized eval set.
condition: When comparing model changes or skill revisions over time.

statement: Keeping eval definitions and results portable lets teams store them locally, integrate them into dashboards, or run them through CI.
condition: When building an evaluation workflow that must persist outside an interactive session.

statement: Running eval cases in independent agents can speed evaluation and reduce context contamination between test runs.
condition: When an eval suite can be split into independent test runs.

statement: Blinded comparator agents can support A/B evaluation between two skill versions or between a skill and no skill to judge whether a change improved output quality.
condition: When comparing two outputs or two skill configurations.

statement: Output-quality evals are insufficient if a skill does not trigger when needed, so trigger behavior needs its own evaluation and tuning.
condition: When a skill must be discoverable among multiple available skills.

statement: As the number of available skills grows, description precision becomes critical because broad descriptions cause false triggers and narrow descriptions cause missed activations.
condition: When many skills may compete for activation.

statement: Description tuning should analyze the current skill description against sample prompts and revise wording to reduce both false positives and false negatives.
condition: When improving whether a skill triggers for the right requests.

statement: Applying description optimization across document-creation skills improved trigger behavior on five of six public skills in the reported test.
condition: In the reported document-creation skill evaluation.

statement: As models improve, natural-language descriptions of desired skill behavior may become more central than detailed implementation instructions.
condition: If future models can infer implementation steps from behavioral specifications.

statement: Because evals already describe desired behavior, they can serve as a bridge from implementation-heavy skill files toward more specification-like skills.
condition: When treating evals as behavioral specifications rather than only regression tests.

statement: A skill is a folder — not merely a single markdown file — that can bundle instructions, scripts, assets, and data which the agent can discover, explore, and manipulate.
The most effective skills exploit the folder structure and available configuration options (including dynamically registered hooks) rather than being a lone instruction file.
Scope each skill to a single clear purpose: the best skills fit cleanly into one category, while skills that try to do too much straddle several and confuse the agent.

Internal skills at Anthropic cluster into nine categories: library/API reference, product verification, data fetching and analysis, business-process and team automation, code scaffolding and templates, code quality and review, CI/CD and deployment, runbooks, and infrastructure operations; this taxonomy is useful for spotting gaps in a skills library.
Library and API reference skills should ship a folder of reference code snippets plus an explicit list of gotchas the agent should avoid.
Verification skills have had the most measurable impact on Claude's output quality in Anthropic's internal use.
Investing heavily in verification skills is worthwhile — it can be worth having an engineer spend a full week making verification skills excellent.

Strengthen verification skills with concrete techniques such as having Claude record a video of its output and enforcing programmatic assertions on state at each step, typically via scripts bundled in the skill.
Business-process and automation skills should save previous results in log files, which helps the model stay consistent and reflect on prior executions of the workflow.
Code scaffolding and template skills are especially valuable when the scaffolding carries natural-language requirements that pure code cannot cover.
Code quality and review skills can embed deterministic scripts and be run automatically, for example via hooks or inside a CI/GitHub Action, for maximum robustness.
Do not state the obvious in a skill: Claude already knows how to code and can read the codebase, so a skill that restates default behaviour adds context without adding value.
A knowledge-oriented skill should focus on information that pushes Claude out of its normal way of thinking rather than repeating what it would do by default.
The highest-signal content in any skill is a Gotchas section built from the common failure points the agent hits, and the skill should be updated over time to capture new gotchas.
Treat the entire file system of a skill as context engineering and progressive disclosure: tell Claude which files exist and it will read them at the appropriate times.
The simplest form of progressive disclosure is to point from SKILL.md to other markdown files, for example moving detailed function signatures and usage examples into a references file.
Avoid over-specifying instructions that railroad Claude; give it the information it needs but leave flexibility to adapt to the situation.
condition: because skills are highly reusable across many contexts

statement: Store a skill's setup context in a config.json in the skill directory, and have the agent ask the user for the information when that config is not yet set up.
condition: when a skill needs user-provided setup context

statement: Instruct Claude to use the AskUserQuestion tool when the agent should present structured, multiple-choice questions to the user.

Write skill descriptions for the model rather than for humans: the description field is what Claude scans at session start to decide whether a skill applies, so it must describe when to trigger the skill rather than summarise it.
Include explicit trigger words (for example 'babysit') in a skill's description so the model reliably activates it.

Skills can hold memory by storing data within them — as simple as an append-only text log or JSON file, or as complex as a SQLite database — so the agent can read its own history and detect what has changed since last run.
Use the ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} environment variable to obtain a stable directory for persisting a skill's data.
Give Claude scripts and libraries so it spends its turns on composition — deciding what to do next — instead of reconstructing boilerplate.

Skills can register on-demand hooks that activate only while the skill is in use and last only for the session, which suits opinionated guardrails (e.g. blocking destructive commands) that you do not want running all the time.
condition: when a hook is too opinionated or risky to run globally

statement: Skills can be shared two ways: checked into a repository under ./.claude/skills, or packaged as a plugin distributed through a Claude Code plugin marketplace.

Checking skills into repos works for small teams across few repos, but every checked-in skill adds to the model's context; at scale an internal plugin marketplace is preferable because it lets teams choose which skills to install and can include a setup flow.
condition: as the number of skills and repositories grows

statement: Curate a skills marketplace organically instead of via a central gatekeeping team: authors publish to a sandbox folder, gain traction, then open a PR to promote the skill into the marketplace.
Skill-to-skill dependencies are not natively managed, but you can reference another skill by name and the model will invoke it if it is installed.
Instrument skill usage with a PreToolUse hook that logs when skills run, so you can identify skills that are popular or under-triggering relative to expectations.
Effective skills tend to start small — a few lines and a single gotcha — and improve iteratively as people add to them when Claude encounters new edge cases.

Building and deploying capable general-purpose agents repeatedly exposes the same gap: an agent has intelligence and broad capability but lacks the domain expertise needed to effectively do real work.
To extend an agent's capabilities, prefer building Skills (packaged domain expertise) over building separate specialized, domain-specific agents.

A Skill is an organized collection of files (a SKILL.md plus optional supporting documents and scripts) that packages domain expertise — workflows, best practices, and procedural knowledge — in a form an agent can access and apply.
Skills turn a capable generalist agent into a knowledgeable specialist.
Code is not merely one use case but a general interface through which an agent can perform almost any kind of digital work.

Because an agent can act through code — calling APIs, using the filesystem, and running Python — the agent scaffolding can be as simple as bash and a filesystem rather than bespoke per-domain tooling.
General capability is not the same as expertise: a broadly capable agent still lacks the accumulated, domain-specific know-how of a seasoned professional.
Without added expertise, agents are often missing important context, cannot easily absorb an organization's expertise, and do not automatically learn from repeated tasks.
Bridge the expertise gap by packaging domain expertise as Skills that the agent can progressively access and apply.
Representing skills as plain files is deliberate: files are a universal primitive, so skills can be version-controlled with Git, stored in shared drives, and shared across a team.
Because skills are just files, skill authoring is not limited to engineers; product managers, analysts, and domain experts can codify their own workflows as skills.
Skills use progressive disclosure: at runtime the model is initially shown only each skill's metadata (the name and description from the YAML frontmatter), not its full contents.

condition: when the model determines the skill is relevant to the current task
statement: The model reads a skill's full SKILL.md only when it determines the skill is relevant to the task, and further detail lives in a references/ directory loaded only on demand.

Progressive disclosure is three-tier by token cost — metadata roughly 50 tokens, a full SKILL.md roughly 500 tokens, and reference files 2,000+ tokens loaded only when needed — so an agent can be equipped with hundreds of skills without overwhelming its context window.
Traditional tools have recurring drawbacks: their instructions are sometimes poorly written, the model often cannot modify or extend them, and they consume context-window space even when unused.
Providing capability as code (scripts) is preferable to opaque tools because code is self-documenting, modifiable by the agent, and need not stay in the context window at all times.

condition: when the same script recurs across tasks
statement: When the agent is repeatedly writing the same script for a task, save that script as a reusable tool inside a skill and have the skill's documentation reference the script rather than inlining the code.

Three kinds of skills are emerging in practice: foundational skills (core document, spreadsheet, and presentation capabilities), partner skills (vendors packaging their services for agent access), and enterprise skills (an organization's internal processes, compliance requirements, and institutional knowledge).

Skills are growing in complexity, from simple documentation or template references toward sophisticated multi-step workflows that coordinate data retrieval, computation, and formatted output across multiple tools.
Skills and MCP servers are complementary: a single skill can orchestrate several MCP-connected sources — web search, internal databases, message history, and documents — to synthesize a result.
Non-engineers can author and test a first skill quickly — reportedly in under 30 minutes — using an interactive skill-creator tool that guides them through the process.

The emerging general-agent architecture has four layers: an agent loop that reasons and decides the next action, an agent runtime that executes (code and filesystem), MCP servers that connect to external tools and data, and a skills library that supplies domain expertise and procedural knowledge.
Keeping the four architecture layers separated — the loop reasons, the runtime executes, MCP connects, and skills guide — keeps the system comprehensible and lets each layer evolve independently.

condition: the skill activates only when the current task matches its domain
statement: Skills are composable and additive: adding a single skill can immediately extend the agent within a domain, and progressive disclosure means the skill activates only when the current task is relevant to it.

The general-agent-plus-MCP-plus-skills pattern generalizes across domains, so the same base agent can be deployed into new verticals (for example financial services or healthcare) by adding domain skills rather than rebuilding the agent.
Treat skills as a portable open standard so that the same skill works across different agent tools and platforms rather than being locked to a single vendor.

Because skills capture and transfer expertise, an agent can start already knowing what a team cares about, and the collective value is expected to grow as reusable skills accumulate across teams and the community.
Model Context Protocol (MCP) connects Claude to external, third-party tools, systems, and services, providing the connectivity layer.
Skills supply the procedural and domain knowledge plus workflow logic Claude needs to use tool connections effectively.
Combining skills with MCP lets a team build agents that follow that team's specific workflows and produce consistent outputs, instead of generic processes that require constant correction.
condition: when both skills and MCP are used together

statement: MCP provides secure, standardized access to external systems such as GitHub, Salesforce, Notion, and internal APIs.
A well-authored skill encodes when to query a system, what to look for in the results, how to format the output, and which edge cases require different handling.
The separation of skills from MCP keeps the architecture composable: a single skill can orchestrate multiple MCP servers, and a single MCP server can support many different skills.
Because responsibilities are separated, adding a new MCP connection lets existing skills incorporate it, and refining one skill improves behaviour across all connected tools.
Pairing a skill with MCP gives clear discovery: the skill encodes which sources to consult and in what order for a given task, so Claude stops guessing where to look.
Skills define multi-step sequences explicitly so that Claude executes the workflow the same way every time, giving reliable orchestration.
Skills define what a finished output looks like (structure, level of detail, and tone) so outputs meet team standards rather than needing manual editing.
MCP servers may include instructions as tool-usage hints and prompts for common tasks to keep tool-specific knowledge close to the tool, but those instructions should be kept generic by design.

As a rule of thumb, MCP instructions should cover how to use the server and its tools correctly, while skill instructions should cover how to use those tools for a given process or a multi-server workflow.

When combining MCP servers and skills, conflicting instructions must be avoided; if the MCP server dictates one output format and the skill dictates another, Claude is forced to guess which to follow.
condition: when combining MCP servers and skills

statement: Let MCP handle connectivity and let skills handle presentation, sequencing, and workflow logic, to prevent instruction conflicts.
Use skills for multi-step workflows involving tools that pull from multiple sources and then create structured documents.
Use skills for processes where consistency matters, such as periodic analyses that must follow the same methodology every time or compliance reviews with mandatory checkpoints.
Use skills to capture and share domain expertise such as research methodologies, code-review standards, and writing guidelines.
Use skills to encode workflows as reusable instructions so institutional knowledge survives when team members leave.
Use an MCP server when you need real-time data access, such as searching Notion pages, reading Slack messages, or querying databases.
Use an MCP server when you need to take actions in external systems, such as creating GitHub issues, updating project-management tools, or sending notifications.
Use an MCP server for file operations such as reading from and writing to Google Drive or accessing local filesystems.
Use an MCP server for API integrations to services that lack native Claude support.
condition: when the target service has no native Claude support

statement: Decision heuristic: if you are explaining how to do something, build a skill; if you need Claude to access something, use an MCP server.
Skills load on demand only when relevant, preserving context window, whereas MCP tool definitions are loaded upfront and are always available once the server is connected.
Skills do not replace MCP; the two solve different problems and the most powerful workflows use both together.

A single skill can coordinate several MCP servers at once, for example searching Google Drive, pulling competitor repositories from GitHub, and gathering market data via web search within one workflow.

Multiple distinct skills can be built for one MCP server, each enhancing the value obtained from that single connection (for example separate meeting-prep, research, and knowledge-capture skills over one Notion connection).

A recommended skill+MCP workflow follows a discovery, orchestration, then performance pattern: the skill selects which sources to query, MCP pulls the live data, the skill applies methodology and formats the output, and the skill validates the result against requirements.
Skills use progressive disclosure to load context on demand and programmatic tool calling to orchestrate MCP tools efficiently.
To start combining the two, connect an MCP server first and then add a skill that uses that connection.
Skills are presented as reusable workflow packages that teach Claude procedures tailored to a user or organization.
The update focuses on making skills easier to deploy, discover, and author.

Claude Code offers seven methods for instructing Claude's behavior: root/subdirectory CLAUDE.md files, rules, skills, subagents, hooks, output styles, and appending the system prompt.
The instruction methods differ along three axes: when the instruction loads into context, whether it persists through compaction, and how much authority (instruction-following weight) it carries.
Root CLAUDE.md loads at session start, stays in context for the whole session, and is memoized — read once and cached, with the cache cleared and re-read after compaction.
A subdirectory CLAUDE.md loads on-demand only when Claude reads a file under that subdirectory, and is dropped from context until that subdirectory is touched again.
Put build commands, directory layout, monorepo structure, coding conventions, and team norms in the root CLAUDE.md.
Keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, give it a single owner, and review changes to it like code.
As CLAUDE.md grows, migrate team-specific conventions into path-scoped rules and procedures into skills so that content loads only when relevant, rather than costing tokens in every session.

In monorepos, give each team's directory its own subdirectory CLAUDE.md so teams load only their own conventions, and let developers use the claudeMdExcludes setting to skip files from teams whose code they never touch.

For standards that must apply to every repository in an organization (security or compliance), deploy a centrally managed CLAUDE.md to developer machines via MDM or config management so it cannot be excluded by individual settings.
Rules are markdown files in .claude/rules/ that give Claude specific constraints or conventions.
Unscoped rules are always loaded at session start and re-injected on compaction, behaving like CLAUDE.md and costing tokens even when not relevant to the task.
A path-scoped rule loads its instructions only when files matching its 'paths' frontmatter are touched, keeping it out of context during unrelated sessions.
condition: the rule declares a 'paths' field and Claude reads a file matching one of those globs

statement: Prefer a path-scoped rule over a nested CLAUDE.md when the instruction is a file-specific constraint or a cross-cutting concern that appears in multiple but not all corners of the codebase.
Skills live in .claude/skills/ as folders of instructions, scripts, and resources, each with a SKILL.md file containing a name, description, and body.
Only a skill's name and description load at session start; its full body loads only when the skill is invoked, either via a slash command or by auto-matching the task.
On compaction, invoked skills are re-injected up to a shared token budget across all invoked skills, and the oldest invoked skills are dropped first once that budget is exceeded.
condition: many skills have been invoked in the session so the shared budget is exceeded

statement: Put procedural instructions such as deploy workflows, release checklists, and review processes in a skill rather than in CLAUDE.md.
Subagents are markdown files in .claude/agents/ using YAML frontmatter (name, description, optional model and tool-access fields) followed by a body that becomes that subagent's system prompt.

A subagent's name, description, and tool list load at session start, but its body never enters the parent conversation and does not auto-invoke; Claude must call it via the Agent tool with a prompt string.
A subagent runs in its own fresh, isolated context window, and only its final message plus metadata returns to the main session.

Use a subagent when a side task (deep search, log analysis, dependency audit) would clutter the main conversation with intermediate results you won't reference again; use a skill when you want the procedure to play out in the main thread so you can see and steer each step.

Hooks are user-defined commands, HTTP endpoints, or LLM prompts that fire on specific Claude lifecycle events such as file edits, tool calls, or session start, giving deterministic control over behavior.
Hooks are registered in settings.json, in managed policy settings, or in skill/agent frontmatter.

There are five hook types — command, HTTP, mcp_tool, prompt, and agent — where command, HTTP, and mcp_tool execute deterministically while prompt and agent hooks use Claude's judgment to determine output.
Hooks have low context cost because their configuration lives outside the main context window, and most hook output is not saved to the main context unless the configuration explicitly returns it.
A blocking hook's standard error is saved into the main context so Claude knows why the call was denied.

Use hooks for anything that should happen deterministically — running linters after edits, posting to Slack on completion, or blocking specific commands — and a PreToolUse hook can inspect any tool call and exit code 2 to deny it.

Output styles are files in .claude/output-styles/ that inject instructions into the system prompt; they load at every session start, are never compacted, and are cached after the first request in a session.
Because output styles sit in the system prompt, they carry the highest instruction-following weight of the covered methods and should be used judiciously.

A custom output style replaces the default output style, dropping Claude Code's default software-engineering instructions (how to scope changes, when to add or omit comments, security handling, and verification habits like running tests before declaring work complete).
exception: the style's frontmatter sets keep-coding-instructions: true

statement: Before writing a custom output style, check the built-in styles — Proactive, Explanatory, and Learning — which cover the most common needs (autonomy, teaching mode, collaborative coding) without maintaining a style file.

The append-system-prompt flag is additive only: it adds instructions to Claude's default role without modifying that role, is passed at invocation time, and applies only to that single invocation rather than persisting as a file across sessions.
Appending the system prompt has diminishing returns for adherence — the more instructions provided this way, the less strictly Claude follows them, particularly when any of them contradict.
Use append-system-prompt for adding specific coding standards, output formatting, or domain-specific knowledge.

When a behavior must happen reliably on 'every time X, always do Y', use a hook in settings.json instead of a CLAUDE.md instruction, because the model choosing to run a tool is different from the tool running automatically.

For something that absolutely must not happen, an instruction is the wrong tool because a prompted rule can fail under pressure, in long sessions, in ambiguous situations, or via prompt injection; a real guardrail must be deterministic, enforced through hooks and permissions.
Managed settings are admin-deployed, cannot be overridden by a user's local config, and are the only way to enforce a deterministic organization-wide guardrail.

All file-based instruction methods have a user-level counterpart that loads for every Claude Code session regardless of repository; keep personal preferences in user-level files and reserve project-level files for team-wide preferences specific to that codebase.
Bundle related skills, subagents, hooks, and output styles into a plugin to share a coherent Claude Code setup across teammates or projects.

statement: Task abstractions can fit multi-agent work better than static todo lists because they can express dependencies, shared updates, and changes across agents.

Loops in Claude Code are agent work cycles that repeat until a defined stop condition is reached.
Loop designs should be distinguished by their trigger, stopping rule, Claude Code primitive, and task fit.
Use the simplest workable approach before introducing a more complex loop pattern.
exception: When a task genuinely requires repetition, scheduling, or external-state monitoring, a richer loop can be justified.

statement: A turn-based loop starts from a user prompt and leaves the user directing each subsequent turn.
Turn-based loops fit shorter tasks that are not recurring or scheduled processes.
condition: When the task is short and irregular.

statement: Specific prompts and stronger verification skills reduce the number of turns needed in manual loops.
condition: When operating a turn-based loop.

statement: In a manual agentic loop, Claude gathers context, acts, checks its work, repeats if needed, and then reports back.
condition: When a user prompt starts a turn-based workflow.

statement: A human review step remains necessary in turn-based work when Claude only returns something it believes is complete.
condition: When completion has not been independently verified.

statement: Manual verification procedures can be encoded as a skill so Claude can check more of its work end-to-end.
condition: When the verification process is repeatable enough to document.

statement: Verification skills should provide tools or connectors that let Claude inspect, measure, or interact with the result.
condition: When self-verification depends on observing the produced system.

statement: Quantitative checks are easier for Claude to self-verify than vague qualitative assessments.
A UI-change verification skill should run the app, exercise the changed interface, inspect the browser console, and evaluate performance before declaring completion.
condition: When verifying a frontend or UI change end-to-end.

statement: If a documented verification step fails, the agent should fix the issue and rerun the verification from the beginning rather than return partially verified work.
condition: When a verification checklist has a failing step.

statement: Goal-based loops are useful when one turn is insufficient and the task has verifiable exit criteria.
condition: When success can be evaluated against explicit criteria.

statement: Defining done explicitly reduces premature stopping because Claude no longer has to infer what is good enough.
condition: When using a goal-based loop.

statement: In goal-based loops, an evaluator can return Claude to work until the goal is met or a turn cap is reached.

statement: Deterministic criteria such as passing tests or reaching a score threshold are especially effective success conditions for goal-based loops.
condition: When the task outcome can be measured deterministically.

statement: Time-based loops fit recurring work and workflows that must react to changing external systems.

statement: A local interval loop stops if the local computer stops running, while a scheduled routine can move the recurring loop to a cloud environment.

condition: When useful work depends on test results, exception reports, support threads, or similar data sources

statement: Claude Code navigates a codebase the way an engineer does: it traverses the file system, reads files, uses grep to find what it needs, and follows references across the codebase.
Claude Code runs locally on the developer's machine and needs no codebase index to be built, maintained, or uploaded to a server.

RAG-based coding tools embed the whole codebase and retrieve chunks at query time; at large scale the embedding pipeline falls behind active teams, so the index is stale and retrieval can return renamed or deleted symbols with no staleness signal.
Live agentic search avoids stale-index failures because each developer's instance works from the current codebase with no central index to maintain.
Agentic search works best when Claude has enough starting context to know where to look; navigation quality is shaped by how well the codebase is set up with CLAUDE.md files and skills.
condition: Claude has enough starting context to know where to look

statement: Asking Claude to find a vague pattern across a very large codebase exhausts the context window before useful work begins, so broad searches must be scoped.
condition: the search target is vague and the codebase is very large

statement: A common misconception is that Claude Code's capability comes from the model alone; in practice the harness built around the model determines performance more than the model by itself.
The Claude Code harness is built from five extension points — CLAUDE.md files, hooks, skills, plugins, and MCP servers — plus two further capabilities, LSP integrations and subagents.
The order in which teams build the harness extension points matters, because each layer builds on the one before it.
CLAUDE.md files come first: they are context files Claude reads automatically at the start of every session — a root file for the big picture and subdirectory files for local conventions.
Because CLAUDE.md files load in every session regardless of task, keep them focused on what applies broadly, or they become a drag on performance.
condition: the file loads in every session regardless of the task

statement: Hooks make the setup self-improving: beyond blocking wrong actions, their higher-value use is continuous improvement — e.g. a stop hook proposes CLAUDE.md updates while context is fresh, and a start hook loads team-specific context dynamically.
For automated checks such as linting and formatting, enforce the rules with hooks deterministically rather than relying on Claude to remember an instruction, which produces more consistent results.
condition: the check is a deterministic gate such as linting or formatting

statement: Skills keep specialized expertise available on demand through progressive disclosure, loading only when the task calls for it so they do not bloat every session.
Skills can be scoped to specific paths so they activate only in the relevant part of the codebase and never auto-load elsewhere.

A plugin bundles skills, hooks, and MCP configuration into one installable package, so a new engineer immediately gets the same context and capabilities as established users, and updates distribute through managed marketplaces.

LSP integrations give Claude symbol-level precision — following a call to its definition, tracing references across files, and telling identically named functions apart — whereas without LSP Claude pattern-matches on text and can land on the wrong symbol.
For multi-language codebases, LSP integration is one of the highest-value investments.
condition: the codebase spans multiple languages

statement: MCP servers connect Claude to internal tools, data sources, and APIs it cannot otherwise reach; the most sophisticated teams expose structured search as an MCP tool Claude calls directly.

Subagents split exploration from editing: an isolated Claude instance with its own context window does a task and returns only the final result to the parent — e.g. a read-only subagent maps a subsystem to a file, then the main agent edits with the full picture.
Do not put reusable expertise in CLAUDE.md; expertise meant to be reused across sessions and projects belongs in a skill.
Do not use prompts for behavior that should run automatically; automatic, consistent behavior belongs in a hook.
Do not build MCP connections before the basic harness layers are working.
Do not run exploration and editing in the same session; delegate exploration to a subagent so editing keeps a clean context.
Too much context in every session degrades performance while too little leaves Claude navigating blind, so effective deployments invest upfront in making the codebase legible to Claude.
Keep CLAUDE.md files lean and layered: the root file should hold only pointers and critical gotchas, or the rest drifts into noise.

Initialize Claude in subdirectories rather than at the repo root so it is scoped to the relevant part; Claude walks up the directory tree loading every CLAUDE.md it finds, so root-level context is never lost.
Scope test and lint commands per subdirectory in that directory's CLAUDE.md, because running the full suite for a one-service change causes timeouts and wastes context on irrelevant output.
condition: the codebase is service-oriented with per-directory test and build commands
exception: compiled-language monorepos with deep cross-directory dependencies, where per-subdirectory scoping is harder and may need project-specific build configuration

statement: Exclude generated files, build artifacts, and third-party code by committing permissions.deny / ignore rules in .claude/settings.json, so every developer gets the same version-controlled noise reduction.
exception: developers who work on code generators may override project-level exclusions in their local settings without affecting the team

statement: When the directory structure does not convey the layout, add a lightweight repo-root markdown map listing each top-level folder with a one-line description; for hundreds of folders layer it (root = highest level, subdirectory CLAUDE.md = next level on demand), and for simpler cases @-mention the specific files or directories.
condition: code is not consolidated in a conventional directory structure

statement: Run LSP servers so Claude searches by symbol instead of by string, because grep on a common function name returns thousands of matches and Claude burns context opening files to find the relevant one.
Even the hierarchical CLAUDE.md approach breaks down in edge cases such as codebases with hundreds of thousands of folders and millions of files, or legacy systems on non-git version control.
exception: codebases with hundreds of thousands of folders and millions of files, or legacy systems on non-git version control

statement: As models evolve, CLAUDE.md instructions, skills, and hooks written for the current model can become unnecessary or actively constraining for a future one — e.g. a rule forcing single-file refactors blocks a newer model's coordinated cross-file edits, and compensating skills/hooks become overhead once the limitation is gone.
Teams should run a meaningful configuration review every three to six months, and also whenever performance feels like it has plateaued after a major model release.
Technical configuration alone does not drive adoption; the organizational layer must be invested in as well.

The fastest-spreading rollouts made a dedicated infrastructure investment before broad access — a small team or even one person wired up the tooling so Claude already fit developer workflows on first contact.

Assign clear ownership of Claude Code: at minimum a single DRI with authority over settings, permissions policy, the plugin marketplace, and CLAUDE.md conventions and responsibility to keep them current; some organizations create a dedicated agent-manager (hybrid PM/engineer) role.
Bottoms-up adoption creates enthusiasm but fragments without someone to centralize and evangelize what works, so knowledge stays tribal and adoption plateaus.

In large or regulated organizations, address governance early: start with a defined set of approved skills, required code-review processes, and limited initial access, then expand as confidence builds.
condition: the organization is large or in a regulated industry

statement: The smoothest deployments establish cross-functional working groups early — engineering, information security, and governance together define requirements and build a rollout roadmap.

Claude Code is designed around conventional software-engineering environments (engineers as primary contributors, Git, standard directory structures); non-traditional setups need extra configuration work.
exception: game engines with large binary assets, unconventional version control, or non-engineer contributors, which require additional configuration work

statement: Dynamic workflows let Claude Code write its own agentic harness on the fly, custom-built for the task at hand.
The default Claude Code harness is built for coding but is useful for many non-coding tasks because many tasks resemble coding tasks.
Some task classes require a custom harness built on top of Claude Code to reach peak performance, including research, security analysis, agent teams, and code review.
condition: for complex, specialized task classes

statement: Dynamic workflows often use more tokens and are best suited to complex, high-value tasks.
condition: for complex, high-value tasks

statement: A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript file executed with special functions that spawn and coordinate subagents.
A dynamic workflow can choose which model each agent uses and whether each subagent runs in its own worktree, selecting the intelligence level and isolation the task needs.
If a dynamic workflow is interrupted, resuming the session lets it pick up from where it left off.
condition: when the workflow is interrupted (e.g., user action or quitting the terminal)

statement: The default harness must plan and execute in a single context window, which is effective for many coding tasks but breaks down on long-running, massively parallel, highly structured, or adversarial tasks.
condition: for long-running, massively parallel, highly structured, or adversarial tasks

statement: Working on a complex task for a long time in a single context window increases susceptibility to specific failure modes.
Agentic laziness is when Claude stops before finishing a complex, multi-part task and declares it done after only partial progress (for example, addressing 35 of 50 security-review items).
Self-preferential bias is Claude's tendency to prefer its own results or findings, especially when asked to verify or judge them against a rubric.
Goal drift is the gradual loss of fidelity to the original objective across many turns, worsened by lossy compaction that can drop edge-case requirements and negative ('don't do X') constraints.
Orchestrating separate Claude subagents with their own context windows and focused, isolated goals combats agentic laziness, self-preferential bias, and goal drift.
Static workflows must work for all edge cases and are therefore usually more generic than dynamic workflows, which a capable model can tailor-make for a specific use case.
You can trigger creation of a dynamic workflow either by asking Claude to make one or by using the trigger word 'ultracode'.
Classify-and-act: use a classifier agent to decide the task type and route to different agents or behavior, or use a classifier at the end to determine the output.

Fan-out-and-synthesize: split a task into many smaller steps, run an agent on each, then synthesize the results; use it when there are many small steps or when each step benefits from its own clean context so they don't cross-contaminate.
condition: when there are many small steps or each step benefits from an isolated context

statement: In fan-out-and-synthesize, the synthesize step is a barrier that waits for all fan-out agents and then merges their structured outputs into one result.
Adversarial verification: for each spawned agent, run a separate agent that adversarially verifies its output against a rubric or criteria.
Generate-and-filter: generate many ideas, filter them by a rubric or verification, dedupe duplicates, and return only the highest-quality, tested ideas.
Tournament: instead of dividing the work, spawn N agents that each attempt the same task with different approaches, then use a judging agent to compare results pairwise until a winner remains.
Loop-until-done: for tasks with an unknown amount of work, keep spawning agents until a stop condition is met (no new findings or no more errors) rather than running a fixed number of passes.
condition: for tasks with an unknown amount of work

statement: For migrations and refactors, break the task into per-unit steps (callsites, failing tests, modules), fix each in its own worktree subagent, have another agent adversarially review, then merge.
When maximally parallelizing subagents on one machine, instruct them not to use resource-intensive commands so you don't run out of machine resources.
condition: when maximizing parallelism on a single machine

statement: Deep-research workflows fan out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify their claims, and synthesize a cited report; the same approach applies to non-web sources such as Slack or a codebase.

For deep verification, have one agent identify all factual claims and spin off a subagent to check each in detail, optionally adding a verifier agent that checks each source subagent's source quality.

Sorting more than about a thousand items in a single prompt degrades quality and won't fit in context; instead sort via a tournament, a pairwise-comparison pipeline, or parallel bucket-rank then merge.
condition: for large lists (roughly 1000+ items)

statement: Comparative (pairwise) judgment is more reliable than absolute scoring.
For rule adherence, build a workflow with one verifier agent per rule and add a skeptic-persona reviewer of the rules to avoid too many false positives.

To evolve rules, mine recent sessions and code-review comments for recurring corrections, cluster them, adversarially verify each candidate (would this rule have prevented a real mistake?), and distill the survivors into CLAUDE.md.

For root-cause investigation, generate independent hypotheses from disjoint evidence (for example, separate agents for logs, files, and data) and subject each to a panel of verifiers and refuters, which structurally prevents single-context self-preferential bias.
A triage workflow should classify each item, dedupe it against what is already tracked, and then act by attempting the fix or escalating to a human.
Use a quarantine pattern in triage: bar agents that read untrusted public content from taking high-privilege actions, which are instead performed by separate acting agents.
Pair repeatable workflows (such as triage, research, or verification) with /loop to run them at regular intervals and with /goal to set a hard completion requirement.
For taste-based exploration such as design or naming, have agents explore several solutions and a review agent judge them against a rubric, finishing when the review agent's criteria are met.
condition: for taste-based tasks like design or naming

statement: Use a classifier agent to route a task to the appropriate model (for example, Sonnet vs Opus) based on researched task complexity.
Do not use dynamic workflows for every task; most traditional coding tasks do not need the extra compute of a workflow such as a panel of five reviewers.
You can cap a dynamic workflow's token usage by prompting an explicit budget, for example 'use 10k tokens'.

Save workflows from the workflow menu and reuse them by checking them into ~/.claude/workflows or distributing them inside a skill, treating skill-bundled workflows as templates rather than verbatim scripts.

Traditional self-service analytics approaches each fail in a characteristic way: wide denormalized tables produce overlapping views with inconsistent metric definitions as the business scales, while ringfenced curated environments miss the long tail of business questions and cause metric and dashboard bloat.

Pointing an LLM agent at a data warehouse and letting it execute queries creates a false sense of precision, because it separates stakeholders from the infrastructure, documentation, and expertise that previously steered them toward carefully curated datasets.

At Anthropic, roughly 95% of business analytics queries are automated via Claude at about 95% aggregate accuracy, freeing the data science team for more strategic work such as causal modeling, forecasting, and machine learning.
Analytics accuracy is fundamentally a context and verification problem, not a code-generation problem.

Unlike coding, which is an open-ended solution space where documentation and tests act as natural guardrails against hallucination, analytics usually has a single correct answer from a single correct source with no deterministic way to prove correctness.

The central problem of agentic analytics is mapping a user's question to specific, up-to-date entities in the data model and knowing the correct way to work with them; once that mapping is right, the resulting SQL execution is trivial.
Three attributes account for the overwhelming majority of inaccurate agent responses: concept-to-entity ambiguity, data staleness, and retrieval failure.

Concept-to-entity ambiguity means that among hundreds of viable fields the agent cannot choose those that best answer a question, for example which actions count as an 'active' user, whether to include fraudulent users, and what lookback window to apply.
Data staleness means sources, business definitions, and schemas change constantly, so data assets and agent knowledge go stale and start returning subtly wrong answers.
Retrieval failure means the correct, properly annotated information exists in the data model, but given the vast search space the agent simply does not find it.

Architect the analytics stack so each layer attacks a specific failure mode: data foundations and sources of truth collapse entity ambiguity, maintenance and validation processes fight staleness, and skills fix retrieval.

Standard data-engineering and data-quality practices - dimensional modeling, shift-left testing, and freshness and completeness checks on critical pipelines - remain as important as ever for accurate analytics agents.
Strong data foundations - the governed data models, transforms, tests, tables, and the metadata describing them - are the single most important driver of analytics-agent accuracy.
Because the end user of the data model is now an agent acting on behalf of a non-expert, analytic results must not require the user to validate their underlying correctness.

Create canonical datasets: curate a small set of governed, clearly owned, consumption-ready, and discoverable single-source-of-truth datasets, aggressively deprecate near-duplicates, and derive physical rollups and caches mechanically from the canonical models rather than maintaining them as alternatives, so that a search for a concept finds one governed answer.
condition: Physical rollups and caches still matter for cost and performance

statement: Enforce canonical models and metric definitions through tooling that structurally routes the agent to them first, through CI that fails review on changes that bypass them, and through mandate that downstream teams build on the governed layer, because governance without enforcement decays back to the multiple-candidates problem.

Colocate nearly all data code - modeling, semantic layer, reference docs, and canonical dashboard definitions - in a single repo with CI that protects cross-layer integrity, so a modeling change that would break a downstream dashboard or invalidate a documented metric is flagged and fixed in the same PR.

Treat metadata - column and table descriptions, canonical metric definitions, grain documentation, valid value ranges, lineage, ownership, and model tiering - as a first-class product maintained with the same rigor as the transformations, so the warehouse is as legible to an agent as a well-documented codebase.
Sources of truth are the reference surfaces the agent consults, ordered by descending trust: the semantic layer, the lineage and transformation graph, the query corpus, and business context.

Require agents to consult the semantic layer of compiled metric and dimension definitions first, so a mapped question returns one governed number consistent with every other company surface, and do not let them fall back to raw SQL for reasons the semantic layer already covers such as custom date filtering, cohorts, or needed joins.
exception: Fall back to raw SQL only after the semantic-layer path is shown not to cover the question

statement: Do not auto-generate semantic-layer metric definitions with an LLM from raw tables and query logs, because it encodes the very ambiguities you are trying to eliminate and was net-negative on evals versus a smaller human-curated layer; instead generate the documentation with Claude but have a human own each definition.
When the semantic layer does not cover a question, use lineage and reference-count-based table ranking to reason about which governed upstream model feeds the concept and which to aggregate from.

Giving the agent raw retrieval access to thousands of historical queries improved accuracy by less than a point because unstructured retrieval cannot map a new question to the right precedent; instead distill the query corpus into structured per-domain reference docs and reusable analysis patterns rather than treating it as a source of truth the agent reads directly.

Supply business context through a company knowledge graph of indexed docs, roadmaps, decision logs, and organizational structure, so the agent can resolve ambient references and ask better clarifying questions rather than answering what was literally asked instead of what was meant.

The common failure across all four source-of-truth layers is poor or stale documentation; use Claude to draft column descriptions, propose metric docs, and flag undocumented models in CI, but keep curation and ownership with humans.

Skills are decisive for accuracy: without skills Claude's analytics accuracy did not exceed 21% on the evals, and adding skills raised it consistently above 95% in aggregate and regularly around 99% in certain domains.

Build pairwise skills: a thin 'knowledge' router skill that narrows a million-field warehouse to a few dozen curated reference files before any query is written, and an 'unbook' process skill that clarifies the question, finds sources, runs the query, loops the result through adversarial review sub-agents, and bundles reusable analysis patterns like retention curves, rate decomposition, and funnel analysis.

Write reference docs for LLM retrieval: describe each table's grain, scope, and exclusions, spell out the mechanics of gotchas, and give explicit routing triggers, without prescriptive query recipes that go stale.

Treat skill maintenance as a first-class engineering concern: colocate skill markdown in the same repo as the transformation models so the PR that changes a model is the PR that updates its doc, and add a code-review hook that flags any reporting-model change not touching a skill file, because otherwise offline accuracy drifts (theirs fell from about 95% to about 65% in a month).

Serve one canonical skill source to every surface - Slack, IDE, dashboard tools, and standalone agent sessions - via automatic sync on merge, and design for portability from the start by avoiding hardcoded repo paths and surface-specific namespaces, so the same question gets the same answer everywhere.

Build offline evals as simple question/answer pairs from three sources - dashboard-based evals auto-generated by Claude and human-validated, long-tail evals generated by feeding Claude business context, and continuously harvested stakeholder corrections - to reveal critical gaps even though they do not measure online performance.

Anchor eval ground truth so it cannot drift: pin each eval to a snapshot date, write it against a stable fact table, or have the grader judge the agent's query rather than its number, and wire the suite into CI so a PR touching a dependency re-runs the affected evals.

Store eval results like telemetry rather than test logs: land every run in a warehouse table with the skill version, git SHA, model ID, per-assertion pass/fail, token count, and wall-clock, so 'did that change help?' becomes a query and slow regressions a single CI run would miss become visible.
Gate each domain's launch on its slice of the eval set clearing a threshold (they initially used about 90%), which forces reference-doc fixes before stakeholders ever see the failures.

Calibrate the number of evals to the complexity of the business area and data model by tracking how well offline accuracy predicts online accuracy; returns diminish past a few dozen per topic and that ceiling drops with each new model generation.

Make every structural skill decision - which sources to expose, whether a sub-agent earns its latency, whether to merge two skills - by ablation: hold the offline eval set fixed, vary exactly one component, and compare pass rates.

Design ablations for null results: their most useful ablation was a negative one, where giving the agent grep access to all prior SQL moved accuracy by less than a point even though transcripts confirmed it read the files, proving the bottleneck was mapping a question to the right entity (structure), not access to prior work.

Ablate at PR granularity: give every meaningful skill edit a before/after run on the relevant eval slice with the delta recorded in the PR description, to keep 'I improved the docs' honest and catch the common case where a well-intentioned addition makes things worse.

Keep a short list of what did not work - for example excessive additional rounds of doc refinement and swapping the adversarial reviewer to a cheaper model - so negative results are recorded cheaply and no one re-runs the same failed experiment.

An adversarial-review skill that aggressively challenges all underlying assumptions on a candidate final answer increased accuracy by 6% within the eval set, but at the cost of 32% more tokens and 72% higher latency.
condition: The 6% accuracy gain comes at 32% more tokens and 72% higher latency

statement: Attach a provenance footer to every response stating the source tier (semantic layer, then curated reference, then raw table), how fresh the underlying data is, and who owns the model, because although it does not make the answer more correct it lets the consumer judge trust and is one of the few mitigations for silent failures.

Add basic data-quality checks that the referenced field is up-to-date, complete, and free of anomalies, because the agent can use the right field in the right way while the underlying data itself is incorrect.

Continuously monitor two production signals - the share of agent queries that resolve through the semantic layer and the share of responses that draw correction language - and review both weekly alongside the offline pass rate.

Automate correction harvesting to close the loop: a scheduled agent scans stakeholder channels every few hours for correction language, drafts a one-line fix to the relevant reference doc, and opens a PR tagged to the domain owner, keeping the fix path deliberately boring so owners actually engage, and feeding the same corrections back into the offline eval set.

The silent failure - a wrong but plausible answer used without objection - is not fully solved; mitigate it with the provenance footer, explicit human sign-off on anything leadership-bound, and a standing daily eval that sanity-checks each domain's top KPIs against the blessed dashboard.

Starting from zero, a handful of canonical datasets, a few dozen offline evals, and a thin knowledge skill capture most of the available upside; the rest of the stack is what you add once those foundations exist.

Before building, align the organization on trade-offs: how much a correct answer matters now versus waiting for models to improve (much infrastructure built for current model shortfalls becomes moot), and whether to run one broad agent or many scoped ones given that more context improves performance but cuts against your access-control and data-privacy posture.
exception: Waiting for model improvements may not fit a company's risk tolerance

statement: The greatest gains come from addressing all three failure modes together: collapse ambiguity into a single governed answer, make that answer easily discoverable, and flag when either has gone stale.
Always check the semantic layer's segments - the named canonical population filters - because hand-rolled WHERE clauses substituting for these segments are the dominant wrong-answer mode.

Resolve date-window conventions before querying: treat 'last week' or 'last month' as the last complete calendar period rather than a trailing 7 or 30 days, and anchor on MAX(date) rather than 'yesterday' because some tables settle late.

Enforce data-integrity rules on the analytics agent: never invent data or columns or make speculative assertions beyond what the data shows, and always use safe division, differentiate observations ('data shows X') from interpretations ('this suggests Y'), and flag limitations.
For restricted or PII data, return the SQL for the user to run themselves rather than returning the results.
Make adversarial SQL review mandatory: spawn a dedicated reviewer sub-agent for every query before the final answer, fix any blocking findings and re-review, and never let the agent self-certify.
