statement: Agent Skills are reusable, filesystem-based resources that give Claude domain-specific expertise (workflows, context, best practices), turning a general-purpose agent into a specialist.
Skills load on-demand, unlike prompts (one-off conversation-level instructions), so the same guidance need not be re-supplied across conversations.
Skills can be composed together to build more complex workflows.
Claude automatically invokes a Skill when it is relevant to the user's request, without requiring explicit invocation.
Skills use progressive disclosure: Claude loads Skill information in stages as needed rather than consuming context upfront.
Level 1 metadata (the name and description from YAML frontmatter) is always loaded at startup and costs roughly 100 tokens per Skill.
Because only lightweight metadata loads at startup, many Skills can be installed with negligible context penalty.
Level 2 content (the SKILL.md body of instructions) is loaded only when the Skill is triggered and should stay under about 5k tokens.
Level 3+ resources (bundled files) are loaded only as needed and carry effectively unlimited token cost since unaccessed files consume zero tokens.
A Skill directory can contain three content types: instructions (markdown), executable code (scripts), and reference resources.
When Claude runs a bundled script via bash, the script's source code never enters the context window; only its output consumes tokens.
Prefer bundled scripts for deterministic, reliable operations, instructions for flexible guidance, and resources for factual lookup.
Reference additional files (e.g. FORMS.md, REFERENCE.md) from SKILL.md so Claude reads them only when a task actually needs them.
There is no practical limit on bundled Skill content because files consume no context until they are accessed.
Every Skill must include a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter.
The only required frontmatter fields are name and description.
The name field must be at most 64 characters and contain only lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens.
The name field must not contain XML tags and must not use the reserved words 'anthropic' or 'claude'.
The description field must be non-empty, at most 1024 characters, and must not contain XML tags.
The description should state both what the Skill does and when Claude should use it, because it drives discovery.
Use Skills only from trusted sources — ones you created yourself or obtained from Anthropic.
A malicious Skill can direct Claude to invoke tools or execute code in ways that do not match the Skill's stated purpose.
Thoroughly audit a Skill before use when it comes from an untrusted or unknown source.
condition: the Skill is from an untrusted or unknown source

statement: Audit every bundled file (SKILL.md, scripts, images, resources) for unusual patterns such as unexpected network calls or file-access operations that do not match the Skill's stated purpose.
Skills that fetch data from external URLs pose particular risk because fetched content may contain malicious instructions.
condition: a Skill fetches data from external URLs

statement: Treat installing a Skill like installing software, being especially careful in production systems that access sensitive data or critical operations.
Using Skills via the Claude API requires three beta headers: code-execution-2025-08-25, skills-2025-10-02, and files-api-2025-04-14.
condition: using Skills via the Claude API

statement: Pre-built Agent Skills are referenced by skill_id (e.g. pptx, xlsx) in the container parameter alongside the code execution tool.
Custom Skills uploaded through the Claude API are shared workspace-wide and accessible to all workspace members.
Custom Skills do not sync across surfaces and must be uploaded separately for each surface where they are used.
Claude Code supports only custom Skills, which are filesystem-based and require no API upload.
condition: using Claude Code

statement: Sharing scope differs by surface: claude.ai is individual-user-only, the Claude API is workspace-wide, and Claude Code is personal (~/.claude/skills/) or project-based (.claude/skills/).
claude.ai does not support centralized admin management or org-wide distribution of custom Skills.
On the Claude API, Skills have no network access and cannot install packages at runtime; only pre-installed packages are available.
condition: running on the Claude API

statement: On claude.ai, Skills may have full, partial, or no network access depending on user/admin settings.
condition: running on claude.ai

statement: In Claude Code, Skills have full network access equivalent to any program on the user's computer.
condition: running in Claude Code

statement: In Claude Code, Skills should install packages locally rather than globally to avoid interfering with the user's computer.
condition: running in Claude Code

statement: Plan each Skill to work within the runtime constraints of the surface where it will run.
Agent Skills are not covered by Zero Data Retention; Skill definitions and execution data are retained under Anthropic's standard data retention policy.
Anthropic provides pre-built Agent Skills for PowerPoint (pptx), Excel (xlsx), Word (docx), and PDF (pdf) document tasks.
Effective Skills are concise, well-structured, and validated through real usage rather than imagined requirements.
A Skill shares the context window with the system prompt, conversation history, other Skills' metadata, and the user's request, so its tokens compete with everything else Claude must hold.
At startup only each Skill's metadata (name and description) is pre-loaded; Claude reads the SKILL.md body only when the Skill becomes relevant, and reads bundled files only as needed.
Keep SKILL.md concise because once it is loaded every token in it competes with conversation history and other context.
Add only context Claude does not already have, assuming the model is already capable, rather than re-explaining common knowledge.
Challenge each piece of SKILL.md content by asking whether Claude truly needs it and whether it justifies its token cost.
Match the level of instruction specificity (degrees of freedom) to the task's fragility and variability.
Use high-freedom text instructions when multiple approaches are valid, decisions depend on context, or heuristics guide the approach.
condition: multiple valid approaches / context-dependent / heuristic-guided task

statement: Use medium-freedom pseudocode or parameterized scripts when a preferred pattern exists but some variation is acceptable.
condition: a preferred pattern exists with acceptable variation

statement: Use low-freedom specific scripts with few or no parameters when operations are fragile, consistency is critical, or an exact sequence must be followed.
condition: operations are fragile / consistency critical / exact sequence required

statement: Test a Skill with every model you plan to use it with, because Skill effectiveness depends on the underlying model.
Instructions that suffice for a powerful model may need more detail for a smaller or faster model, so aim for instructions that work well across all target models.
SKILL.md frontmatter requires exactly two fields: name and description.
The name field must be at most 64 characters, use only lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens, contain no XML tags, and avoid the reserved words 'anthropic' and 'claude'.
The description field must be non-empty, at most 1024 characters, contain no XML tags, and state both what the Skill does and when to use it.
Prefer gerund-form Skill names (verb + -ing) because they clearly describe the activity or capability the Skill provides.
Avoid vague, overly generic, or reserved-word Skill names (e.g. helper, utils, tools, documents) that do not convey what the Skill does.
Write Skill descriptions in the third person, because the description is injected into the system prompt and inconsistent point-of-view can cause discovery problems.
Make descriptions specific and include key terms plus the concrete triggers and contexts for when the Skill should be used.
The description is the critical signal Claude uses to select the right Skill from among potentially 100+ available Skills.
Keep the SKILL.md body under 500 lines for optimal performance, and split content into separate files when approaching that limit.
Structure a Skill for progressive disclosure: SKILL.md is a concise overview that points Claude to detailed files, which are loaded only when needed.
Keep reference files one level deep from SKILL.md, because deeply nested references lead Claude to partial reads (e.g. head -100) and incomplete information.
For reference files longer than 100 lines, include a table of contents at the top so Claude can see the full scope even when previewing with a partial read.
condition: reference file longer than 100 lines

statement: Break complex operations into clear sequential steps, and for particularly complex workflows provide a checklist Claude can copy and check off.
Avoid time-sensitive information that will become outdated; place legacy details in an 'old patterns' section instead of dated conditionals.
Use one consistent term per concept throughout a Skill, because inconsistent terminology hinders Claude's ability to follow instructions.
Provide output templates and match template strictness to needs: an exact mandatory template for strict formats, a labelled sensible-default for flexible guidance.
For Skills whose output quality depends on seeing examples, provide concrete input/output example pairs rather than abstract descriptions.
Create evaluations before writing extensive documentation, so the Skill solves real observed problems rather than imagined ones.

Follow evaluation-driven development: identify gaps by running Claude without the Skill, build about three test scenarios, establish a no-Skill baseline, write minimal instructions, then iterate against the baseline.
Develop Skills iteratively using Claude itself, where one instance (Claude A) helps design and refine the Skill and another instance (Claude B) tests it on real tasks.
When the testing instance misses or mishandles something, return to the authoring instance with the specific observed behaviour and refine the Skill accordingly.
Strengthen a rule that Claude keeps missing by making it more prominent or using stronger imperative language (e.g. 'MUST filter' instead of 'always filter').
condition: Claude repeatedly fails to follow an existing rule

statement: Iterate on Skills based on observed real-usage signals (unexpected exploration paths, missed references, ignored bundled files) rather than on assumptions.
Always use forward slashes in file paths, even on Windows, because Windows-style backslash paths cause errors on Unix systems.
Do not present multiple tool or library options unnecessarily; give a sensible default with an escape hatch for edge cases.
In scripts bundled with a Skill, handle error conditions explicitly rather than punting failures to Claude.
Justify and document every configuration parameter to avoid voodoo constants, since if the author cannot determine the right value Claude cannot either.
Provide pre-made utility scripts even when Claude could write the code itself, because bundled scripts are more reliable, save tokens, save time, and ensure consistency across uses.
Utility scripts can be executed via bash without loading their contents into context, so only the script's output consumes tokens.
State explicitly in the instructions whether Claude should execute a given script or read it as reference, to prevent ambiguous use.
For most utility scripts prefer execution over reading, because execution is more reliable and efficient.
condition: ordinary utility scripts
exception: complex logic that must be read as reference

statement: When inputs can be rendered as images, have Claude analyze them visually to understand layouts and structures.
condition: inputs can be rendered as images

statement: Use the plan-validate-execute pattern (have Claude first produce a structured plan, validate it with a script, then execute) to catch errors early in complex, open-ended tasks.

Insert a verifiable intermediate output (a machine-checkable plan file validated before applying changes) for batch operations, destructive changes, complex validation rules, and high-stakes operations.
condition: batch, destructive, complex-validation, or high-stakes operations

statement: Make validation scripts verbose with specific error messages that list valid options (e.g. the available field names), so Claude can fix the problem.
Skills run in a code execution environment with filesystem access, bash, and code execution, subject to platform-specific limitations.
On claude.ai the execution environment can install packages from npm and PyPI and pull from GitHub, whereas the Claude API has no network access and no runtime package installation.
condition: claude.ai vs Claude API platform

statement: List a Skill's required packages in its SKILL.md and verify they are available in the target code execution environment.
Reference files, data, and documentation bundled with a Skill consume no context tokens until they are actually read.
Name bundled files descriptively so their names indicate their content (e.g. form_validation_rules.md rather than doc2.md).
Organize a Skill's directories by domain or feature to aid Claude's discovery of the right file.
Prefer writing scripts for deterministic operations rather than asking Claude to generate the operation's code each time.
condition: deterministic operations

statement: Test file-access patterns with real requests to verify Claude can navigate the Skill's directory structure.
When a Skill uses MCP tools, always reference them by fully qualified name in the form ServerName:tool_name to avoid 'tool not found' errors, especially when multiple MCP servers are available.
condition: Skill uses MCP tools

statement: Do not assume packages or tools are already installed; state dependencies explicitly and include their installation step.
Include validation, verification steps, and feedback loops for critical or quality-critical operations before sharing a Skill.
condition: critical or quality-critical operations

statement: The code execution tool must be enabled in a request in order to use Skills.
A request may include at most 8 Skills in the container parameter.
When a Skill creates a document, the response returns a file_id for each created file, and the Files API must be used to download the actual file content.
condition: when a Skill creates a document such as Excel, PowerPoint, PDF, or Word

statement: A container can be reused across multiple messages by passing the previous response's container id in the container parameter.
A fresh, isolated container is created for each request unless an existing container ID is specified.
exception: an existing container ID is specified in the container parameter

statement: The API may return a pause_turn stop reason for long-running Skill operations; the response can be sent back unchanged to let Claude continue its turn, or modified to interrupt and add guidance.
condition: for long-running Skill operations

statement: Multiple Skills can be combined in a single request to handle workflows spanning several document types or domains.
A custom Skill bundle is a directory containing a SKILL.md file at the top level with name and description YAML frontmatter, plus any supporting scripts or resources.
Custom Skills are uploaded as either a zip archive or individual file objects; the Python SDK also provides a files_from_dir helper that accepts a directory path.
A Skill upload must include a SKILL.md file at the top level, have all files specify a common root directory in their paths, and have a total combined size under 30 MB.
The Skill name frontmatter field must be at most 64 characters, use only lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens, contain no XML tags, and avoid the reserved words 'anthropic' and 'claude'.
The Skill description frontmatter field must be at most 1024 characters, non-empty, and contain no XML tags.
To delete a Skill, all of its versions must be deleted first; attempting to delete a Skill that still has versions returns a 400 error.
exception: the Skill still has existing versions, which returns a 400 error

statement: Specifying a Skill version of 'latest' always resolves to the most recent version, while specifying an exact version pins the Skill for stability.

When Skills are specified, Claude sees each Skill's name and description metadata in the system prompt, the Skill files are copied into the container at /skills/{directory}/, and full Skill instructions are loaded only when relevant (progressive disclosure).
Skills run in the code execution container with no network access and cannot make external API calls.
Skills cannot install packages at runtime; only pre-installed packages are available in the container.
Skills should be pinned to specific versions for production stability and set to 'latest' during active development.
Changing the Skills list in a container breaks prompt caching, so the Skills list should be kept consistent across requests for best caching performance.
condition: when using prompt caching

statement: Skill-related errors should be handled by catching BadRequestError and checking whether the error message references a skill before re-raising.
Including unused Skills should be avoided because it impacts performance.
Agent Skills are not eligible for Zero Data Retention; Skill definitions and execution data are retained according to Anthropic's standard data retention policy.
The List Skills endpoint returns both Anthropic and custom Skills, and its source parameter filters results by Skill type.
A skill is a SKILL.md file of instructions that extends what Claude can do; Claude adds it to its toolkit and applies it when relevant, or the user invokes it directly with /skill-name.
Create a skill when you repeatedly paste the same instructions, checklist, or multi-step procedure into chat, or when a CLAUDE.md section has grown into a procedure rather than a fact.
A skill's body loads only when the skill is used, so long reference material costs almost nothing until it is needed, unlike CLAUDE.md content which is always loaded.

Custom commands have merged into skills: a file at .claude/commands/deploy.md and a skill at .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md both create /deploy and behave the same way, and existing .claude/commands/ files keep working.
Claude Code skills follow the Agent Skills open standard and extend it with invocation control, subagent execution, and dynamic context injection.

Bundled skills such as /code-review, /batch, /debug, /loop, and /claude-api are available in every session unless disabled via the disableBundledSkills setting; they are prompt-based and invoked like any other skill.
The /run, /verify, and /run-skill-generator bundled skills require Claude Code v2.1.145 or later.

/run and /verify infer how to launch an app from the project type and from the README, package.json, or Makefile, but this inference becomes unreliable for projects that need a database, an env file, a graphical session, or a multi-step build.
condition: the project needs anything beyond a standard launch

statement: Run /run-skill-generator once per project (and again when the build or launch process changes) to record the launch recipe as a per-project skill at .claude/skills/run-<name>/ so /run and /verify follow the recorded recipe.

A skill's storage location determines its scope: enterprise (managed settings, all org users), personal (~/.claude/skills/, all your projects), project (.claude/skills/, this project only), and plugin (<plugin>/skills/, where the plugin is enabled).

When skills share a name across levels, precedence is enterprise over personal over project, and a skill at any level overrides a bundled skill of the same name; plugin skills use a plugin-name:skill-name namespace so they cannot conflict.
Skills also load from nested .claude/skills/ directories below the working directory when Claude reads or edits a file in that subdirectory, which lets a monorepo package provide its own skills.

A nested skill whose name clashes with another appears under a directory-qualified name such as apps/web:deploy; typing /deploy runs the project-root skill and /apps/web:deploy runs the nested variant explicitly.

A skill entry can be a symlink to a directory elsewhere on disk; Claude Code follows the symlink to read SKILL.md and loads the skill only once even if the target is reachable from more than one location.
Adding a .claude-plugin/plugin.json to a skill folder loads it as a plugin named <name>@skills-dir so it can bundle agents, hooks, and MCP servers.
condition: in a project .claude/skills/ this first requires accepting the workspace trust dialog

statement: Live change detection makes adding, editing, or removing a skill under a watched skills directory take effect within the current session without restarting, but creating a top-level skills directory that did not exist at session start requires a restart so it can be watched.
exception: a newly created top-level skills directory requires a restart

statement: Live change detection covers SKILL.md text only; for a skill folder that is also a plugin, changes to hooks/, .mcp.json, agents/, and output-styles/ require /reload-plugins to take effect.
exception: plugin subdirectory changes need /reload-plugins

statement: Project skills load from .claude/skills/ in the starting directory and in every parent directory up to the repository root, so starting Claude in a subdirectory still picks up root-level skills.
Each skill is a directory with SKILL.md as the required entrypoint; other files such as templates, example outputs, scripts, and reference docs are optional.

--add-dir and /add-dir load .claude/skills/ from the added directory automatically, but the permissions.additionalDirectories setting in settings.json grants file access only and does not load skills.
Reference content in a skill runs inline to add knowledge Claude applies to current work, while task content gives step-by-step instructions and is often invoked directly with /skill-name.
Keep the SKILL.md body concise because once a skill is invoked its content stays in context across turns, making every line a recurring token cost; state what to do rather than narrating how or why.
Among frontmatter fields only description is recommended; all fields are optional, and description tells Claude when to apply the skill.
Put the key use case first in the description because the combined description and when_to_use text is truncated at 1,536 characters in the skill listing.

disable-model-invocation: true prevents Claude from auto-loading a skill (leaving only manual /name invocation), prevents preloading the skill into subagents, and as of v2.1.196 prevents a scheduled task firing with the skill as its prompt.
user-invocable: false hides a skill from the / menu so only Claude can invoke it, useful for background knowledge that is not a meaningful user action.

allowed-tools grants the listed tools without per-use approval while the skill is active but does not restrict which tools are available; disallowed-tools removes tools from the pool while the skill is active until the next message.

For project skills, allowed-tools takes effect only after the user accepts the workspace trust dialog, so review project skills before trusting a repository because a skill can grant itself broad tool access.
condition: the skill is checked into a project .claude/skills/ directory

statement: The model frontmatter field overrides the model only for the rest of the current turn and is not saved to settings; the session model resumes on the next prompt.
The paths frontmatter field limits automatic activation to files matching its glob patterns.

A skill's invoked command name comes from its location (directory name under .claude/skills/, file name under .claude/commands/, plugin-namespaced for plugin skills); the frontmatter name sets only the display label except for a plugin-root SKILL.md where name sets the command name.

Skill content supports substitutions: $ARGUMENTS (all args), $ARGUMENTS[N] or $N (0-based indexed args), $name (declared named argument), and the variables ${CLAUDE_SESSION_ID}, ${CLAUDE_EFFORT}, ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}, and ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}.
The ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} substitution requires Claude Code v2.1.196 or later and applies to both the skill body and the allowed-tools frontmatter.
Indexed arguments use shell-style quoting, so wrap multi-word values in quotes to pass them as a single argument; escape a literal $ before a digit, ARGUMENTS, or an argument name with a backslash.
Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines and move detailed reference material to separate supporting files, referenced from SKILL.md so Claude knows what each contains and when to load it.

The inline !`<command>` syntax runs a shell command as preprocessing before the skill content is sent to Claude and replaces the placeholder with the command output; it is not something Claude executes.

Inline !`command` is recognized only when ! appears at the start of a line or immediately after whitespace; if ! follows another character the placeholder is left as literal text and the command does not run, and multi-line commands must use a fenced ```! block.
condition: ! is at line start or immediately after whitespace

statement: Injection substitution runs once over the original file and command output is inserted as plain text without being re-scanned, so a command cannot emit a placeholder for a later pass to expand.

disableSkillShellExecution: true disables !command execution for user, project, plugin, and additional-directory skills (replacing each command with a disabled-by-policy message), but bundled and managed skills are not affected.
exception: bundled and managed skills are unaffected

statement: Include the word ultrathink anywhere in skill content to request deeper reasoning when the skill runs.
Add context: fork to a skill's frontmatter to run it in isolation: the skill content becomes the subagent's prompt and the subagent has no access to the conversation history.
context: fork only makes sense for skills with explicit task instructions; a guidelines-only skill gives the subagent the guidelines but no actionable prompt, so it returns without meaningful output.
condition: the skill contains an explicit task, not just guidelines

statement: With context: fork the system prompt comes from the agent type and the task is the SKILL.md content, and CLAUDE.md is also loaded except when the agent is Explore or Plan.
exception: Explore and Plan agents do not load CLAUDE.md

statement: A subagent that declares a skills field uses its own markdown body as the system prompt and Claude's delegation message as the task, and it also loads the preloaded skills plus CLAUDE.md.

The agent frontmatter field selects which subagent configuration executes a forked skill (built-in Explore, Plan, general-purpose, or any custom agent from .claude/agents/); if omitted, general-purpose is used.

The built-in Explore and Plan agents skip CLAUDE.md and git status to keep their context small, so a forked skill using agent: Explore sees only the SKILL.md content and the agent's own system prompt.
By default Claude can invoke any skill that does not set disable-model-invocation: true.
A few built-in commands are available through the Skill tool, including /init, /review, and /security-review, while others such as /compact are not.
Disable all skills by adding the Skill tool to deny rules in /permissions.
Allow or deny specific skills with permission rules where Skill(name) is an exact match and Skill(name *) is a prefix match with any arguments.
Adding disable-model-invocation: true removes a skill from Claude's context entirely, which is how you hide an individual skill from Claude.
The user-invocable field controls only / menu visibility, not Skill tool access, so use disable-model-invocation: true to block programmatic invocation by Claude.
The skillOverrides setting controls skill visibility from settings instead of the skill's own frontmatter, and the /skills menu writes it to .claude/settings.local.json.

Each skillOverrides value is one of on (name and description, listed in menu), name-only (name only, in menu), user-invocable-only (hidden from Claude, in menu), or off (hidden everywhere); a skill absent from skillOverrides is treated as on.

As of v2.1.199, the off state also hides a skill from Remote Control clients and Agent SDK callers, and invoking a hidden skill by its full name returns the skillOverrides error instead of running it.
Plugin skills are not affected by skillOverrides and must be managed through /plugin instead.
exception: plugin skills

statement: Seeing a skill trigger tells you Claude found it, not that it did what you intended, so measure separately whether Claude invokes the skill on the prompts it should and whether the output matches expectations.

Evaluate a skill by a baseline comparison: run each realistic prompt in a fresh session with the skill available and again with it disabled, then compare; a fresh session matters because leftover authoring context masks gaps in the written instructions.
condition: a fresh session is used for each run

statement: The skill-creator plugin automates the comparison loop, storing test cases in evals/evals.json, spawning an isolated subagent per test case, writing pass/fail evidence to grading.json, aggregating a with-skill versus without-skill benchmark to benchmark.json, running blind A/B version comparisons, tuning descriptions, and opening an HTML review viewer.
Install skill-creator with /plugin install skill-creator@claude-plugins-official, then run /reload-plugins to make its skills available in the current session.

If a plugin is not found in any marketplace, refresh it with /plugin marketplace update claude-plugins-official, or add it with /plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-official if it was never added, then retry the install.
condition: the plugin is reported missing from any marketplace

statement: Skills can be distributed at different scopes: project skills by committing .claude/skills/ to version control, plugins by creating a skills/ directory in a plugin, and managed deployment organization-wide through managed settings.
Skills can bundle and run scripts in any language, giving Claude capabilities beyond a single prompt, such as generating interactive HTML visual output while Claude handles orchestration.
Reference a bundled script path with ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR} so it resolves correctly whether the skill is installed at the personal, project, or plugin level.

If a skill is not triggering, check that the description includes keywords users would naturally say, verify the skill appears in the available-skills list, rephrase the request to match the description, or invoke it directly with /skill-name.
condition: the skill does not trigger when expected

statement: If a skill's frontmatter YAML is malformed, Claude Code loads the body with empty metadata so /skill-name still works but Claude has no description to match against; run with --debug to see the parse error.
condition: the frontmatter YAML is malformed

statement: If a skill triggers too often, make its description more specific or add disable-model-invocation: true to allow only manual invocation.
condition: the skill triggers when unwanted

statement: Skill descriptions are shortened to fit a listing character budget that scales at 1% of the model's context window, and when it overflows the descriptions of the least-invoked skills are dropped first so the skills you actually use keep their full text.
Run /doctor to see how many skill descriptions are being shortened or dropped and which skills are affected.

Raise the skill listing budget with the skillListingBudgetFraction setting or the SLASH_COMMAND_TOOL_CHAR_BUDGET environment variable; each entry's combined description and when_to_use text is capped at 1,536 characters regardless of budget, configurable via skillListingMaxDescChars.
Agent Skills extend Claude with specialized, task-specific expertise such as creating documents, analyzing data, and processing files.
Anthropic ships four pre-built Agent Skills in the API: PowerPoint (pptx), Excel (xlsx), Word (docx), and PDF (pdf).
Using the Skills API requires a Claude API key, Python 3.7+ or curl, and basic familiarity with making API requests.
condition: using the Skills API as shown in the quickstart

statement: You can enumerate the available Anthropic-managed Skills by calling the Skills list endpoint filtered to the anthropic source.
The Skills list API returns each Skill's metadata, namely its name and description.
Claude loads Skill metadata at startup so it knows which Skills exist, which is the first level of progressive disclosure — Skills are discovered without their full instructions being loaded.
Skills are selected for a request via the container parameter of the Messages API.
The container.skills field lists which Skills Claude is permitted to use for that request.
A skill entry's type of "anthropic" marks it as an Anthropic-managed Skill, and skill_id names the specific Skill (for example pptx).
Setting a skill entry's version to "latest" pins it to the most recently published version of that Skill.
The code execution tool must be enabled (via the request's tools parameter) for Agent Skills to run.
condition: invoking Agent Skills through the API

statement: Enabling Skills requires the beta headers, including code-execution and the skills-2025-10-02 beta.
Any version of the code execution tool satisfies the Skills requirement, including newer revisions (code_execution_20260120 and later), not only code_execution_20250825.
Whichever code execution tool version is used, its tool type and its beta header must be kept consistent with each other.
condition: choosing a code execution tool version

statement: The skills-2025-10-02 beta header must always be included when using Skills, regardless of the code execution tool version.
Claude automatically matches the user's task to the relevant Skill rather than requiring the caller to invoke it explicitly.
When Claude determines a Skill is relevant it loads that Skill's full instructions — the second level of progressive disclosure — and then executes the Skill's code.
Files produced by a Skill are created inside the code execution container and returned as a file reference containing a file ID in the response.
To obtain a Skill-generated file, extract its file ID from the code execution tool result and download it through the Files API.
When extracting the generated file ID, both result block types must be checked because a Skill may run through either the Python or the bash code execution tool.
condition: parsing the response for a generated file
exception: one path suffices only if you know which code-execution tool the Skill used

statement: A generated file is retrieved by calling the Files download endpoint with the file ID and writing the returned content to a local path.
The same request pattern generates other document types by swapping the skill_id — xlsx for spreadsheets, docx for Word documents, and pdf for PDFs.
Custom, domain-specific Skills can be built and uploaded in addition to the pre-built ones.
Agent skills extend Codex with task-specific capabilities by packaging instructions, resources, and optional scripts so Codex can follow a workflow reliably.
Agent skills build on the open agent skills standard.
Skills are the authoring format for reusable workflows, whereas plugins are the installable distribution unit for reusable skills and apps in Codex.
Design the workflow itself as a skill, then package it as a plugin when you want other developers to install it.
condition: when you want other developers to install/distribute the workflow

statement: Skills are available in the Codex CLI, the IDE extension, and the Codex app.
Skills use progressive disclosure: Codex begins with only each skill's name, description, and file path, and loads the full SKILL.md instructions only when it decides to use that skill.

The initial list of available skills is capped at 2% of the model's context window, or 8,000 characters when the context window is unknown, and Codex shortens skill descriptions first to stay within that budget.
For large skill sets, Codex may omit some skills from the initial list and show a warning.
The initial-list context budget applies only to the initial skills list; once Codex selects a skill it still reads that skill's full SKILL.md instructions.
A skill is a directory containing a SKILL.md file plus optional scripts and references.
A skill's SKILL.md file must include a name and a description.
Codex can activate a skill explicitly (mentioned directly in the prompt, via /skills or by typing $ in the CLI/IDE) or implicitly (chosen automatically when the task matches the skill's description).

Write concise skill descriptions with clear scope and boundaries, front-loading the key use case and trigger words, because implicit matching depends on the description and descriptions may be shortened.
Use Record & Replay to draft a skill from a demonstration when the workflow is easier to show than to describe.
condition: when the workflow is easier to show than to describe

statement: The built-in $skill-creator asks what the skill does, when it should trigger, and whether it should stay instruction-only or include scripts, with instruction-only as the default.
A skill can be created manually by making a folder with a SKILL.md file whose frontmatter declares name and description, followed by the instructions for Codex to follow.
Codex detects skill changes automatically; restart Codex if an update does not appear.
condition: if a skill update does not appear automatically

statement: Codex reads skills from repository, user, admin, and system locations, scanning .agents/skills in every directory from the current working directory up to the repository root.

Repository-scoped skills live in .agents/skills at the current working directory, at a parent folder, or at the repository root; user skills live in $HOME/.agents/skills; admin skills live in /etc/codex/skills; system skills are bundled with Codex by OpenAI.
If two skills share the same name, Codex does not merge them and both can appear in skill selectors.
Codex supports symlinked skill folders and follows the symlink target when scanning skill locations.
To distribute a reusable skill beyond a single repository, bundle two or more skills, or ship a skill alongside an app integration, package them as a plugin.
condition: when distributing a skill beyond a single repo, bundling multiple skills, or shipping with an app integration

statement: A plugin can include one or more skills and can optionally bundle app mappings, MCP server configuration, and presentation assets in a single package.
Use $skill-installer <name> to add curated skills for local use, and the installer can be prompted to download skills from other repositories.
Disable a skill without deleting it by adding a [[skills.config]] entry with enabled = false pointing at its SKILL.md path in ~/.codex/config.toml, then restarting Codex.
Add agents/openai.yaml to a skill to configure its Codex-app UI metadata, invocation policy, and declared tool dependencies.
allow_implicit_invocation defaults to true; setting it to false stops Codex from implicitly invoking the skill based on the prompt.
exception: explicit $skill invocation still works even when allow_implicit_invocation is false

statement: Keep each skill focused on a single job.
Prefer instructions over scripts in a skill unless you need deterministic behavior or external tooling.
exception: unless you need deterministic behavior or external tooling

statement: Write imperative skill steps with explicit inputs and outputs.
Test prompts against the skill description to confirm the skill triggers as intended.
Codex customization is composed of several complementary layers — AGENTS.md project guidance, memories, skills, MCP, and subagents — that work together rather than compete.
AGENTS.md gives Codex durable, repo-specific project guidance that travels with the repository and applies before the agent starts work.
AGENTS.md should be kept small, containing only the instructions that matter.
AGENTS.md should hold the rules Codex must follow every time in a repo, such as build and test commands, review expectations, repo-specific conventions, and directory-specific instructions.
When the agent makes incorrect assumptions about the codebase, correct them in AGENTS.md and ask the agent to update AGENTS.md so the fix persists across future sessions.
AGENTS.md should be treated as a feedback loop, codifying corrections so future sessions inherit them.
Add a rule to AGENTS.md when the agent makes the same mistake repeatedly.
condition: the agent makes the same mistake repeatedly

statement: Add routing guidance to AGENTS.md indicating which directories or files to prioritize when the agent finds the right files but reads too many documents.
condition: the agent reads too many documents to find the right files

statement: Codify recurring pull-request feedback into AGENTS.md when the same feedback is left more than once.
condition: the same PR feedback is left more than once

statement: An AGENTS.md update can be delegated to a Codex cloud task by tagging @codex in a pull-request comment with the request.
Automations can run recurring checks (for example daily) that look for guidance gaps and suggest additions to AGENTS.md.
AGENTS.md should be paired with enforcing infrastructure — pre-commit hooks, linters, and type checkers — so recurring mistakes are prevented before a human sees them.
Codex can load guidance from multiple locations, including a global file in the Codex home directory and repo-specific files; files closer to the working directory take precedence.
The global AGENTS file should be used to shape how Codex communicates with the developer (review style, verbosity, defaults), while repo files stay focused on team and codebase rules.
Skills give Codex reusable capabilities for repeatable workflows and support richer instructions, scripts, and references while remaining reusable across tasks.
Skills are often the best fit for reusable workflows because they support richer instructions, scripts, and references.
Skill metadata is loaded and visible to the agent, so Codex can discover and choose skills implicitly without bloating context up front.
A skill is typically a SKILL.md file plus optional scripts, references, and assets.
A skill directory can include a scripts/ folder of CLI scripts that Codex invokes as part of the workflow, such as seeding data or running validations.
A skill should be paired with MCP when the workflow needs external systems such as issue trackers, design tools, or docs servers.
condition: the workflow needs external systems

statement: Skills should be used for repeatable workflows, team-specific expertise, and procedures that need examples, references, or helper scripts.

Skills can be global (in the user directory) or repo-specific (checked into .agents/skills); repo skills belong in .agents/skills when the workflow applies to that project, and the user directory is for skills wanted across all repos.

Codex uses progressive disclosure for skills: it starts with name/description metadata for discovery, loads SKILL.md only when the skill is chosen, and reads references or runs scripts only when needed.
Clear skill descriptions improve triggering reliability.
If a plugin already exists for a workflow, install it first to reuse a proven setup.
condition: a plugin already exists for the workflow

statement: A skill should be packaged as a plugin to distribute the workflow across teams or bundle it with app integrations; skills remain the authoring format while plugins are the installable distribution unit.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the standard way to connect Codex to external tools and context providers, and is especially useful for remotely hosted systems such as Figma, Linear, GitHub, or internal knowledge services.
MCP should be used when Codex needs capabilities that live outside the local repo, such as issue trackers, design tools, browsers, or shared documentation systems.
condition: Codex needs capabilities outside the local repo

statement: In the MCP model the host is Codex, the client is the MCP connection inside Codex, and the server is the external tool or context provider.
MCP servers can expose tools (actions), resources (readable data), and prompts (reusable prompt templates), which helps reason about trust and capability boundaries.
Subagents let you create agents with different roles and tool configurations so each subagent stays focused and uses the right tools for its job.
MCP is often most useful when paired with skills, where a skill defines the workflow and names the MCP tools to use.
When a skill depends on MCP, declare that dependency in agents/openai.yaml so Codex can install and wire the MCP server automatically.
condition: a skill depends on MCP

statement: Customization should be built in order: first AGENTS.md (with pre-commit hooks and linters to enforce rules), then plugins or skills for reusable workflows, then MCP when workflows need external systems, then subagents to delegate specialized or noisy tasks.
Codex reads AGENTS.md instruction files before starting any work, so guidance can be layered globally and per-project for consistent expectations across repositories.
Codex builds its instruction chain once per run, which in the TUI usually means once per launched session.
Codex's global scope is its home directory, which defaults to ~/.codex.
exception: the CODEX_HOME environment variable is set to a different path

statement: At the global scope Codex reads AGENTS.override.md if it exists and otherwise reads AGENTS.md, using only the first non-empty file at that level.
condition: an AGENTS.override.md file exists in the Codex home directory

statement: For project scope Codex starts at the project root (typically the Git root) and walks down to the current working directory.
When Codex cannot find a project root it checks only the current directory for instruction files.
condition: no project root can be located

statement: In each directory along the path Codex checks for AGENTS.override.md, then AGENTS.md, then any fallback names in project_doc_fallback_filenames, including at most one file per directory.

Codex concatenates discovered instruction files from the root downward joined by blank lines, so files closer to the current directory override earlier guidance by appearing later in the combined prompt.
Codex skips empty instruction files during discovery.
Codex stops adding instruction files once the combined size reaches project_doc_max_bytes, which defaults to 32 KiB.
condition: the combined instruction size reaches project_doc_max_bytes

statement: When the combined-size cap is hit, raise project_doc_max_bytes or split instructions across nested directories to keep critical guidance intact.
condition: the combined instruction size hits the project_doc_max_bytes cap

statement: Create ~/.codex/AGENTS.md to hold persistent, reusable global defaults that every repository inherits.
Use ~/.codex/AGENTS.override.md for a temporary global override without deleting the base AGENTS.md, and remove the override to restore the shared guidance.
Add an AGENTS.md at the repository root to record project-level norms while still inheriting the global defaults.
Add an AGENTS.override.md in nested directories when a specific team or service needs different rules from the repository default.
Place overrides as close as possible to the specialized work, because Codex stops searching once it reaches the current directory.
To make Codex treat an alternate filename (e.g. TEAM_GUIDE.md) as instructions, add it to project_doc_fallback_filenames in ~/.codex/config.toml.
After changing Codex configuration, restart Codex or run a new command so the updated configuration loads.
With fallback filenames configured, Codex checks each directory in the order AGENTS.override.md, AGENTS.md, then the listed fallback names in sequence.
Filenames not listed in project_doc_fallback_filenames are ignored for instruction discovery.
Set the CODEX_HOME environment variable to point Codex at a different home directory, such as a project-specific automation profile.
Verify instruction setup by running Codex from a repository root with a prompt that summarizes current instructions; Codex should echo global and project guidance in precedence order.

To audit which instruction files Codex loaded, enable a plaintext TUI log with codex -c log_dir=./.codex-log and inspect codex-tui.log, or read the most recent session-*.jsonl when session logging is enabled.
If instructions appear stale, restart Codex in the target directory; Codex rebuilds the instruction chain on every run, so there is no cache to clear manually.
When no instructions load, verify you are in the intended repository, confirm codex status reports the expected workspace root, and ensure the instruction files are non-empty.
When the wrong guidance appears, look for an AGENTS.override.md higher in the directory tree or under the Codex home, and rename or remove it to fall back to the regular file.
condition: incorrect or unexpected guidance is being applied

statement: When Codex ignores fallback filenames, confirm the names are listed in project_doc_fallback_filenames without typos and then restart Codex so the configuration takes effect.
condition: fallback-named instruction files are being ignored

statement: When instructions are truncated, raise project_doc_max_bytes or split large instruction files across nested directories.
condition: instruction content is being truncated

statement: If profiles are confused, check $CODEX_HOME before launching Codex, since a non-default value points Codex at a different home directory than the one being edited.
condition: the wrong Codex profile/home appears to be in use

statement: Keep AGENTS.md as a file separate from README.md so agent-specific context does not clutter human-facing documentation.

Place the AGENTS.md file at the root of the repository.
Cover the sections an agent needs to work effectively: project overview, build and test commands, code style guidelines, testing instructions, and security considerations.
Include extra operational instructions in AGENTS.md such as commit-message and pull-request guidelines, security gotchas, large-dataset notes, and deployment steps.
In a large monorepo, add a nested AGENTS.md inside each subproject or package rather than relying only on a single top-level file.

statement: Explicit user chat prompts override all AGENTS.md instructions.

statement: Treat AGENTS.md as living documentation and update it as the project evolves.

statement: A single AGENTS.md file is compatible across a growing ecosystem of AI coding agents and tools, so one file can serve many agents.
Provide explicit setup commands in AGENTS.md covering how to install dependencies, start the dev server, and run tests.
Require that a commit pass all tests before it is merged.
After moving files or changing imports, run the linter to confirm ESLint and TypeScript (or equivalent) rules still pass.
