statement: Add or update tests for any code you change, even when not explicitly asked to.
Run lint and tests before committing.
Agent skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Copilot loads when relevant to improve its performance on specialized tasks.
To create an agent skill, author a SKILL.md file and optionally other resources (supplementary Markdown files or scripts) that the SKILL.md instructions reference.
Project skills, scoped to a single repository, are placed in a .github/skills, .claude/skills, or .agents/skills directory in that repository.
Personal skills, shared across projects, are placed in a ~/.copilot/skills or ~/.agents/skills directory in the user's home directory.
Each skill must have its own subdirectory within the skills directory.
Skill subdirectory names should be lowercase and use hyphens in place of spaces.
A SKILL.md file is a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter followed by a Markdown body.
The SKILL.md frontmatter field 'name' is required and must be a unique, lowercase identifier using hyphens for spaces, typically matching the skill's directory name.
The SKILL.md frontmatter field 'description' is required and states what the skill does and when Copilot should use it.
The SKILL.md frontmatter field 'license' is optional and describes the license applying to the skill.
The Markdown body of SKILL.md holds the instructions, examples, and guidelines that Copilot follows.

When a skill is invoked, Copilot automatically discovers all files in the skill's directory and makes them available alongside the instructions, so scripts and resources placed there can be referenced from SKILL.md.
The SKILL.md frontmatter 'allowed-tools' field pre-approves the tools a skill may use without prompting for confirmation each time.
If a tool is not listed in the skill's allowed-tools field, Copilot prompts the user for permission before using it.
condition: the tool is not listed in the allowed-tools field

statement: Skill instructions in the SKILL.md body should tell Copilot when and how to run any included script.
A skill created by someone else can be added by downloading its skill directory (a directory containing SKILL.md and optionally other files) and moving it to a project or personal skills location.
The 'gh skill' GitHub CLI command discovers, installs, updates, and publishes agent skills from GitHub repositories.
'gh skill search TOPIC' searches for skills by topic.
'gh skill preview OWNER/REPOSITORY SKILL' renders a skill's SKILL.md and file tree in the terminal without installing it.
'gh skill install OWNER/REPOSITORY [SKILL]' installs a skill; run with no arguments for a fully interactive flow.
A specific skill version can be installed using an @TAG or @SHA suffix on the skill argument.
The '--pin' flag locks an installed skill to a specific version or commit SHA so it is skipped during updates.
The '--agent' flag installs a skill for a specific agent host and the '--scope' flag controls the install scope.
By default, skills are installed for Copilot at project scope.
When a skill is installed with 'gh skill', provenance metadata (source repository, ref, and tree SHA) is written into the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter.
'gh skill update' uses the provenance metadata in SKILL.md to check for upstream changes, and can update a specific skill or all skills with '--all'.
Pinned skills are skipped during 'gh skill update'; updating a pinned skill requires reinstalling it with a new '--pin' value.
condition: the skill is pinned

statement: 'gh skill publish --dry-run' validates skills against the Agent Skills specification and checks remote settings (tag protection, secret scanning, code scanning) without publishing.
'gh skill publish --fix' auto-fixes metadata issues in skill files without publishing them.
'gh skill publish' validates and publishes a repository's skills.
Copilot decides when to use a skill based on the user's prompt and the skill's description.
When Copilot chooses to use a skill, the SKILL.md file is injected into the agent's context, giving it access to the instructions and any included scripts or examples.
To ensure Copilot code review reads and uses a skill, name the skill directory with a review-focused name such as 'code-review'.
condition: the skill is intended for Copilot code review on GitHub

statement: Existing skills in the .github/skills directory can be used automatically by Copilot code review when they are relevant to the review.
condition: the skills reside in the .github/skills directory

statement: Custom instructions are recommended for simple instructions relevant to almost every task, while skills are recommended for detailed instructions Copilot should access only when relevant.
Custom instructions let you supply persistent contextual detail to Copilot automatically instead of repeating that context in every prompt.
The added context from custom instructions is not shown in the chat input but is available to Copilot to generate higher-quality responses.
There are three main types of custom instructions on GitHub.com: personal, repository, and organization.
Personal custom instructions apply only to the individual who sets them and are configured in a popup on the Copilot Chat page on GitHub.com.
Repository-wide custom instructions are specified in a .github/copilot-instructions.md file and apply to all requests made in the repository's context.

Path-specific custom instructions are specified in one or more NAME.instructions.md files within or below the .github/instructions directory and apply only to requests whose files match the specified path.
Use path-specific instructions to avoid overloading repository-wide instructions with information that only applies to certain file types or directories.
Agent instructions are specified in files named AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, or GEMINI.md and behave like repository-wide instructions.
condition: the Copilot feature in use supports agent instructions
exception: agent instructions are not supported by all Copilot features

statement: Organization custom instructions are added by organization owners and apply to all members of the organization regardless of where their Copilot subscription comes from.
Custom instruction precedence, from highest to lowest, is: personal, then repository (path-specific, then repository-wide, then agent), then organization.
Even though personal instructions take the highest priority, all relevant sets of instructions are still provided to Copilot.
Avoid providing conflicting sets of custom instructions across the personal, repository, and organization levels.
If response quality is a concern, repository custom instructions can be temporarily disabled.
condition: response quality is a concern

statement: Custom instructions are most effective when written as short, self-contained natural-language statements.
Choose whether an instruction belongs at the personal, repository, or organization level based on the scope over which you want it to apply.
Because custom instructions are sent with every chat message, they should be broadly applicable to most requests made in the repository.
An effective instructions file should provide a project overview, the repository's folder structure, coding standards and conventions, and the tools, libraries, or frameworks used.
In a large and diverse repository, instructions that request referring to external resources when formulating a response may cause problems.
In a large and diverse repository, instructions to answer in a particular style may cause problems.
In a large and diverse repository, instructions to always respond with a certain level of detail may cause problems.

Instructions such as pointing Copilot to a style guide in another repository, forcing use of @terminal, imposing a conversational style, or capping answer/word length may not produce the intended results.
Common repository custom-instruction use cases are test generation, code review, and commit-message generation.

Organization custom instructions can enforce organization-wide preferences such as always responding in a chosen language, disabling code blocks in responses, or routing security questions to a designated knowledge base.
Prompt files are Markdown files (*.prompt.md) that store reusable prompt instructions and relevant context for a specific chat interaction.
Prompt files are only available in VS Code, Visual Studio, and JetBrains IDEs.
Custom instructions add codebase-wide context to every AI workflow, whereas prompt files add instructions to a single, specific chat interaction.
Common prompt-file use cases are code generation, sharing domain expertise, team collaboration, and onboarding.
You can keep multiple prompt files in a workspace, each defining a prompt for a different purpose.
On GitHub.com and in VS Code, all three repository custom instruction types are available: repository-wide, path-specific, and agent instructions.
In Visual Studio, only two repository custom instruction types are available: repository-wide and path-specific.
A prompt file typically states its goal, asks the user for any inputs it needs that were not provided, and then lists the concrete requirements and reference files for the task.
A reusable prompt file can encapsulate task-specific standards, such as required libraries, typing rules, and validation conventions, so a common task is generated consistently.

A prompt file can capture a reusable review checklist, such as a REST API security review covering authentication/authorization, input validation and sanitization, rate limiting, and security logging and monitoring.
In Xcode, repository custom instructions consist of a single file, .github/copilot-instructions.md, created in the repository.
In Eclipse there are two types of repository custom instructions: workspace custom instructions and project custom instructions.
Eclipse workspace custom instructions apply to all projects in a workspace and let you specify workspace-wide instructions and preferences in a single file.
Eclipse project custom instructions apply to a specific project and are specified in a single .github/copilot-instructions.md file in that project.
Repository custom instructions let you give GitHub Copilot repository-specific guidance and preferences on GitHub.
For Copilot code review, the personal setting to use custom instructions must be enabled for repository custom instructions to take effect; it is enabled by default.
condition: applies to Copilot code review

statement: Copilot on GitHub supports three types of repository custom instructions: repository-wide, path-specific, and agent instructions.
Repository-wide custom instructions apply to all requests made in the context of a repository.
Repository-wide custom instructions are specified in a copilot-instructions.md file in the .github directory of the repository.
Path-specific custom instructions apply to requests made in the context of files that match a specified path.
Path-specific custom instructions are specified in one or more NAME.instructions.md files within or below the .github/instructions directory of the repository.
When a path-specific instruction file matches the file Copilot is working on, the instructions from both the path-specific file and any repository-wide instructions file are used together.
condition: a path-specific file matches the working file and a repository-wide instructions file also exists

statement: Agent instructions are used by AI agents and can be provided as one or more AGENTS.md files stored anywhere within the repository.
When Copilot is working, the nearest AGENTS.md file in the directory tree takes precedence.
condition: multiple AGENTS.md files exist in the directory tree

statement: As an alternative to AGENTS.md, a single CLAUDE.md or GEMINI.md file stored in the repository root can be used for agent instructions.
A repository-wide custom instructions file can either be written from scratch or generated for you by the Copilot cloud agent.
To have the Copilot cloud agent generate a copilot-instructions.md file, open the agents tab, select the target repository in the prompt-field dropdown, paste the onboarding prompt, and submit it.
The repository onboarding task for generating custom instructions should be performed only once per repository.
Generated custom instructions must be no longer than two pages.
Custom instructions must not be task specific.
A repository-wide instructions file must be created at .github/copilot-instructions.md, creating the .github directory first if it does not already exist.
Custom instructions are written in natural language using Markdown format.
Whitespace between instructions is ignored, so instructions may be written as a single paragraph, one per line, or separated by blank lines.
To create path-specific instructions, create the .github/instructions directory (optionally with subdirectories) and add NAME.instructions.md files whose names end in .instructions.md.
A path-specific instruction file must begin with a frontmatter block containing the applyTo keyword, using glob syntax to specify which files or directories the instructions apply to.
Multiple glob patterns in an applyTo value are specified by separating them with commas.
Adding the excludeAgent keyword to a path-specific file's frontmatter prevents that file from being used by the named agent, with a value of either code-review or cloud-agent.
If the excludeAgent keyword is not included in the frontmatter block, both Copilot code review and Copilot cloud agent will use the instructions.
condition: excludeAgent keyword is absent from the frontmatter

statement: Custom instructions become available for use as soon as the file is saved and are automatically added to requests submitted to Copilot.
In Copilot Chat, a conversation can use repository custom instructions by adding the repository that contains the instructions file as an attachment.
condition: using Copilot Chat at github.com/copilot

statement: When Copilot Chat uses repository custom instructions, the instructions file is added as a reference for the generated response, verifiable by expanding the references list and checking for the copilot-instructions.md file.
Custom instructions are enabled for Copilot code review by default and can be disabled or re-enabled in the repository settings on GitHub.com.
To toggle custom instructions for Copilot code review, open the repository's Settings, select Copilot then Code review, and toggle the 'Use custom instructions when reviewing pull requests' option.

In applyTo glob syntax, * matches all files in the current directory, ** or **/* matches all files in all directories, *.py matches .py files in the current directory, **/*.py recursively matches .py files in all directories, src/*.py matches .py files directly in src but not its subdirectories, and src/**/*.py recursively matches .py files under src.

A Claude skill should be packaged as a folder whose required entry point is SKILL.md, with scripts, references, and assets added only when the workflow needs executable helpers, on-demand documentation, or reusable output materials.

A skill should rely on progressive disclosure: frontmatter must be compact enough to be loaded continually, SKILL.md should hold the core operating guidance, and linked files should be loaded only when needed.
Progressive disclosure reduces context cost while preserving access to specialized expertise.
A skill should be composable and avoid assuming it is the only active capability.
A portable skill should avoid product-specific assumptions unless its dependencies are available across the intended Claude surfaces.
condition: when the author wants the same skill to work across Claude.ai, Claude Code, and API environments

statement: For an MCP integration, skills should encode the workflow knowledge and best practices that turn raw tool access into reliable user outcomes.
condition: when the user already has a working MCP server

statement: Before writing a skill, the author should identify two or three concrete use cases the skill must enable.
A useful skill use case definition should state the user trigger, ordered workflow steps, required tools, embedded domain knowledge, and expected result.
Document and asset creation skills should embed style guidance, templates, and quality checks when consistent output quality is the goal.
condition: when the skill creates documents, presentations, apps, designs, code, or similar artifacts

statement: Workflow automation skills should define step-by-step methods with validation gates, reusable templates, and iteration loops.
condition: when the skill coordinates a repeatable multi-step process

statement: MCP-enhancement skills should coordinate tool calls in sequence, embed domain expertise, and handle common tool errors.
condition: when the skill improves how Claude uses one or more MCP servers

statement: Skill success criteria should combine trigger accuracy, workflow efficiency, API reliability, reduced user redirection, output consistency, and correction rate rather than relying on a single metric.
Triggering quality should be tested with obvious in-scope requests, paraphrased in-scope requests, and unrelated out-of-scope requests.
Functional skill tests should check output validity, successful tool/API calls, error handling, and edge cases.
Performance comparisons should measure the same task with and without the skill enabled, including tool calls, token use, retries, and correction burden.
The skill folder name should use kebab-case with no spaces, underscores, or capital letters, and the required skill file should be named exactly SKILL.md.
A skill folder should not contain a README.md; human-facing repository documentation should live outside the skill folder.
The minimal frontmatter must include a kebab-case name and a description that states both what the skill does and when it should be used.
The description field should include concrete trigger phrases and relevant file types so Claude can decide when to load the skill.
A skill description should stay under 1024 characters and avoid XML angle brackets.
Skill names should not use reserved Claude or Anthropic naming patterns because frontmatter is surfaced in the system prompt.
A strong skill description should be specific about the task and triggers; vague descriptions and descriptions without usage triggers are likely to underperform.
SKILL.md instructions should provide concrete steps, runnable commands where appropriate, examples, and troubleshooting guidance instead of generic advice.
Detailed documentation should be moved to references and linked from SKILL.md so the main instruction file stays focused.
Skill authors should iterate on one challenging task until Claude succeeds before broadening the skill to many scenarios.
Undertriggering should be addressed by making the description more detailed and adding relevant user-facing keywords.
condition: when the skill fails to load for relevant requests

statement: Overtriggering should be addressed by adding negative triggers and narrowing the skill description scope.
condition: when the skill loads for irrelevant requests

statement: Execution failures should be addressed by improving instructions and adding explicit error handling.
condition: when the skill loads but produces inconsistent results, failed API calls, or user corrections

statement: For public distribution, host the skill in a clear repository, document installation and example usage, and connect the skill documentation to any related MCP documentation.
condition: when distributing a skill beyond a private user or team

statement: Skill positioning should emphasize the user outcome and the combined MCP-plus-skill workflow rather than the internal folder and metadata mechanics.
condition: when writing user-facing documentation or marketing for a skill

statement: Sequential workflow skills should make ordering, inter-step dependencies, validation points, and rollback behavior explicit.
condition: when the user outcome requires ordered multi-step execution

statement: Multi-MCP workflow skills should separate phases, pass data deliberately between services, validate before each phase transition, and centralize error handling.
condition: when a workflow spans multiple services

statement: Iterative refinement skills should define quality criteria, run validation, address identified issues, repeat until a stopping condition, and then finalize.
condition: when output quality improves through revision

statement: Context-aware tool-selection skills should use explicit decision criteria, provide fallbacks, and explain the selected tool or storage path to the user.
condition: when the same user outcome can be served by different tools or storage targets

statement: Domain-specific intelligence skills should apply domain checks before action, document decisions, and maintain an audit trail.
condition: when the skill adds specialized governance, compliance, or domain reasoning beyond tool access

statement: The skill-creator skill can generate initial skill drafts, review descriptions and structure, identify triggering risks, and suggest tests, but it does not replace automated test execution or quantitative evaluation.
Invalid frontmatter should be fixed by using complete YAML delimiters and valid quotation rather than leaving metadata as plain text or unterminated strings.
condition: when a skill upload or validation reports invalid frontmatter

statement: Invalid skill names should be corrected to lowercase kebab-case without spaces or capital letters.
condition: when a skill upload or validation reports an invalid skill name

statement: A skill that never loads automatically should have its description revised for specificity, realistic trigger phrases, and relevant file-type cues.
condition: when the symptom is undertriggering

statement: Asking Claude when it would use a named skill can expose how Claude interprets the skill description and what trigger information is missing.
condition: when debugging undertriggering

statement: A skill that loads for unrelated queries should add negative trigger guidance.
condition: when the symptom is overtriggering

statement: Overbroad descriptions should be narrowed to the specific domain, artifact type, or workflow the skill actually handles.
condition: when the symptom is overtriggering

statement: Skill scope should explicitly exclude adjacent domains when those adjacent requests should be handled elsewhere.
condition: when the skill is prone to overtriggering

statement: MCP connection failures should first be checked by confirming that the MCP server is connected in the relevant Claude surface.
condition: when a skill loads but MCP calls fail

statement: MCP authentication failures should be investigated by checking API-key validity, required permissions or scopes, and refreshed OAuth tokens.
condition: when a skill loads but MCP calls fail

statement: Testing the MCP server directly without the skill helps determine whether a failure belongs to the MCP connection rather than the skill instructions.
condition: when a skill loads but MCP calls fail

statement: Skill instructions that call MCP tools should verify tool names against server documentation and preserve case sensitivity.
condition: when diagnosing MCP tool-call failures

statement: When Claude does not follow a skill, make the instructions concise, use bullets or numbered lists, and move detailed reference material out of SKILL.md.
condition: when the skill loads but instructions are not followed

statement: Critical instructions should appear near the top of SKILL.md, be clearly marked, and be repeated when necessary.
condition: when the skill loads but critical steps are skipped

statement: Ambiguous validation guidance should be replaced with explicit checks and preconditions.
condition: when the skill loads but validations are inconsistently applied

statement: Critical validations should be implemented as bundled scripts when deterministic checking is more reliable than language-only instruction.
condition: when validation correctness is important enough to justify executable support

statement: Encouragement to be thorough is more effective in the user prompt than in SKILL.md.
Large-context skill problems can come from oversized skill content, too many simultaneously enabled skills, or loading all content instead of using progressive disclosure.
condition: when skill behavior becomes slow or degraded

statement: To reduce context load, move detailed documentation into references, link to it from SKILL.md, and keep SKILL.md under about 5,000 words.
condition: when skill content is too large or responses degrade

statement: If many skills are enabled at once, evaluate whether selective enablement or grouped skill packs would reduce context pressure.
condition: when more than roughly 20 to 50 skills are enabled simultaneously

statement: A pre-upload checklist should verify concrete use cases, required tools, folder structure, SKILL.md naming, frontmatter validity, actionable instructions, error handling, examples, references, trigger tests, functional tests, tool integration, and packaging.
condition: before uploading or distributing a skill

statement: After upload, the author should test skills in real conversations, monitor undertriggering and overtriggering, collect feedback, iterate on descriptions and instructions, and update metadata versions.
condition: after uploading a skill

statement: Bug reports for public skills should include the skill name, the error message, and reproduction steps.
condition: when reporting a skill defect

statement: First-time skill builders should start with the best-practices guide and then consult API documentation as needed.
condition: when building a first skill

statement: Optional frontmatter and metadata fields can be used to record licensing, compatibility, allowed tool access, authorship, versioning, category, tags, documentation, and support details.
YAML frontmatter should be parsed as data and must not contain executable code.
Complete production skill examples should be used as templates because maintained repositories can include additional current patterns beyond a static guide.
condition: when adapting an existing pattern for a new skill

statement: Skill files should be concise, structured, and validated against real usage so agents can discover and apply them effectively.
Only a skill's metadata is preloaded at startup; the main skill file and any bundled files consume context only after the agent decides they are relevant.
Even though full skill content is lazy-loaded, authors should keep the main skill file short because loaded content competes with conversation history and other context.
Skill authors should omit explanations that capable agents can already infer, and include only context that materially changes task execution.

condition: when a task admits multiple valid approaches and depends on context
statement: For tasks with multiple acceptable approaches and contextual judgment, text-based heuristic guidance is preferable to rigid procedure.

condition: when a preferred pattern exists and configuration changes behavior
statement: For tasks with a preferred pattern but acceptable variation, pseudocode or parameterized scripts give the agent enough structure without over-constraining it.

condition: when the operation is fragile, error-prone, or consistency-critical
statement: For fragile, error-prone, or consistency-critical operations, a skill should provide exact commands or tightly constrained scripts.
The amount of freedom a skill gives the agent should increase with task variability and decrease with operational risk.

condition: when the skill is intended for use across multiple models
statement: A skill should be tested with every model intended to use it because instruction sufficiency and verbosity tolerance vary by model capability.

condition: when the same skill targets models with different capabilities
statement: Instructions that are adequate for a stronger reasoning model may need more concrete guidance for a faster or smaller model.
Skill frontmatter requires a human-readable name and a one-line description, and those fields shape discoverability.
Skill names should use a consistent activity-oriented pattern so users and agents can identify capabilities quickly.
Vague, overly broad, or inconsistent skill names reduce referenceability and weaken skill collection organization.
A skill description should be written in third person because it is injected into the agent context and point-of-view mismatch can impair discovery.
A skill description should include both the capability and the triggering contexts or keywords that should cause selection.
The main skill file should act as an overview and navigation layer, with detailed instructions, references, examples, and scripts loaded only as needed.

condition: when the main skill file is becoming long or broad
statement: When a skill approaches substantial length, authors should move detailed material into separate files rather than overloading the main skill file.

condition: when a skill spans multiple domains or datasets
statement: Domain-specific reference files reduce irrelevant context by letting agents load only the domain needed for the current task.

condition: when details are needed only for some task variants
statement: Advanced or conditional material should be linked from the main skill file so agents can load it only for tasks that require it.
Skill reference links should stay one level deep from the main skill file because nested reference chains increase the chance that agents preview only partial information and miss needed details.

condition: when a reference file is longer than about 100 lines
statement: Long reference files should begin with a contents overview so agents can assess scope and navigate to relevant sections even during partial reads.

condition: when a task has multiple dependent steps
statement: Complex skills should express workflows as clear ordered steps, and especially complex workflows can provide a checklist for progress tracking.

condition: when the task has a validator or review checklist
statement: Critical validation steps should be embedded directly in workflows so the agent checks work immediately, fixes failures, and repeats until validation passes.
Skill content should avoid time-sensitive mainline instructions and instead separate current guidance from legacy patterns to reduce future staleness.
Skills should use consistent terminology throughout so agents can map concepts and instructions reliably.
Templates are useful when an output must follow a required structure, but flexible templates should explicitly allow adaptation when task context matters.

condition: when examples clarify desired output better than prose rules
statement: Input-output examples are valuable when output quality depends on style, format, or level-of-detail expectations that are hard to specify abstractly.

condition: when the same skill supports multiple task variants
statement: Conditional workflows should route agents through task-type decisions before giving variant-specific procedures.
Authors should create representative evaluations before writing extensive skill documentation so the skill targets observed gaps instead of speculative needs.
Evaluation-driven skill development should compare baseline behavior without the skill against behavior after minimal instructions are added, then iterate from results.
A practical skill evaluation should specify the skill under test, the user query, required files, and expected behavior so success can be judged consistently.
Effective skill development can alternate between an authoring agent that refines the skill and a fresh using agent that exposes real execution gaps.
Skill iteration should be based on observed agent behavior, including missed references, unexpected navigation paths, overused sections, and ignored bundled files.

condition: when usage observations show repeated access to the same bundled content
statement: If an agent repeatedly needs a bundled file, authors should consider moving that material into the main skill file.

condition: when usage observations show a bundled file is ignored
statement: If agents never use a bundled file, authors should treat it as a signal that the file may be unnecessary or insufficiently signposted.
Skill file paths should use forward slashes so references work across operating systems.
Windows-style path separators can break skill references on Unix-like systems.
Skill instructions should give a recommended default approach and reserve alternatives for cases where they are genuinely needed.
Offering too many equivalent implementation choices can confuse the agent and weaken execution consistency.

condition: when a skill includes executable scripts
statement: Scripts bundled with skills should handle predictable error conditions directly instead of failing and leaving recovery entirely to the agent.

condition: when scripts expose numeric limits, retries, timeouts, thresholds, or similar constants
statement: Configuration constants in skill scripts should be justified and documented so agents can understand when a value is intentional rather than arbitrary.

condition: when a script contains unexplained configuration values
statement: If an author cannot justify a configuration value, the agent is unlikely to infer the right value reliably during execution.

condition: when a task has repeatable executable logic
statement: Reusable utility scripts are preferable to regenerated code for deterministic skill operations because they improve reliability, save context, save time, and standardize repeated work.

condition: when a skill bundles executable code
statement: Skill instructions should state whether a script is meant to be executed or read as reference, because those modes have different context and reliability tradeoffs.

condition: when the script is a normal utility rather than an explanation of complex logic
statement: For most utility scripts, execution is preferred over reading source because the agent can use the script behavior without loading implementation details into context.

condition: when inputs have spatial or visual structure
statement: When task inputs can be rendered visually, skills can use image conversion plus visual inspection to help agents understand layout and structure.

condition: when work is batch-oriented, destructive, high-stakes, or subject to complex validation rules
statement: Complex open-ended operations should use a plan-validate-execute workflow with a structured intermediate plan before applying changes.

condition: when a structured plan can be checked before execution
statement: Validating intermediate plan files catches missing fields, conflicts, omissions, and invalid updates before the original artifact is modified.

condition: when a validation script is bundled with a skill
statement: Validation scripts should produce specific, actionable error messages so the agent can repair the plan or input efficiently.

condition: when a skill depends on packages or external libraries
statement: Skill authors should list required packages and verify that the intended execution environment can provide them.

condition: when a skill may run in different Anthropic execution environments
statement: Package installation capabilities differ by environment: some hosted surfaces can install packages or fetch repositories, while API execution lacks network installation.
Skill authors should account for lazy file access: names and descriptions are always available, while full files, references, data, and scripts affect context only when read or executed.

condition: when the agent executes a bundled utility script
statement: Executing a script through the shell generally consumes context only through its output, not through the full script source.
Skill directories should use descriptive file names so agents can infer file purpose while navigating the filesystem.

condition: when a skill includes multiple references or domains
statement: Skill directories should be organized by domain or feature to make task-relevant references easy to find and irrelevant references easy to skip.

condition: when large reference files, examples, documentation, or datasets are useful
statement: Skills can bundle comprehensive resources without immediate context cost, provided agents are guided to load only the resources needed for the task.

condition: when an operation is repeatable and mechanically checkable
statement: Deterministic operations inside skills should be implemented as scripts rather than asking agents to generate equivalent code during each run.

condition: when a skill relies on multiple files or folders
statement: Skill authors should test real file access patterns to ensure agents can navigate the directory structure and reach the intended resources.

condition: when a skill instructs the agent to use MCP tools
statement: Skills that reference MCP tools should use fully qualified server-and-tool names to avoid lookup failures.

condition: when multiple MCP servers may be available
statement: Unqualified MCP tool names are more likely to fail when multiple servers expose tools or when the agent must disambiguate tool location.

statement: The source reports that a similar think-tool configuration produced gains for Claude 3.5 Sonnet as well as Claude 3.7 Sonnet, suggesting the pattern may generalize across those Claude model generations.
Good automated evaluations let teams ship AI agents more confidently and make problems and behavioral changes visible before they reach users; their value compounds over an agent's lifecycle.

The autonomy, intelligence, and flexibility that make AI agents useful also make them harder to evaluate, because agents act over many turns—calling tools, modifying state, and adapting to intermediate results.
Evaluating 'an agent' means evaluating the agent harness (scaffold) and the model working together, not the model in isolation.

Grade the outcome (the final state in the environment at the end of a trial), not just what the transcript says the agent did—e.g. verify a reservation exists in the environment's database rather than trusting a 'flight booked' message.
Run multiple trials per task, because model outputs vary between runs, to produce more consistent results.

Frontier models can find creative valid solutions that a static eval scores as failures, so an eval 'failure' may actually be a better solution than the reference (e.g. Opus 4.5 exploiting a policy loophole to book a flight on tau2-bench).
Without evals, debugging is reactive and teams cannot distinguish real regressions from noise, automatically test changes against many scenarios before shipping, or measure improvements.
Build evals early: in early development product requirements translate naturally into test cases, whereas waiting forces you to reverse-engineer success criteria from a live system.
condition: in early agent development

statement: Evals can serve as the highest-bandwidth communication channel between product and research teams by defining metrics researchers can optimize against.
Agent evaluations typically combine three grader types—code-based, model-based, and human—each grading some portion of the transcript or the outcome.
Prefer deterministic (code-based) graders where possible, LLM graders where necessary or for added flexibility, and human graders judiciously for additional validation.
Code-based graders are fast, cheap, objective, reproducible, and easy to debug, but brittle to valid variations that don't match expected patterns and limited for subjective tasks.

Model-based (LLM) graders are flexible, scalable, and capture nuance for open-ended output, but are non-deterministic, more expensive than code, and require calibration against human graders for accuracy.
Human graders are the gold standard and match expert user judgment, but are expensive, slow, and often require scarce human experts.
Per-task scoring can be weighted (combined grader scores must hit a threshold), binary (all graders must pass), or a hybrid.
Capability ('quality') evals should start at a low pass rate, targeting tasks the agent struggles with so the team has a hill to climb.
Regression evals should have a nearly 100% pass rate; a decline in score signals that something is broken.
Once an agent is launched and optimized, high-pass-rate capability evals can graduate into a regression suite run continuously to catch drift.

Effective evals for coding agents rely on well-specified tasks, stable test environments, and thorough tests of the generated code; deterministic graders are natural because you can check whether the code runs and the tests pass.

For coding agents, once you have pass/fail outcome tests it is useful to also grade the transcript—e.g. heuristic code-quality rules and LLM rubrics for how the agent calls tools or interacts with the user.
In practice coding-agent evaluations typically rely on unit tests for correctness plus an LLM rubric for overall code quality, adding other graders and metrics only as needed.

For conversational agents the quality of the interaction itself is part of what is evaluated, so effective evals rely on verifiable end-state outcomes plus rubrics capturing both task completion and interaction quality.
Conversational-agent evals often require a second LLM to simulate the user for extended multi-turn interactions.
Conversational-agent success is multidimensional—e.g. combine a state check (ticket resolved), a transcript constraint (finished in under N turns), and an LLM rubric (appropriate tone).

For research agents, quality can only be judged relative to the task, so combine grader types: groundedness checks (claims supported by retrieved sources), coverage checks (key facts a good answer must include), and source-quality checks (sources are authoritative, not just first retrieved).
Given the subjective nature of research quality, LLM-based rubrics for research agents should be frequently calibrated against expert human judgment.

Evaluate computer-use agents by running them in a real or sandboxed environment and verifying the intended outcome through backend state (e.g. confirm an order was actually placed), not merely that a confirmation page appeared.

Browser-use agents require balancing token efficiency against latency: DOM-based interaction is fast but token-heavy while screenshot-based interaction is slower but more token-efficient, so build evals that check the agent selects the right tool for each context.
pass@k measures the probability an agent produces at least one correct solution in k attempts and rises as k increases; use it when only one success matters (e.g. pass@1 for coding).
pass^k measures the probability that all k trials succeed and falls as k increases; use it for customer-facing agents where consistent, reliable behavior every time is essential.
Start with as few as 20-50 simple tasks drawn from real failures rather than waiting for hundreds, because early on each system change has a large, noticeable effect so small samples suffice.
condition: in early agent development

statement: Seed the initial eval set from what you already test manually plus your bug tracker and support queue, converting user-reported failures into test cases and prioritizing by user impact.

Write unambiguous tasks: a good task is one where two domain experts would independently reach the same pass/fail verdict, and everything the grader checks should be clear from the task description so agents don't fail due to ambiguous specs.
With frontier models, a 0% pass rate across many trials (e.g. 0% pass@100) is most often a signal of a broken task or grader, not an incapable agent.
condition: using frontier models

statement: Create a reference solution (a known working output that passes all graders) for each task to prove the task is solvable and verify the graders are correctly configured.
Build balanced problem sets that test both where a behavior should occur and where it should not, to avoid class-imbalanced evals and the one-sided optimization they cause.

Build a robust eval harness with a stable environment and isolate each trial by starting from a clean environment, because unnecessary shared state (leftover files, cached data, git history from prior trials, resource exhaustion) causes correlated failures or inflated performance and makes results unreliable.

Grade what the agent produced, not the specific path it took (e.g. an exact tool-call sequence), because checking rigid step sequences yields brittle tests that punish valid approaches eval designers didn't anticipate.
For tasks with multiple components, build in partial credit so an agent that completes some steps is scored above one that fails immediately.

Calibrate LLM-as-judge graders against human experts, give the LLM a way out (e.g. return 'Unknown' when it lacks information) to avoid hallucination, and use clear structured rubrics grading each dimension with an isolated judge rather than one judge for all dimensions.

Subtle failure modes—grading bugs, agent-harness constraints, or ambiguity—can produce low scores despite good agent performance, so carefully double-check tasks and graders (e.g. Opus 4.5 rose from 42% to 95% on CORE-Bench after fixing rigid grading, ambiguous specs, and non-reproducible tasks).
Make graders resistant to bypasses or hacks so that passing genuinely requires solving the problem rather than exploiting unintended loopholes.
You cannot know whether your graders are working well without reading transcripts and grades from many trials, so invest in transcript-viewing tooling and regularly read transcripts.
A failed-task transcript tells you whether the agent made a genuine mistake or your grader rejected a valid solution, and often surfaces key details about agent and eval behavior.
Failures should seem fair—it should be clear what the agent got wrong and why—so that when scores don't climb you can be confident it is due to agent performance and not a broken eval.

Do not take eval scores at face value until someone digs into the eval's details and reads transcripts; if grading is unfair, tasks are ambiguous, valid solutions are penalized, or the harness constrains the model, revise the eval.
An eval at 100% pass rate tracks regressions but provides no signal for improvement.

Eval saturation occurs when an agent passes all solvable tasks, leaving no room for improvement; near saturation large capability gains show up as small score increases, making results deceptive (e.g. SWE-Bench Verified moved from ~30% to >80% within a year).
An eval suite is a living artifact that needs ongoing attention and clear ownership to remain useful.
A durable eval-maintenance model is to have a dedicated evals team own the core infrastructure while domain experts and product teams contribute most eval tasks and run the evaluations themselves.

For AI product teams, owning and iterating on evaluations should be as routine as maintaining unit tests, because teams can waste weeks on AI features that 'work' in early testing but fail unstated expectations a good eval would surface early.
Defining eval tasks is one of the best ways to stress-test whether product requirements are concrete enough to start building.

Practice eval-driven development: build evals that define planned capabilities before agents can fulfill them, then iterate until the agent performs well; capability evals starting at a low pass rate make progress on such bets visible.

The people closest to product requirements and users (product managers, customer success, salespeople) are best positioned to define success, so enable them to contribute eval tasks (e.g. as a PR via Claude Code).

Automated evals give faster iteration, full reproducibility, no user impact, and can run on every commit, but require up-front and ongoing maintenance and can create false confidence if they don't match real usage patterns.

Production monitoring reveals real user behavior and provides ground truth on how agents actually perform, but is reactive (problems reach users first), noisy, and requires instrumentation investment.
A/B testing measures actual user outcomes and controls for confounds, but is slow, requires sufficient traffic, and only tests changes you deploy.
User feedback surfaces unanticipated problems with real examples, but is sparse, self-selected, skewed toward severe issues, and relying on users to catch issues risks negative user impact.

Manual transcript review builds intuition for failure modes and catches subtle quality issues automated checks miss, but is time-intensive, doesn't scale, and gives inconsistent, mostly qualitative coverage.

Systematic human studies give gold-standard judgments and handle subjective or ambiguous tasks, but are expensive, slow, and require reconciling inter-rater disagreement; reserve them for calibrating LLM graders or evaluating subjective outputs.

Map evaluation methods to lifecycle stages: automated evals pre-launch and in CI/CD, production monitoring post-launch for drift, A/B testing to validate significant changes once traffic suffices, ongoing user-feedback triage and weekly transcript sampling, and systematic human studies for calibration.

No single evaluation layer catches every issue (like the Swiss-cheese safety model), so combine multiple methods so failures slipping through one layer are caught by another; the most effective teams pair automated evals for iteration, production monitoring for ground truth, and periodic human review for calibration.
Eval frameworks are only as good as the eval tasks run through them, so pick a framework that fits your workflow quickly and then invest your energy in high-quality test cases and graders.

The constant fundamentals across agent types are: start early, source realistic tasks from observed failures, define unambiguous and robust success criteria, design graders thoughtfully combining multiple types, make problems hard enough for the model, iterate to improve signal-to-noise, and read the transcripts.
Harness design has a substantial impact on the effectiveness of long-running agentic coding, not just the underlying model.
On complex long-running tasks an agent tends to drift off course over time, driven by two recurring failure modes: loss of coherence as context fills, and unreliable self-evaluation.
Models lose coherence on lengthy tasks as the context window fills up.
Some models exhibit 'context anxiety', wrapping up work prematurely as they approach what they believe is their context limit.
condition: observed in some models as they near their perceived context limit

statement: A context reset — clearing the context window entirely and starting a fresh agent, paired with a structured handoff carrying the prior agent's state and next steps — addresses both coherence loss and context anxiety.
Compaction (summarizing earlier conversation in place so the same agent continues on a shortened history) preserves continuity but does not give a clean slate, so context anxiety can persist.
A context reset succeeds only if the handoff artifact carries enough state for the next agent to pick up the work cleanly.
condition: the handoff artifact must contain sufficient state for clean continuation

statement: Context resets add orchestration complexity, token overhead, and latency to each harness run.

Because Claude Sonnet 4.5 exhibited context anxiety strongly enough that compaction alone was insufficient, context resets were essential to its harness; with Opus 4.5 the behaviour was largely gone, so context resets could be dropped and the build run as one continuous session with the SDK's automatic compaction.
condition: model exhibits strong context anxiety (e.g. Sonnet 4.5)
exception: model that no longer exhibits context anxiety (e.g. Opus 4.5) does not need context resets

statement: When asked to evaluate their own work, agents tend to confidently praise it even when the quality is obviously mediocre to a human.
The self-praise problem is most pronounced on subjective tasks such as design, where there is no binary pass/fail check equivalent to a verifiable software test.
condition: subjective tasks lacking a verifiable binary check

statement: Even on tasks with verifiable outcomes, agents still sometimes show poor judgment that impedes task performance.
Separating the agent doing the work from the agent judging it is a strong lever for improving output quality.
Separation alone does not eliminate evaluator leniency, because the evaluator is still an LLM inclined to be generous toward LLM-generated output.
exception: the evaluator remains an LLM and stays lenient unless deliberately tuned

statement: Tuning a standalone evaluator to be skeptical is far more tractable than making a generator critical of its own work, and once external feedback exists the generator has something concrete to iterate against.
Absent any intervention, Claude gravitates toward safe, predictable layouts that are technically functional but visually unremarkable.
Aesthetic quality cannot be fully reduced to a single score, but it can be improved with grading criteria that encode explicit design principles and preferences.

Reframing an unanswerable subjective question ('is this design beautiful?') into a criteria-anchored one ('does this follow our principles for good design?') gives the model a concrete target to grade against.

Four grading criteria were used for frontend design — design quality (coherent whole), originality (deliberate custom decisions vs templates/AI defaults), craft (technical execution), and functionality (usability) — shared with both the generator and evaluator.

Weight the criteria the model is weak on (design quality and originality) more heavily than the ones it already handles well by default (craft and functionality), so the criteria push the model toward aesthetic risk-taking rather than generic 'AI slop'.
Calibrate the evaluator with few-shot examples that include detailed score breakdowns, which aligns its judgment with the operator's preferences and reduces score drift across iterations.

Giving the evaluator a browser tool (Playwright MCP) so it interacts with the live running page before scoring — rather than grading a static screenshot — yields more grounded assessments, at the cost of real wall-clock time per cycle.

Instruct the generator to make a strategic decision after each evaluation: refine the current direction when scores are trending well, or pivot to a different approach when the current one is not working.
The exact wording of grading criteria steers output in ways the operator may not anticipate, so the prompt language attached to criteria directly shapes the character of the output.

Even the first iteration, with no evaluator feedback yet, is noticeably better than an unprompted baseline, indicating the criteria and their language steer the model away from generic defaults before any feedback loop runs.
The generator-evaluator (GAN-inspired) pattern maps naturally onto the software development lifecycle, where code review and QA play the same structural role as a design evaluator.
A three-agent architecture — planner, generator, evaluator — was used, with each agent addressing a specific observed gap in prior runs.

Use a planner that expands a short 1-4 sentence prompt into a full product spec, instructing it to be ambitious in scope but to stay at product context and high-level technical design rather than granular implementation detail.

Keep the planner's spec high-level because if it fixes granular technical details upfront and gets them wrong, those errors cascade into downstream implementation; constrain agents on the deliverables and let them find the path as they work.
Have the generator work in sprints, implementing one feature at a time from the spec, and self-evaluate its work at the end of each sprint before handing off to QA, with git for version control.

The evaluator should exercise the running application through a browser tool the way a real user would — testing UI features, API endpoints, and database state — and grade each unit of work against both the bugs it finds and explicit criteria (product depth, functionality, visual design, code quality), each with a hard threshold that fails the unit if unmet.

Before each sprint, have the generator and evaluator negotiate a 'sprint contract' agreeing on what 'done' means and how completion will be verified before any code is written, to bridge the gap between a high-level spec and testable implementation.

Have agents communicate through files — one writes a file, another reads and responds in that file or a new one — which keeps work faithful to the spec without over-specifying implementation too early.
The full harness run cost roughly 20x more than the solo single-agent run ($200 over 6 hours vs $9 over 20 minutes), but produced a markedly higher-quality result.

The solo single-agent run produced an application whose central feature was broken — entities rendered but did not respond to input because the wiring between entity definitions and the game runtime was broken with no surface indication — while the full-harness run produced a working, more polished, more feature-rich application.

The evaluator kept implementation aligned with the spec by walking granular contract criteria (e.g. 27 criteria for a single sprint) and filing findings specific enough to act on without further investigation.
Out of the box Claude is a poor QA agent: it identifies legitimate issues then talks itself into approving the work anyway, and it tends to test superficially rather than probing edge cases.

Tune an evaluator by reading its logs, finding cases where its judgment diverged from the operator's, and updating the QA prompt to fix those cases — expect several rounds before its grading is reasonable.
Even a tuned evaluator leaves verification headroom: small layout issues, unintuitive interactions, and undiscovered bugs in deeply nested features it did not exercise thoroughly still slip through.

Every component in a harness encodes an assumption about what the model cannot do on its own, and those assumptions are worth stress-testing because they may be wrong and can go stale as models improve.
Follow 'find the simplest solution possible, and only increase complexity when needed' when maintaining an agent harness.

Simplify a harness methodically by removing one component at a time and reviewing its impact, rather than cutting back radically, because a radical cut makes it hard to tell which pieces were actually load-bearing.

A more capable model (e.g. Opus 4.6, which plans more carefully, sustains agentic tasks longer, operates reliably in larger codebases, and has better self-review and long-context retrieval) reduces the scaffolding a harness needs.
condition: a more capable successor model is available

statement: The sprint-decomposition construct can be removed once the model can natively sustain coherent multi-hour work without it (e.g. Opus 4.6 built coherently for over two hours without sprint decomposition).
condition: the model can sustain coherent long-running work without decomposition

statement: Keep the planner even after simplification: without it the generator under-scopes, starting to build without speccing and producing a less feature-rich application.

An evaluator's value is not fixed — it depends on where the task sits relative to what the model can do reliably solo: it gives real lift for work at or beyond the model's solo capability, and becomes unnecessary overhead for work well within it.
condition: task sits at or beyond what the model can do reliably on its own
exception: task is well within the model's reliable solo capability

statement: Building app-embedded AI features (a generator producing a proper tool-driven agent inside the app) required substantial prompting iteration because that knowledge is recent enough that the model's training data covers it thinly.
condition: the target capability is recent and thinly represented in training data

statement: Good practice when building against a model: experiment directly with that model, read its traces on realistic problems, and tune its performance toward the desired outcome.
When a new model lands, re-examine the harness: strip away pieces no longer load-bearing and add new pieces that unlock capability that was not previously possible.
condition: a new, more capable model has been released

statement: Long-running agents must operate in discrete sessions, and each new session begins with no memory of prior sessions.
Because context windows are limited and most complex projects cannot be completed within a single window, agents need a mechanism to bridge state between sessions.
Context-management features such as compaction are not sufficient on their own to let an agent make consistent progress across many context windows.
A frontier coding model run in a loop across multiple context windows will fall short of building a production-quality web app when given only a high-level prompt.
condition: the agent is given only a high-level, one-line prompt with no scaffolding

statement: A common failure mode is the agent attempting to do too much at once (one-shotting the app), which causes it to run out of context mid-implementation and leave a feature half-implemented and undocumented.
Compaction does not always pass perfectly clear instructions to the next agent session.
A second common failure mode is a later agent instance observing that progress has been made and prematurely declaring the entire project complete.

An effective harness decomposes the work into two parts: an initializer agent that establishes the environment for all required features, and coding agents that make incremental progress while leaving the environment clean.
A 'clean state' means code appropriate for merging to a main branch: no major bugs, orderly and well-documented, so a developer could start new work without first cleaning up an unrelated mess.
The very first session should use a specialized initializer prompt that differs from the prompt used for subsequent coding sessions.
The initializer agent should set up an init.sh script, a progress log file (e.g. claude-progress.txt), and an initial git commit recording the files added.
Every subsequent coding session should be prompted to make incremental progress and then leave structured updates for the next session.
The key enabler is letting a fresh-context agent quickly understand the current state of work, achieved through a progress file combined with git history.
The initializer agent should write a comprehensive feature-requirements file that expands the user's initial prompt into many concrete end-to-end feature descriptions.
Every feature in the feature list should initially be marked as failing so that later coding agents have a clear outline of what full functionality looks like.
Coding agents should be permitted to edit the feature file only by changing a feature's pass/fail status, not by adding, removing, or rewriting features.
Use strongly-worded instructions forbidding the agent from removing or editing tests, because doing so could lead to missing or buggy functionality.
The feature list should be stored as JSON rather than Markdown, because the model is less likely to inappropriately change or overwrite a JSON file.
Coding agents should work on only one feature at a time; this incremental constraint is critical to curbing the agent's tendency to do too much at once.
After each code change the agent should leave the environment clean, best elicited by committing progress to git with descriptive commit messages and writing progress summaries to a progress file.
Committing progress to git lets the agent revert bad code changes and recover previously working states of the codebase.
Leaving structured artifacts (git commits and progress notes) improves efficiency by removing the need for the next agent to guess prior state and repair basic functionality.
A further failure mode is the agent marking a feature complete without proper end-to-end testing.
Without explicit prompting the agent tends to run unit tests or curl commands against a dev server but fails to verify that a feature works end-to-end.
condition: the agent is not explicitly prompted to test end-to-end

statement: When explicitly prompted to use browser-automation tools and to test as a human user would, the agent verified web-app features end-to-end reliably.
condition: the agent is explicitly prompted to use browser automation and test as a human user

statement: Providing the agent with testing tools such as browser automation dramatically improved performance by surfacing bugs that were not obvious from the code alone.

End-to-end testing via vision and browser automation cannot catch every kind of bug; for example, the agent could not see browser-native alert modals through the Puppeteer MCP, so features relying on them were buggier.
exception: bugs invisible to the vision/browser-automation tooling, such as browser-native alert modals not exposed via the automation MCP

statement: Each coding session should begin with orientation steps: run pwd to confirm the working directory, read the git log and progress file, then read the feature list and pick the highest-priority not-yet-done feature.
Pre-baking the testing and orientation routine into the harness saves tokens each session because the agent does not have to re-derive how to test the code.
The initializer should write an init.sh script that runs the development server, and each session should run a basic end-to-end test before implementing a new feature.
Running a basic end-to-end test at the start of a session lets the agent detect and fix a broken state before adding new features, which would otherwise compound existing bugs.

It remains unclear whether a single general-purpose coding agent performs best across contexts, or whether specialized agents (e.g. testing, QA, or code-cleanup agents) in a multi-agent architecture would perform better.

These harness lessons were developed for full-stack web-app development and are likely, though not proven, to generalize to other long-horizon agentic domains such as scientific research or financial modeling.
The initializer and coding agents differ only in their initial user prompt; the system prompt, tool set, and overall harness are otherwise identical.
Open-ended research cannot be served by a fixed, linear one-shot pipeline; the agent must operate autonomously across many turns, revising its approach based on intermediate findings.
Subagents operating in parallel with their own context windows enable compression and separation of concerns, reducing path dependency and enabling independent investigations.
A multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as lead and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on Anthropic's internal research eval.
Multi-agent systems excel especially at breadth-first queries that pursue multiple independent directions simultaneously.
On the BrowseComp evaluation, token usage alone explained 80% of performance variance, and token usage plus number of tool calls plus model choice together explained 95%.
Multi-agent systems work mainly because they let the system spend enough tokens on the problem, distributing work across agents with separate context windows to add parallel-reasoning capacity.
Agents typically use about 4x more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15x more tokens than chat.
Multi-agent systems are only economically viable for tasks whose value is high enough to justify their much higher token cost.
condition: the value of the task is high enough to pay for increased token usage

statement: Multi-agent systems are a poor fit for domains that require all agents to share the same context or that involve many dependencies between agents, such as most coding tasks.
exception: tasks requiring shared context or heavy inter-agent dependencies (e.g. most coding tasks)

statement: Reserve multi-agent systems for valuable tasks that involve heavy parallelization, information exceeding a single context window, and interfacing with numerous complex tools.
condition: tasks with heavy parallelization, information exceeding one context window, or many complex tools

statement: Use an orchestrator-worker architecture in which a lead agent coordinates the process and delegates to specialized subagents that run in parallel.
Prefer multi-step dynamic search that adapts to new findings over static Retrieval-Augmented-Generation retrieval of fixed similar chunks.
The lead agent should save its plan to external memory to persist context, because if the context window exceeds 200,000 tokens it is truncated and the plan would otherwise be lost.
condition: context window may exceed 200,000 tokens

statement: A dedicated citation agent should process the gathered documents and report to attribute each claim to its source before returning results.

To iterate on agent prompts effectively, build simulations using the exact prompts and tools and watch agents work step-by-step, which surfaces failure modes such as stopping late, verbose queries, or wrong tool selection.

Give each subagent an explicit objective, output format, guidance on tools and sources, and clear task boundaries; vague delegation causes subagents to duplicate work, leave gaps, or misinterpret the task.

Embed explicit effort-scaling rules in prompts: roughly 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls for simple fact-finding, 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each for direct comparisons, and more than 10 subagents with divided responsibilities for complex research.

Tool design and selection are as critical as human-computer interfaces; give agents explicit tool-selection heuristics and ensure every tool has a distinct purpose and a clear, high-quality description.
Bad or low-quality tool descriptions can send agents down completely wrong paths.

Let agents improve themselves: Claude 4 models can diagnose failure modes and rewrite prompts and tool descriptions, and a tool-testing agent that rewrote a flawed tool's description produced a 40% decrease in task-completion time for later agents.
Prompt agents to start with short, broad queries and progressively narrow, because agents otherwise default to overly long, specific queries that return few results.

Use extended thinking as a controllable planning scratchpad for the lead agent, and interleaved thinking after tool results for subagents to evaluate result quality, identify gaps, and refine the next query.
Introduce parallelism at two levels—the lead agent spinning up 3-5 subagents in parallel and subagents calling 3+ tools in parallel—which cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries.
Prompt agents with good heuristics and explicit guardrails rather than rigid rules, since strict instructions do not generalize to the many valid paths agents may take.
Start evaluating agents immediately with a small sample of about 20 queries representing real usage, because early large effect sizes are visible with only a few test cases.
exception: do not delay evaluation until a large hundreds-of-case suite is built

statement: A single LLM-as-judge call with one prompt that outputs a 0.0-1.0 score and a pass/fail grade against a rubric (factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, tool efficiency) was more consistent and human-aligned than using multiple judges.
Human evaluation remains essential because testers catch edge cases automated evals miss, such as hallucinations on unusual queries, system failures, and subtle source-selection biases.

Multi-agent systems exhibit emergent behavior—small changes to the lead agent can unpredictably change subagent behavior—so the best prompts are collaboration frameworks defining division of labor, problem-solving approaches, and effort budgets.
In agentic systems, minor changes and minor failures cascade into large, compounding behavioral changes, making complex long-running agents hard to engineer.

Because agents are stateful and errors compound, build systems that resume from the point of failure rather than restarting, and combine AI adaptability with deterministic safeguards such as retry logic and regular checkpoints.
Informing the agent when a tool is failing and letting it adapt works well for graceful error handling.

Add full production tracing and monitor agent decision patterns and interaction structures—without inspecting individual conversation contents—to diagnose non-deterministic failures while preserving user privacy.
Use rainbow deployments to gradually shift traffic from old to new versions so that updates do not disrupt agents already mid-execution.

Synchronous subagent execution simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks—the lead cannot steer running subagents and the system blocks on the slowest one—whereas asynchronous execution adds parallelism at the cost of harder result coordination, state consistency, and error propagation.

For agents that mutate persistent state over many turns, evaluate the correct final end-state rather than judging each turn, and break complex workflows into discrete checkpoints where specific state changes should have occurred.
condition: agents modify persistent state across multi-turn conversations

statement: Manage long-horizon conversations by having agents summarize completed phases into external memory and, as context limits approach, spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts while maintaining continuity through handoffs.
condition: conversations span so many turns that a standard context window becomes insufficient

statement: Have subagents write their outputs to an external filesystem and pass lightweight references back to the coordinator to avoid the 'game of telephone', preventing information loss and reducing token overhead, especially for structured outputs.
condition: outputs are structured (e.g. code, reports, data visualizations)

statement: Agent harnesses encode assumptions about what the model cannot do on its own, and those assumptions should be questioned frequently because they go stale as models improve.

A harness workaround added for one model can become dead weight on a stronger model: context resets added to stop Claude Sonnet 4.5 ending tasks prematurely near its context limit ('context anxiety') were unnecessary on Claude Opus 4.5, where the behaviour was gone.

Design an agent system for 'programs as yet unthought of' by virtualizing its components into abstractions general enough to outlast any particular implementation, mirroring how OS abstractions like process and file outlasted the hardware beneath them.

An agent can be virtualized into three components: a session (an append-only log of everything that happened), a harness (the loop that calls the model and routes its tool calls to infrastructure), and a sandbox (an execution environment where the model runs code and edits files).
Each virtualized agent component should be implementable and swappable independently without disturbing the others.
Be opinionated about the shape of the interfaces around the model, not about what implementation runs behind them.
Placing session, harness, and sandbox in a single shared container has real benefits: file edits are direct syscalls and there are no service boundaries to design.

Coupling all agent components into one container creates a 'pet' (in the pets-vs-cattle sense): the server becomes a named, hand-tended individual, so if the container fails the session is lost and an unresponsive container must be nursed back to health.
condition: when session, harness, and sandbox share one container

statement: When all components share one container, the only debugging window (a WebSocket event stream) cannot localize failures, so a harness bug, a dropped event-stream packet, and a container going offline all present identically.
condition: when components share one container observed only via an event stream

statement: If the debugging container also holds user data, opening a shell inside it to investigate is effectively no debugging capability at all.
condition: when the container also holds user data

statement: Baking into the harness the assumption that everything the model works on lives in the same container forces customers who want the agent to reach resources in their own VPC to either peer their network or run the harness themselves.
condition: when the harness assumes co-located resources

statement: Decouple the 'brain' (the model and its harness) from the 'hands' (sandboxes and tools that perform actions) and from the 'session' (the event log), making each an interface that assumes little about the others and can fail or be replaced independently.
Have the harness call the sandbox/container the same way it calls any other tool, through a uniform interface such as execute(name, input) -> string, rather than living inside the container.

Once the harness treats the container as an external tool, the container becomes cattle: if it dies the harness catches the failure as a tool-call error and returns it to the model, and on retry a fresh container is reinitialized from a standard recipe (e.g. provision({resources})).

Keeping the session log outside the harness makes the harness itself cattle, because nothing in the harness needs to survive a crash: a new harness can be rebooted (wake(sessionId)), refetch the event log (getSession(id)), and resume from the last event.
During the agent loop the harness should durably record events by writing them to the session (e.g. emitEvent(id, event)) so the run is recoverable.

Running untrusted model-generated code in the same container as credentials is a security flaw: a prompt injection then only has to convince the model to read its own environment, and an attacker who obtains those tokens can spawn fresh unrestricted sessions and delegate work to them.
condition: when generated code and credentials share an environment

statement: Narrowly scoping a token is only a partial mitigation because it encodes an assumption about what the model cannot do with a limited token, and that assumption weakens as models get smarter.
The structural fix for credential exposure is to make tokens unreachable from the sandbox where the model's generated code runs, rather than relying on scoping alone.
Keep credentials out of the sandbox by either bundling auth with a resource or holding it in a vault outside the sandbox.

For Git access, clone the repository using its access token during sandbox initialization and wire the token into the local git remote, so push and pull work from inside the sandbox without the agent ever handling the token.

For custom tools, store OAuth tokens in a secure vault and route MCP tool calls through a dedicated proxy that takes a session-associated token, fetches the matching credentials from the vault, and makes the external call, so the harness is never made aware of any credentials.
Long-horizon tasks often exceed the model's context window, and the standard mitigations (compaction, a memory tool, context trimming) all force irreversible decisions about what context to keep.
Irreversibly retaining or discarding context risks failure because it is hard to know in advance which tokens future turns will need.
