Context removed by a compaction step is recoverable only if it was stored, since the harness drops the compacted messages from the context window.
condition: when messages are transformed by a compaction step

statement: Store context as an object that lives outside the context window and that the model can programmatically access (e.g. code that filters or slices it), rather than deciding up front what to discard.
A durable session log can serve as the context object outside the context window, so context is stored durably in the log rather than only inside a sandbox or REPL.

Expose the event log through an interface that lets the brain interrogate context by positional slices (e.g. getEvents()), so it can resume where it stopped reading, rewind before a moment, or reread context before an action.

Let the harness transform fetched events before passing them to the context window (for example organizing context for a high prompt-cache hit rate), so arbitrary context engineering lives in the harness.

Separate recoverable context storage (the session's job) from arbitrary context management (the harness's job), because the specific context engineering future models will need cannot be predicted; the interface should only guarantee the session is durable and available for interrogation.

Placing the brain inside a container forces one container per brain and makes every session pay the full container setup cost up front (clone repo, boot process, fetch events) before any inference, even sessions that never touch the sandbox.
condition: when the brain runs inside the container

statement: Time-to-first-token (TTFT) — how long a session waits between accepting work and producing its first response token — is the latency users feel most acutely.

Provisioning containers lazily via a brain-issued tool call only when needed lets inference start as soon as pending events are pulled from the session log, so sessions that need no container do not wait for one.
Decoupling the brain from the container and provisioning lazily reduced measured p50 TTFT by roughly 60% and p95 by over 90%.
Scaling to many brains can be done by starting many stateless harnesses and connecting them to hands only when needed.

Connecting one brain to many execution environments requires the model to reason about where to send work, a harder cognitive task than operating in a single shell, which is why a single-container design fits only less-capable models.
condition: as model intelligence scales

statement: Modeling each hand as a uniform tool (execute(name, input) -> string) lets the harness support any custom tool, any MCP server, and first-party tools without knowing whether the sandbox is a container, a phone, or anything else.
Because no hand is coupled to any particular brain, brains can pass hands to one another.

A meta-harness should be opinionated only about the interfaces around the model — that it can manipulate state (a session), perform computation (a sandbox), and scale to many brains and many hands — while making no assumptions about the number, location, or specific harness those brains and hands use.
As AI coding capability improves, a technical evaluation that reliably distinguishes human skill levels today can become trivially solvable by a future model, destroying its evaluative signal.
Each new frontier-model release should be expected to defeat an existing technical take-home, so evaluations must be treated as perishable and periodically redesigned rather than fixed assets.
A take-home should be genuinely engaging and enjoyable so candidates are motivated to participate and to show their skill at high resolution.
Give a longer time horizon (on the order of 2 to 4 hours) because real engineering work rarely involves sub-hour deadlines, while balancing the horizon against how onerous it is for candidates.
condition: balance chosen duration against candidate burden and pipeline scheduling overhead

statement: Use a realistic working environment for the evaluation: no observer, no expected narration, candidate works in their own editor.
Allow time within the evaluation for comprehension of existing systems and for building debugging tooling, since these are hard to assess in a short live interview.

A high-signal evaluation should avoid problems that hinge on a single insight, give candidates many chances to demonstrate ability, produce a wide scoring distribution, and contain enough depth that even strong candidates do not finish everything.
Avoid requiring narrow or specific domain knowledge; candidates with strong fundamentals can learn specifics on the job, and requiring niche expertise unnecessarily shrinks the candidate pool.
An evaluation problem should be representative of the real work the job involves.
Favor problems with fast development loops, interesting depth, and room for creativity.
When the job itself uses AI assistance, the evaluation should explicitly permit AI tools rather than ban them, so it reflects real working conditions.
condition: the role actually involves working with AI assistance

statement: Longer-horizon problems are harder for AI to solve completely, so permitting AI use can still require candidates to demonstrate their own skill.
To rebuild an evaluation the model has defeated, run the strongest available model on it to identify where it starts struggling, and make that failure point the new starting difficulty.
Remove problem elements the model has already fully solved (for example, multicore parallelism), because they add no discriminating signal and only slow the development loop.
Shortening the time limit (for example from 4 hours to 2 hours) can reduce scheduling overhead and multi-week pipeline delays and make the test easier to fit into a weekend.
condition: the shorter window still leaves enough depth to distinguish candidates

statement: Banning AI assistance is a poor solution because it is hard to enforce and does not reflect a job where people work alongside AI.

Requiring candidates to substantially outperform what the model achieves alone risks making the dominant strategy passively watching the model, because the model works faster than a human can read and steer.

Problems for which the model has abundant training data (such as data transposition or memory-bank-conflict optimization) are poor choices for an AI-resistant evaluation, because the model draws on a large base of prior experience.
To give human reasoning an advantage over a model's larger experience base, choose problems that are sufficiently out-of-distribution or novel.
Making an evaluation sufficiently out-of-distribution to resist AI conflicts with the goal of resembling the real job, forcing a trade-off between AI-resistance and realism.
A heavily constrained, unusual instruction set (as in Zachtronics-style puzzles) forces unconventional problem solving and can remain resistant to current models.

Verify a candidate evaluation's AI-resistance against the strongest available (including pre-release) model, not just a casual run, because a problem that appears model-proof in a quick attempt may be solved with more effort.
When probing AI-resistance, use extended thinking budgets and a test-time-compute harness, since increasing the model's compute or thinking time often surfaces a solution a short attempt missed.
Have colleagues who are less steeped in the specific problem verify that humans can still outperform the model, to confirm the signal is not an artifact of the designer's own expertise.
Patching a single model-found shortcut is insufficient; the model may still find the intended solution through deeper analysis, so re-test after each patch.
Deliberately withholding visualization and debugging tools makes building such tools part of what the evaluation tests, and judgment about how much to invest in tooling becomes part of the signal.
Including a bug the candidate must find and fix exercises their ability to build debugging tooling.
An evaluation composed of more independent sub-problems tends to have lower variance than one built around a single deep problem.
A well-designed take-home can be more predictive than paper credentials, letting strong candidates with limited formal experience demonstrate skill.
When realism can no longer be preserved against AI, an evaluation that simulates novel work can still carry hiring signal even though it no longer resembles the real job.
Anthropic's performance-engineering take-home was used from early 2024, completed by over 1,000 candidates, and helped hire dozens of engineers, providing an empirical basis for these design lessons.
Model capability on the take-home climbed steadily across generations: Claude Opus 4 beat most human applicants within the time limit, and Claude Opus 4.5 matched even the strongest candidates.
Model performance continues to improve with additional test-time compute (for example, the same model reached progressively lower cycle counts as harness compute and thinking time increased).
Human experts retain an advantage over current models at sufficiently long time horizons: the fastest human unlimited-time solution still substantially exceeds the model's best result.
condition: the time horizon is long enough (well beyond a couple of hours)

statement: The context window is the most important resource to manage in Claude Code, because it holds the entire conversation and fills up quickly during debugging or codebase exploration.
LLM performance degrades as the context window fills: Claude may forget earlier instructions or make more mistakes as context approaches its limit.

Give Claude a check it can run itself (tests, a build, a linter, a diff against a fixture, or a screenshot comparison) so it can iterate to a pass/fail signal without the human acting as the verification loop.
When prompting, state explicit verification criteria (e.g. concrete example test cases and an instruction to run the tests after implementing) instead of only describing the desired function.
For UI changes, have Claude take a screenshot of the result and compare it against the target design, then list and fix the differences.
Instruct Claude to address the root cause of a failure rather than suppressing the error or fixing only the symptom.

Choose how hard the verification gates the stop: iterate within one prompt, set it as a /goal condition re-checked every turn, enforce it as a deterministic Stop hook, or have a verification subagent give a second opinion.
A Stop hook blocks a turn from ending until the check passes, but Claude Code overrides the hook and ends the turn after 8 consecutive blocks.
Have Claude show evidence of success (test output, the command run and its result, or a screenshot) rather than merely asserting the work is done.
Separate research and planning from implementation, using plan mode, to avoid having Claude solve the wrong problem.
Skip planning and ask Claude to act directly when the scope is clear and the fix is small; plan when the approach is uncertain, the change spans multiple files, or the code is unfamiliar.
condition: scope is clear and the fix is small vs. approach uncertain, multi-file, or unfamiliar code

statement: Give precise instructions that reference specific files, state constraints, and point to example patterns, because more precise prompts require fewer corrections.
Scope a task by naming the file, the scenario to cover, and testing preferences (such as avoiding mocks).
Point Claude to the source that can answer a question (for example, its git history) rather than asking abstractly.
Direct Claude to an existing pattern in the codebase (naming a good example file) so a new component follows established conventions.
When reporting a bug, provide the symptom, the likely location, and what a fix looks like, and ask Claude to write a failing test that reproduces it before fixing.
Vague, open-ended prompts are useful when you are exploring and can afford to course-correct, because they surface issues you would not have thought to ask about.
condition: you are exploring and can afford to course-correct

statement: Provide rich context by referencing files with @, pasting images, giving documentation URLs, piping data into Claude, or telling Claude to fetch what it needs itself.
Maintain a CLAUDE.md file (generated initially with /init) holding persistent project context such as Bash commands, code style, and workflow rules that Claude cannot infer from code alone.
Keep CLAUDE.md short and include only broadly applicable rules; put knowledge or workflows that are only sometimes relevant into skills so they load on demand instead of bloating every conversation.
A bloated or over-long CLAUDE.md causes Claude to ignore instructions because important rules get lost in the noise, so prune each line by asking whether removing it would cause mistakes.

In CLAUDE.md, include project-specific and non-obvious information (custom Bash commands, non-default style rules, test runners, repo etiquette, environment quirks, gotchas) and exclude anything Claude can infer or already knows.
Improve instruction adherence by adding emphasis such as 'IMPORTANT' or 'YOU MUST', and check CLAUDE.md into git so the team can contribute.
CLAUDE.md files can import other files with @path syntax and can be placed at home, project root, project-local (gitignored), and parent/child directory scopes.
Reduce permission interruptions with auto mode (a classifier that blocks only risky actions), permission allowlists for known-safe commands, or OS-level sandboxing.

Prefer CLI tools (such as gh, aws, gcloud) for interacting with external services because they are the most context-efficient interface; install the gh CLI to avoid unauthenticated GitHub rate limits.
Use hooks for actions that must happen every time, because hooks are deterministic and guaranteed whereas CLAUDE.md instructions are only advisory.
Create skills as SKILL.md files under .claude/skills/ to give Claude project- or domain-specific knowledge and reusable workflows that are applied automatically or invoked directly.
Set disable-model-invocation: true on skill workflows that have side effects so they are triggered manually rather than automatically by the model.
condition: the workflow has side effects you want to trigger manually

statement: Define custom subagents under .claude/agents/ for isolated tasks; they run in their own context with their own allowed tools, keeping the main conversation uncluttered.
Onboard to an unfamiliar codebase by asking Claude Code the same questions you would ask a senior engineer, with no special prompting required.
For larger features, have Claude interview you first using the AskUserQuestion tool, then write a self-contained SPEC.md and execute it in a fresh session with clean context.
condition: the feature is large

statement: Write self-contained specs that name the files and interfaces involved, state what is out of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step.
Course-correct as soon as Claude goes off track using Esc to stop, Esc+Esc or /rewind to restore state, 'undo that' to revert, and /clear to reset context between unrelated tasks.

After correcting Claude more than twice on the same issue in one session, run /clear and restart with a more specific prompt, because a clean session with a better prompt outperforms a long session of accumulated corrections.
condition: you have corrected the same issue more than twice in one session

statement: Manage context aggressively: use /clear between unrelated tasks, rely on auto-compaction near limits, use /compact <instructions> for control, and /btw for side questions that should not enter history.
Delegate research to subagents ('use subagents to investigate X') so they explore in a separate context window and report back summaries, keeping the main conversation clean.
Use rewind checkpoints (created on every prompt) to try risky approaches and restore conversation and/or code, but note checkpoints only track Claude's own changes and are not a replacement for git.
exception: checkpoints do not track changes made by external processes, so they are not a git replacement

statement: Resume prior work with claude --continue or claude --resume and name sessions with /rename so each workstream keeps its own persistent context.
Run Claude non-interactively with claude -p in CI, pre-commit hooks, or scripts, using --output-format json or stream-json to parse results programmatically.
Run multiple Claude sessions in parallel (via worktrees, the desktop app, the web, or agent teams) to speed up work and to get unbiased review from a fresh context that did not write the code.
Use a Writer/Reviewer split across sessions (or have one Claude write tests and another write the code to pass them) so review is done in a context not biased toward the code just written.
Fan out large migrations or analyses by looping claude -p over tasks, using --allowedTools to scope permissions for batch operations.

Run autonomously with auto mode (claude --permission-mode auto -p), but note that in non-interactive -p runs auto mode aborts if the classifier repeatedly blocks actions, since there is no user to fall back to.
exception: in non-interactive -p runs auto mode aborts when the classifier repeatedly blocks actions

statement: Before treating a task as done, add an adversarial review step in which a subagent reviews only the diff and criteria in a fresh context (e.g. the /code-review skill) and reports gaps back to the session.

Instruct a reviewer to flag only gaps affecting correctness or stated requirements and treat the rest as optional, because a reviewer asked to find gaps will report some even when the work is sound, leading to over-engineering.
The best-practice patterns are starting points that work well in general rather than fixed rules, and may not be optimal for every situation.

Sometimes deviate from the defaults deliberately: let context accumulate when deep in one complex problem, skip planning for exploratory tasks, or use a vague prompt to see how Claude interprets a problem before constraining it.
condition: the task is complex/exploratory or you want to see Claude's unconstrained interpretation

statement: Build intuition for when to be specific versus open-ended by paying attention to what works: when output is great, note the prompt structure, context, and mode used; when Claude struggles, diagnose whether context was too noisy, the prompt too vague, or the task too big for one pass.
Infrastructure configuration alone can produce agentic-benchmark score differences that exceed the margins separating leaderboard positions.
On Terminal-Bench 2.0 the score gap between the most- and least-resourced infrastructure setups was about 6 percentage points (p < 0.01).

Agentic coding evaluations differ from static benchmarks because the runtime environment is an active part of solving the task (writing programs, running tests, installing dependencies, iterating over turns), not a passive container.
Two agents given different resource budgets or time limits are not effectively taking the same test.
Specifying recommended per-task resources is not the same as enforcing them consistently, and the enforcement methodology can change what a benchmark actually measures.
Container runtimes enforce resources with two distinct parameters: a guaranteed allocation reserved up front and a separate hard limit at which the container is killed.
Setting the guaranteed allocation equal to the hard kill limit leaves zero headroom, so a transient memory spike can OOM-kill a container that would otherwise have succeeded.
condition: when guaranteed allocation and hard kill limit are set to the same value

statement: Treating per-task resource specs as both a floor and a hard ceiling drove high infrastructure error rates, with as many as 6% of tasks failing on pod errors unrelated to the model's ability.
The Terminal-Bench leaderboard relies on a sandboxing provider whose more lenient implementation allows temporary overallocation without killing the container, favoring infrastructure stability.
Across six resource configurations from strict per-task enforcement (1x) to uncapped, agent success rates rose as resource headroom increased.
Infrastructure error rates fell monotonically with added headroom, from 5.8% under strict enforcement to 0.5% when uncapped, with the strict-to-3x drop (5.8% to 2.1%) significant at p < 0.001.
From 1x to 3x resources, success scores varied only within noise (p = 0.40) because most tasks crashing at 1x would have failed regardless of resources.
Beyond roughly 3x resources, success rates begin climbing faster than infrastructure errors decline.

Between 3x and uncapped, extra resources let agents attempt approaches that only work with generous allocations (large dependencies, expensive subprocesses, memory-intensive test suites), lifting success ~4 points while infra errors fell only 1.6 points.
Up to about 3x the per-task specs, additional resources mainly fix transient-spike reliability problems, making the eval more stable without making it easier.
condition: up to roughly 3x the per-task resource specs

statement: Above about 3x, additional resources actively help the agent solve problems it otherwise could not, which shows that resource limits can change what the eval measures.
condition: above roughly 3x the per-task resource specs

statement: Tight resource limits reward lean, efficient strategies while generous limits reward agents that exploit heavyweight tools, so a single score without a stated resource configuration makes those differences hard to interpret.

Different models adopt different default strategies (for example installing a full data-science stack versus implementing the math from the standard library), and the resource configuration determines which default happens to succeed.

The resource-headroom effect replicated across multiple Anthropic models with a consistent direction but varying magnitude, and the same trend appears to hold on non-Claude models though it was not rigorously tested.

A crossover experiment on SWE-bench (RAM up to 5x across 227 problems, 10 samples each) reproduced the same monotonic effect but with smaller magnitude (only 1.54 points higher at 5x than 1x), consistent with SWE-bench tasks being less resource-intensive.
Resource allocation is not the only hidden variable; under certain configurations time limits also affect the score.
Because agentic evals are end-to-end system tests, any component of the setup (cluster health, hardware specs, concurrency level, egress bandwidth) can act as a confounder on the final score.
Pass rates have been observed anecdotally to fluctuate with time of day, likely because API latency varies with traffic, though this effect was not formally quantified.
The boundary between model capability and infrastructure behavior is blurrier than a single benchmark score implies.
For coding evals meant to be published, running them at multiple times and on multiple days helps average out infrastructure noise.
The ideal is to run each eval under identical hardware for both the scaffold and the inference stack to guarantee reproducibility, though this is not always practical.
exception: when running identical hardware is not practical

statement: Evals should specify both the guaranteed allocation and a separate hard kill threshold per task rather than a single pinned value, so containers get breathing room against spurious OOM kills while a ceiling still prevents score inflation.
The band between the resource floor and ceiling should be calibrated so that scores at the floor and at the ceiling fall within noise of each other.

In Terminal-Bench 2.0 a 3x ceiling over per-task specs cut infra error rates by roughly two-thirds (5.8% to 2.1%, p < 0.001) while keeping the score lift within noise (p = 0.40), a reasonable tradeoff whose exact multiplier varies by benchmark and should be reported.
Labs should treat resource configuration for agentic evals as a first-class experimental variable, documented and controlled with the same rigor as prompt format or sampling temperature.
Benchmark maintainers should publish recommended resource specs and also specify the enforcement methodology to close the reproducibility gap.
Consumers of benchmark results should treat small score differences on agentic evals as carrying more uncertainty than the reported precision suggests.
Leaderboard differences below about 3 percentage points deserve skepticism until the eval configuration is documented and matched.

Infrastructure confounders stack on top of naive binomial confidence intervals (which already span 1-2 points) rather than falling within them, and at the extremes of the allocation range the spread reaches about 6 points.
A model provider can shield its eval infrastructure from these confounders by dedicating hardware, but external evaluators cannot easily do the same.
An Agent Skill is a directory that must contain, at minimum, a SKILL.md file.
A skill directory may optionally include scripts/, references/, and assets/ subdirectories, plus any additional files or directories.
The SKILL.md file must contain YAML frontmatter followed by Markdown body content.
The SKILL.md frontmatter must include a name field and a description field, which are both required.
The name frontmatter field must be 1 to 64 characters long.
The name field may only contain unicode lowercase alphanumeric characters (a-z, 0-9) and hyphens.
The name field must not start or end with a hyphen.
The name field must not contain consecutive hyphens.
The skill's name field must match the name of its parent directory.
The description frontmatter field must be 1 to 1024 characters and non-empty.
The description field should describe both what the skill does and when to use it.
The description field should include specific keywords that help agents identify relevant tasks.
The optional license field specifies the license applied to the skill and is recommended to be kept short, either a license name or a reference to a bundled license file.
The compatibility field must be 1 to 500 characters when it is provided.
condition: the compatibility field is provided

statement: The compatibility field should only be included when the skill has specific environment requirements such as intended product, required system packages, or network access.
condition: the skill has specific environment requirements

statement: The optional metadata field is a map from string keys to string values that clients can use to store properties not defined by the Agent Skills spec.
Metadata key names should be made reasonably unique to avoid accidental conflicts.
The optional allowed-tools field is a space-separated string of tools that are pre-approved to run.
The allowed-tools field is experimental and its support may vary between agent implementations.
exception: an agent implementation does not support the experimental field

statement: The Markdown body after the frontmatter contains the skill instructions and has no format restrictions.
A SKILL.md body should include step-by-step instructions, examples of inputs and outputs, and common edge cases.
An agent loads the entire SKILL.md file once it decides to activate a skill, so longer SKILL.md content should be split into referenced files.

The scripts/ directory contains executable code that agents can run, and scripts should be self-contained or clearly document their dependencies, include helpful error messages, and handle edge cases gracefully.
The languages supported for scripts depend on the agent implementation, with common options including Python, Bash, and JavaScript.
The references/ directory contains additional documentation that agents load on demand, so individual reference files should be kept focused and small to reduce context usage.
The assets/ directory contains static resources such as templates, images, and data files.
Agents load skills progressively, pulling in more detail only as a task requires it.
At startup, only the metadata (the name and description fields, roughly 100 tokens) is loaded for all skills.
The full SKILL.md body is loaded only when the skill is activated, and its instructions are recommended to stay under 5000 tokens.
Resource files in scripts/, references/, or assets/ are loaded only when they are required.
The main SKILL.md should be kept under 500 lines, with detailed reference material moved to separate files.
File references within a skill should use relative paths from the skill root directory.
File references should be kept one level deep from SKILL.md, avoiding deeply nested reference chains.
Skills can be validated with the skills-ref reference library, which checks that the SKILL.md frontmatter is valid and follows all naming conventions.
Agent Skills are a lightweight, open format for extending an AI agent's capabilities with specialized knowledge and workflows.
At its core a skill is a folder that contains a SKILL.md file as its required entry point.
A skill's SKILL.md file combines metadata with instructions that tell the agent how to perform a specific task.
The minimum metadata a SKILL.md must declare is a name and a description.
condition: These two fields are the stated minimum; more metadata may be added.

statement: Beyond SKILL.md a skill may also bundle scripts, reference materials, templates, and other resources.
condition: These bundled resources are optional, not required.

statement: The conventional skill layout keeps the required SKILL.md at the folder root and organizes optional executable code under scripts/, documentation under references/, and templates or other resources under assets/.
Agents frequently lack the context they need to do real work reliably, and skills address this by packaging that context for on-demand loading.
Skills package procedural knowledge together with company-, team-, and user-specific context into portable, version-controlled folders that agents load on demand.
Skills give agents domain expertise by capturing specialized knowledge as reusable instructions and resources.
Skills give agents repeatable workflows by turning multi-step tasks into consistent, auditable procedures.
A skill can be built once and reused across products.
condition: Reuse works only across agents/clients that are compatible with the skills format.

statement: Agents load skills through progressive disclosure, which proceeds in three stages: discovery, then activation, then execution.
In the discovery stage, at startup agents load only each skill's name and description — just enough to recognize when the skill might be relevant.
In the activation stage the agent reads the full SKILL.md instructions into context.
condition: Activation happens when the task matches the skill's description.

statement: In the execution stage the agent follows the skill's instructions and may execute bundled code or load referenced files.
condition: Bundled code and referenced files are loaded only as needed.

statement: Because a skill's full instructions load only when a task calls for them, agents can keep many skills available while incurring only a small context footprint.

Asking an LLM to generate a skill from its general training knowledge alone, without domain-specific context, produces vague, generic procedures instead of the specific API patterns, edge cases, and project conventions that make a skill valuable.
Effective skills are grounded in real, domain-specific expertise, so skill creators should feed domain-specific context into the creation process rather than relying on the model's general knowledge.
To create a skill from a hands-on task, complete a real task in conversation with an agent while supplying context, corrections, and preferences, then extract the reusable pattern into the skill.

When extracting a skill from a completed task, capture the sequence of steps that worked, the corrections that steered the agent, the input/output data formats, and the project-specific context the agent did not already know.

A skill synthesized from a team's actual project artifacts (internal docs, runbooks, style guides, API specs, schemas, config files, code-review comments, issue trackers, version-control history, and real failure cases with resolutions) outperforms one synthesized from generic best-practice references, because it captures the team's own schemas, failure modes, and recovery procedures.

Refine a skill by running it against real tasks and feeding all of the results back into the creation process, not only the failures, asking what triggered false positives, what was missed, and what could be cut.
Even a single execute-then-revise iteration noticeably improves skill quality, and complex domains often benefit from several iterations.

Read the agent's execution traces rather than only its final outputs, because wasted or unproductive steps reveal instructions that are too vague, instructions that do not apply to the current task, or too many options presented without a clear default.

When a skill activates, its full SKILL.md body loads into the agent's context window alongside conversation history and other active skills, so every token in the skill competes with everything else for the agent's attention.

Skill content should focus on what the agent would not know on its own — project-specific conventions, domain-specific procedures, non-obvious edge cases, and the particular tools or APIs to use — and omit general knowledge the model already has.
For each piece of skill content, ask 'Would the agent get this wrong without this instruction?' and cut the content if the answer is no.
If the agent already handles the entire task well without the skill, the skill may not be adding value.

A skill should encapsulate a coherent unit of work that composes well with other skills; skills scoped too narrowly force multiple skills to load for one task and risk conflicting instructions, while skills scoped too broadly become hard to activate precisely.

Concise, stepwise guidance with a working example tends to outperform exhaustive documentation, because overly comprehensive skills make the agent struggle to extract what is relevant and can trigger unproductive paths from instructions that do not apply.
Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines and 5,000 tokens, holding just the core instructions needed on every run, and move detailed reference material into separate files such as a references/ directory.

Tell the agent when to load each reference file (for example, 'read references/api-errors.md if the API returns a non-200 status') rather than giving a generic 'see references/ for details', so context is loaded on demand.
Match the specificity of an instruction to the fragility of the task rather than applying the same level of prescriptiveness to every part of a skill.
Give the agent freedom and explain the purpose behind an instruction rather than dictating exact steps.
condition: when multiple approaches are valid and the task tolerates variation

statement: Give the agent prescriptive, exact instructions and forbid deviation.
condition: when operations are fragile, consistency matters, or a specific sequence must be followed

statement: When multiple tools or approaches could work, pick a single default and mention alternatives only briefly rather than presenting several options as equal.

A skill should teach the agent how to approach a class of problems rather than prescribing what to produce for one specific instance, so that the approach generalizes even when individual details are specific.

A gotchas section listing environment-specific facts that defy reasonable assumptions is among the highest-value content in a skill, provided the entries are concrete corrections to real mistakes rather than general advice.
condition: the entries are concrete, environment-specific corrections, not generic advice

statement: Keep gotchas in SKILL.md itself so the agent reads them before encountering the situation, because with a separate reference file the agent may not recognize the trigger to load it for non-obvious issues.
When an agent makes a mistake you have to correct, add the correction to the skill's gotchas section as a direct way to improve the skill iteratively.
To get output in a specific format, provide a concrete template rather than describing the format in prose, because agents pattern-match well against concrete structures.
Keep short templates inline in SKILL.md, and store longer or conditionally-needed templates in an assets/ directory referenced from SKILL.md so they load only when needed.
An explicit checklist helps the agent track progress and avoid skipping steps, especially when steps have dependencies or validation gates.
Instruct the agent to validate its own work before moving on using a loop of doing the work, running a validator, fixing issues, and repeating until validation passes.
For batch or destructive operations, have the agent produce an intermediate plan in a structured format, validate that plan against a source of truth, and only then execute.
condition: for batch or destructive operations

statement: Validation error messages should be informative enough for the agent to self-correct, for example by listing the available valid field names when a referenced field is not found.
If the agent independently reinvents the same logic on each run, write that logic once as a tested script and bundle it in a scripts/ directory.
condition: when the agent repeatedly reinvents the same logic across runs

statement: Running structured evaluations (evals) determines whether a skill works reliably across varied prompts and edge cases and whether it outperforms using no skill, while giving a feedback loop for systematic improvement.
A test case has three parts: a prompt (a realistic user message), a human-readable expected-output description of what success looks like, and optional input files the skill works with.
Test prompts should use realistic context such as file paths and column names, because vague prompts like 'process this data' are too vague to test anything useful.
Store test cases in an evals/evals.json file inside the skill directory.
Start with only 2-3 test cases rather than over-investing before seeing the first round of results, and expand the set later.
Vary test prompts across different phrasings, levels of detail, and formality.
Include at least one test prompt that exercises a boundary condition, such as malformed input, an unusual request, or a case where the skill's instructions might be ambiguous.
When first authoring test cases, do not define specific pass/fail checks; write only prompts and expected outputs, and add assertions after seeing what the first run produces.
Run each test case twice — once with the skill and once without it (or with a previous version) — to establish a baseline for comparison.

Organize eval results in a workspace directory alongside the skill, giving each full pass through the loop its own iteration-N/ directory, and each test case an eval directory with with_skill/ and without_skill/ subdirectories containing outputs/, timing.json, and grading.json.
The evals.json file is authored by hand, whereas grading.json, timing.json, and benchmark.json are produced during the eval process by the agent, scripts, or the author.
Each eval run should start with a clean context free of leftover state from previous runs or skill development, so the agent follows only what the SKILL.md specifies.
Subagent environments (for example Claude Code) provide run isolation naturally because each child task starts fresh; without subagents, use a separate session for each run.
condition: running without subagent isolation

statement: For each run, provide the skill path (or no skill for the baseline), the test prompt, any input files, and the output directory.

When improving an existing skill, use its previous version as the baseline: snapshot it before editing, point the baseline run at the snapshot, and save baseline outputs to old_skill/ instead of without_skill/.
condition: when improving an existing skill rather than testing a new one

statement: Timing data lets you weigh the skill's time and token cost against the baseline, since a skill that improves quality but triples token usage is a different trade-off than one that is both better and cheaper.
Record each run's token count and duration in timing.json (total_tokens and duration_ms) when the run completes.
In Claude Code, the subagent task-completion notification includes total_tokens and duration_ms, which must be saved immediately because they are not persisted anywhere else.
condition: running in Claude Code

statement: Assertions are verifiable statements about what an output should contain or achieve, and should be added only after seeing the first round of outputs because you often do not know what 'good' looks like until the skill has run.

Good assertions are programmatically verifiable, specific and observable, or countable; avoid weak assertions that are too vague to grade or too brittle, such as requiring an exact phrase that correct output with different wording would fail.

Not everything needs an assertion: qualities like writing style, visual design, or whether output 'feels right' are hard to decompose and are better caught during human review, so reserve assertions for objectively checkable things.
Grading records PASS or FAIL for each assertion against the actual outputs, with specific evidence that quotes or references the output rather than stating an opinion.

Give outputs and assertions to an LLM to evaluate each one, but for mechanically checkable assertions (valid JSON, correct row count, file dimensions) use a verification script, because scripts are more reliable than LLM judgment and reusable across iterations.
Require concrete evidence for a PASS and do not give the benefit of the doubt; an output with the right label but missing substance is a FAIL.
While grading, review the assertions themselves — not just the results — to catch ones that are too easy, too hard, or unverifiable, and fix them for the next iteration.

To compare two skill versions, use blind comparison: present both outputs to an LLM judge without revealing which version produced which so it scores holistic qualities free from bias, which complements assertion grading.

After each iteration, compute per-configuration summary statistics (pass_rate, time, tokens as mean and stddev) plus a delta into benchmark.json; the delta reveals what the skill costs versus what it buys.
Standard deviation is only meaningful with multiple runs per eval, so in early iterations with 2-3 single-run test cases focus on raw pass counts and the delta.
condition: only when there are multiple runs per eval

statement: Remove or replace assertions that always pass in both configurations, since they add no signal and inflate the with-skill pass rate.
Investigate assertions that always fail in both configurations — the assertion may be broken, the test too hard, or it may check the wrong thing — and fix them before the next iteration.
Study assertions that pass with the skill but fail without it, because that is where the skill clearly adds value, and identify which instructions or scripts made the difference.
When the same eval passes sometimes and fails other times (high stddev), tighten the skill's instructions by adding examples or more specific guidance to reduce ambiguity.
condition: when results are inconsistent across runs (high stddev)

statement: Investigate time and token outliers by reading the eval's execution transcript to find the bottleneck.

Review results with a human because assertion grading only checks what you thought to write assertions for, whereas a human catches unanticipated issues and outputs that are technically correct but miss the point.

Record specific, actionable feedback per test case (for example 'missing axis labels', not 'looks bad'); empty feedback means the output passed review, and improvements should focus on test cases with specific complaints.

Iteration draws on three signals — failed assertions (specific gaps), human feedback (broader quality issues), and execution transcripts (why things went wrong) — which are most effectively turned into changes by giving all three plus the current SKILL.md to an LLM to propose improvements.
Generalize fixes from feedback to address underlying issues broadly rather than adding narrow patches, because the skill is used across many prompts, not just the test cases.

Keep the skill lean, since fewer better instructions often outperform exhaustive rules; if pass rates plateau despite adding more rules the skill may be over-constrained, so try removing instructions.

Prefer reasoning-based instructions ('Do X because Y tends to cause Z') over rigid directives ('ALWAYS do X, NEVER do Y'), because models follow instructions more reliably when they understand the purpose.
Bundle repeated work into the skill's scripts/ directory when every run independently writes a similar helper script.
condition: when multiple runs independently reimplement the same helper

statement: The eval loop is iterative: propose improvements from the signals and SKILL.md, review and apply the changes, rerun all test cases in a new iteration-N+1/ directory, grade and aggregate, and review with a human, repeating until you are satisfied, feedback is consistently empty, or improvement between iterations is no longer meaningful.
A skill only provides value if it is activated, so triggering reliability is a prerequisite for a skill being useful.
The description field in a SKILL.md frontmatter is the primary mechanism an agent uses to decide whether to load a skill for a given task.
An under-specified skill description causes the skill to fail to trigger on prompts where it should apply.
An over-broad skill description causes the skill to trigger on prompts where it should not apply.
Agents use progressive disclosure: at startup they load only each skill's name and description, and read the full SKILL.md into context only once a task matches the description.
Because only the description is loaded at triggering time, the description alone carries the entire burden of deciding when the skill is relevant.
Agents typically consult a skill only for tasks requiring knowledge or capabilities beyond what the agent can handle alone.
condition: the task is non-trivial for the agent

statement: A simple one-step request may fail to trigger a skill even when the description matches perfectly, because the agent can complete it with basic tools.
condition: the request is simple/one-step and handleable with basic tools

statement: Write skill descriptions in imperative phrasing that instructs the agent when to act (e.g. 'Use this skill when...') rather than describing what the skill does.
Frame a skill description around user intent and what the user is trying to achieve, not the skill's internal implementation or mechanics.
Err on the side of a pushy description that explicitly lists the contexts where the skill applies, including cases where the user does not name the domain directly.
Keep a skill description concise — a few sentences to a short paragraph — to cover scope without bloating the agent's context across many skills.
A skill description must stay within the hard specification limit of 1024 characters.
To test triggering, build a set of realistic user prompts each labeled with whether it should or should not trigger the skill (eval queries).
Aim for about 20 eval queries, roughly 8-10 that should trigger and 8-10 that should not.
Vary should-trigger queries along phrasing, explicitness, detail, and complexity to test whether the description captures the skill's full scope.
The most useful should-trigger queries are ones where the skill would help but the connection is not obvious from the query alone, since those are where description wording makes the difference.
The most valuable should-not-trigger queries are near-misses that share keywords or concepts with the skill but actually need something different.
Obviously-irrelevant negative queries (no keyword overlap) test almost nothing and are weak negative examples.
Make eval queries realistic by including file paths, personal context, specific details, and casual language with occasional typos and abbreviations.
Test triggering by running each query through the agent with the skill installed and observing whether the agent invokes the skill via client observability such as logs or tool-call histories.
A query passes if it should trigger and the skill was invoked, or if it should not trigger and the skill was not invoked.
Because model behavior is nondeterministic, run each query multiple times (three is a reasonable start) and compute a trigger rate as the fraction of runs that invoked the skill.
A should-trigger query passes if its trigger rate is above a threshold (0.5 is a reasonable default) and a should-not-trigger query passes if its trigger rate is below that threshold.
Split the eval query set into a train set (~60%) used to guide description changes and a validation set (~40%) reserved to check whether improvements generalize, to avoid overfitting.
Ensure both the train and validation splits contain a proportional mix of should-trigger and should-not-trigger queries, shuffle randomly, and keep the split fixed across iterations.
Use only train-set failures to guide description revisions and keep validation-set results out of the revision process.
When should-trigger queries fail, the description is likely too narrow — broaden its scope or add context about when the skill is useful.
condition: should-trigger queries are failing

statement: When should-not-trigger queries falsely trigger, the description is likely too broad — add specificity about what the skill does not do or clarify the boundary with adjacent capabilities.
condition: should-not-trigger queries are false-triggering

statement: Avoid adding specific keywords from failed queries (overfitting); instead address the general category or concept those queries represent.
If refinement stalls after several iterations, try a structurally different description framing rather than incremental tweaks.
condition: several refinement iterations have not improved results

statement: Re-check that the description stays under the 1024-character limit during optimization, since descriptions tend to grow as they are revised.
Around five optimization iterations is usually enough; if performance is not improving the problem may lie in the queries (too easy, too hard, or mislabeled) rather than the description.
Select the best description by its validation-set pass rate, recognizing that the best iteration may not be the last one because later iterations can overfit the train set.

When applying the result, update the description field, verify it is under the 1024-character limit, and verify triggering with manual sanity checks plus 5-10 fresh queries never used during optimization.
Fresh queries that were never part of the optimization process give an honest check of whether the description generalizes.
A skill can instruct an agent both to run one-off shell commands and to bundle reusable executable scripts under a scripts/ directory.
Reference an existing package directly in SKILL.md instructions instead of creating a scripts/ directory when that package already provides the needed functionality.
condition: an existing package already does what the skill needs

statement: Several tool runners auto-resolve a package's dependencies at runtime, letting a skill invoke the tool without a separate manual install step.
uvx runs Python packages in isolated, aggressively cached environments and ships with uv, but is not bundled with Python and therefore requires a separate install.
pipx runs Python packages in isolated environments, is installable through OS package managers, and is a mature alternative to uvx with broader OS-package-manager availability.
npx runs npm packages by downloading them on demand, ships with npm and Node.js so it needs no extra install, and caches packages after first use.
bunx is Bun's drop-in equivalent of npx and is appropriate only when the environment provides Bun rather than Node.js.
condition: the environment has Bun rather than Node.js

statement: deno run executes scripts directly from URLs or specifiers, requires explicit permission flags such as --allow-read for filesystem or network access, and uses -- to separate Deno's own flags from the tool's flags.
condition: the script needs filesystem or network access (permission flags)

statement: go run compiles and runs Go packages directly and is built into the go command, needing no extra tooling.
Pin tool versions (for example npx eslint@9.0.0) so that a referenced command behaves the same over time.
State a skill's prerequisites explicitly in SKILL.md rather than assuming the agent's environment already has them, and use the compatibility frontmatter field for runtime-level requirements.
Move a command into a tested script under scripts/ once it grows complex or hard to get right; a bare one-off command is only reliable for invoking a tool with a few flags.
condition: the command is complex or hard to get right on the first try

statement: Reference bundled files using relative paths from the skill directory root, because the agent resolves those paths automatically and absolute paths are unnecessary.
List the available scripts in SKILL.md so the agent knows they exist.

Script execution paths written in code blocks are resolved relative to the skill directory root because the agent runs commands from there, and the same convention applies in references/*.md support files.
For reusable logic, bundle a script under scripts/ that declares its dependencies inline so the agent can run it with a single command and no separate manifest file or install step.
condition: the skill needs reusable logic

statement: PEP 723 defines a standard format for inline Python script metadata, with dependencies declared in a TOML block inside # /// markers.
uv run creates an isolated environment, installs the declared dependencies, and runs the script; pipx run also supports PEP 723 scripts.
Pin dependency versions with PEP 508 specifiers, constrain the interpreter with requires-python, and use uv lock --script to produce a reproducible lockfile.

Deno's npm: and jsr: import specifiers make a script self-contained by default and cache dependencies globally, though packages with native addons (node-gyp) may not work and packages shipping pre-built binaries work best.
exception: packages with native addons (node-gyp) may not work

statement: Bun auto-installs missing packages at runtime when no node_modules directory is found, with versions pinned directly in the import path.
exception: a node_modules directory exists anywhere up the directory tree, which disables auto-install and falls back to Node.js resolution

statement: Ruby's bundler/inline lets a script declare its gems directly in a gemfile block, and versions must be pinned explicitly because there is no lockfile.
exception: an existing Gemfile or BUNDLE_GEMFILE in the working directory can interfere

statement: When an agent runs a script it reads the script's stdout and stderr to decide what to do next.

Never require interactive input in a script: agents run in non-interactive shells and cannot answer TTY prompts, so a blocking prompt hangs indefinitely; accept all input via command-line flags, environment variables, or stdin.

Document a script's interface with --help output (a brief description, the available flags, and usage examples), since that output is the primary way an agent learns the interface, and keep it concise because it consumes the agent's context window.
Write error messages that state what went wrong, what was expected, and what to try, because an opaque error wastes an agent turn and directly shapes the agent's next attempt.

Emit structured output such as JSON, CSV, or TSV rather than free-form text so both the agent and standard tools can consume it, and separate data from diagnostics by sending data to stdout and progress or warnings to stderr.
Make scripts idempotent because agents may retry commands, so a create-if-not-exists behaviour is safer than create-and-fail-on-duplicate.
Reject ambiguous input with a clear error rather than guessing, and prefer enums or closed sets to constrain inputs.
Provide a --dry-run flag so the agent can preview the effect of a destructive or stateful operation before running it.
condition: the operation is destructive or stateful

statement: Use distinct exit codes for different failure types (such as not-found, invalid-arguments, or auth-failure) and document each code in --help so the agent can tell them apart.
Guard destructive operations with explicit confirmation flags such as --confirm or --force, or other safeguards appropriate to the risk level.
condition: the operation is destructive

statement: Keep output size predictable because many agent harnesses truncate output beyond roughly 10-30K characters and can lose critical information; default to a summary or limit and support pagination via --offset, or require an --output flag for large output.
An Agent Skill is a folder that contains a SKILL.md file.
A minimal, working Agent Skill can be a single SKILL.md file under 20 lines.
SKILL.md begins with a YAML frontmatter block delimited by --- containing name and description fields, followed by a Markdown body of instructions.
The skill's name field must match the name of the folder that contains the SKILL.md file.
The name field is a short identifier for the skill.
The description field tells the agent when to use the skill and is the signal the agent uses to decide whether to activate it.
The body of SKILL.md holds the instructions the agent follows once the skill activates.
By default, VS Code discovers skills placed in the .agents/skills/ directory relative to the project root.
Agent Skills use an open, agent-agnostic format, so the same skill runs unchanged in any compatible agent, including VS Code, Claude Code, and OpenAI Codex.
Agents load skills through progressive disclosure, which lets an agent have access to many skills without loading all of their full instructions into context up front.
During discovery, at the start of a chat session the agent scans the default skill directories and reads only each skill's name and description, just enough to judge relevance.
During activation, the agent matches the user's request against a skill's description and only then loads that skill's full SKILL.md body into context.
During execution, the agent follows the instructions in the skill body, adapting them (such as substituting parameters) to the specifics of the user's request.
To verify a skill is available in VS Code, open Copilot Chat in Agent mode and type /skills to confirm the skill appears in the list.
If a skill does not appear in the /skills list, verify the SKILL.md file is located at the expected path (e.g. .agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md) relative to the project root.
condition: the skill fails to appear in the /skills list

statement: Tool-use reliability varies across models: some models consistently follow skill instructions and run commands, while others may answer on their own without invoking the tool.
If the agent answers without running the skill's terminal command, switching to a different model from the model dropdown can make it follow the skill.
condition: the agent responds without running the skill's terminal command

statement: Using an Agent Skill in VS Code requires GitHub Copilot and selecting Agent mode from the chat mode dropdown.

Skills-compatible agents should load skill content in three progressive-disclosure tiers (catalog metadata, full instructions, then bundled resources) so base context stays small while specialized knowledge remains available on demand.
Tier 1 (catalog) loads only each skill's name and description at session start, costing roughly 50-100 tokens per skill.
Tier 2 loads the full SKILL.md body only when a skill is activated, and that body should be kept under about 5000 tokens.
Tier 3 loads a skill's bundled resources (scripts, references, assets) only when the instructions actually reference them.
At session startup the agent should discover all available skills and load their metadata.

Skill discovery should scan multiple scopes — at minimum project-level (relative to the working directory) and user-level (relative to the home directory); further scopes such as organization-wide or agent-bundled depend on the deployment model.
Within each scope the agent should scan both the client-specific skills directory and the shared '.agents/skills/' convention directory.
Scanning the '.agents/skills/' convention gives cross-client interoperability, making skills installed by other compliant clients automatically visible and vice versa.
Discovery should treat a skill as any subdirectory that contains a file named exactly 'SKILL.md'.
Discovery should skip directories that will not contain skills, such as '.git/' and 'node_modules/'.
Discovery should optionally respect '.gitignore' and set scan bounds (for example a max depth of 4-6 levels and a cap around 2000 directories) to prevent runaway scanning in large trees.

On skill name collisions apply a deterministic precedence rule where project-level skills override user-level skills; within the same scope pick first-found or last-found consistently and log a warning when a skill is shadowed.

Loading of project-level skills should be gated on a trust check (loading them only if the user has marked the project folder trusted) to stop untrusted repositories from injecting instructions into the agent's context.
condition: when project-level skills come from a potentially untrusted repository

statement: For a cloud-hosted or sandboxed agent, project-level skills travel with the cloned repository and can be scanned from its directory tree.
condition: when the agent operates on a cloned repository

statement: User-level and organization-level skills do not exist inside a sandbox and must be provisioned externally — e.g. cloning a configuration repo, accepting skill URLs/packages, or letting users upload skill directories.
condition: when the agent runs in a container or on a remote server

statement: Built-in skills can be packaged as static assets within the agent's deployment artifact so they are available in every session without external fetching.

A SKILL.md has YAML frontmatter between '---' delimiters followed by a markdown body; parsing extracts name and description (required) plus optional fields, and treats the trimmed remainder as the body.

The parser should handle technically-invalid YAML from other clients — most commonly unquoted values containing colons — via a fallback that quotes them or converts them to block scalars before retrying.

Validation should be lenient: warn but still load the skill on a name/directory mismatch or a name exceeding 64 characters, but skip the skill and log an error when the description is missing/empty or the YAML is completely unparseable.
Each skill record needs at minimum name, description, and location (absolute path to SKILL.md), stored in a map keyed by name for fast lookup during activation.
The skill body can be stored at discovery time for faster activation, or read from disk at activation time for lower aggregate memory use and to pick up file changes between activations.
A skill's base directory (the parent of its location) should be derived to resolve relative paths and enumerate bundled resources.
Skills should be disclosed to the model as a catalog of name, description, and optionally location, in any structured format (XML, JSON, or a bulleted list).

Include each skill's location in the catalog to enable file-read activation and give the model a base path for relative references; it may be omitted only when a dedicated activation tool already returns the skill directory in its result.
exception: unless a dedicated activation tool provides the skill directory path in its result

statement: The catalog can be placed either as a labeled system-prompt section (simplest, broadest compatibility) or embedded in a dedicated activation tool's description (cleaner system prompt).
Include a concise behavioral-instruction block alongside the catalog telling the model how and when to load skills, worded to match the supported activation mechanism.

Skills excluded for any reason (disabled, permission-denied, or opted out of model invocation) should be hidden entirely from the catalog rather than listed and blocked at activation, to avoid the model wasting turns on skills it cannot use.
When no skills are discovered, omit the catalog and behavioral instructions entirely rather than showing an empty skills block or registering a skill tool with no valid options.
condition: when no skills are discovered

statement: Activation should rely on model-driven judgment (the model reading the catalog and deciding a skill is relevant) rather than harness-side keyword or trigger matching.
File-read activation — the model calling its standard file-read tool on the SKILL.md path — is the simplest mechanism and needs no special infrastructure.
condition: when the model has file-read access

statement: A dedicated activation tool is required when the model cannot read files directly and is useful even when it can, because it lets you control returned content, wrap it in structured tags, list bundled resources, enforce permissions, and track activation.
A dedicated activation tool should constrain its name parameter to the set of valid skill names (e.g. an enum) to prevent the model from hallucinating nonexistent skill names.
Users should be able to activate skills directly, independent of the model, via a slash-command or mention syntax that the harness intercepts and injects.

When a dedicated activation tool returns skill content, wrap it in identifying tags so the model can distinguish skill instructions from other content and the harness can preserve them during context compaction.
condition: when using a dedicated activation tool

statement: A dedicated activation tool may enumerate a skill's bundled resources but must not eagerly read them — the model loads specific files on demand when the instructions reference them.
If the agent has a permission system gating file access, skill directories should be allowlisted so bundled resources load without triggering a user-confirmation prompt on every reference.
condition: when the agent has a permission system that gates file access

statement: Skill content should be exempted from context compaction/pruning, because silently losing durable skill instructions mid-session degrades performance with no visible error.
condition: when the agent truncates or summarizes older messages as the context window fills

statement: Activations should be deduplicated by tracking which skills are already in context and skipping re-injection of an already-loaded skill.

A skill may optionally be run in a separate subagent session that performs the task and returns a summary, which is useful when the skill's workflow is complex enough to warrant a dedicated focused session.
Agent skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Copilot can load to improve its performance on specialized tasks.
condition: when the skill is relevant to the current task

statement: The Agent Skills specification is an open standard that is used by a range of different AI systems, not only Copilot.
Users can author their own skills to teach Copilot to perform a task in a specific, repeatable way.
Skills can be sourced from shared online repositories such as anthropics/skills and GitHub's community-created github/awesome-copilot collection, in addition to authoring your own.
The `gh skill` command in the GitHub CLI discovers and installs skills from GitHub repositories.
Copilot supports project skills stored in the repository under `.github/skills`, `.claude/skills`, or `.agents/skills`.
Copilot supports personal skills stored in the home directory under `~/.copilot/skills` or `~/.agents/skills`, which are shared across projects.
Agent Skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that GitHub Copilot loads on demand when relevant to perform specialized tasks.
Agent Skills implement an open standard that is portable across skills-compatible agents, including GitHub Copilot in VS Code, the Copilot CLI, and the Copilot cloud agent.

Choose Agent Skills over custom instructions when you need reusable capabilities that work across multiple AI tools, want to bundle scripts or examples alongside instructions, or want to define specialized on-demand workflows such as testing, debugging, or deployment.

Choose custom instructions over skills when you need to define project-specific coding standards, language or framework conventions, code-review or commit-message guidelines, or rules applied to file types via glob patterns.
Custom instructions are always applied (or applied via glob patterns) and are limited to VS Code and GitHub.com, whereas skills are task-specific, loaded on demand, and portable across agents.
A skill is defined by a directory that contains a SKILL.md file specifying the skill's behavior.
Project skills live in a repository under .github/skills/, .claude/skills/, or .agents/skills/.
Personal skills live in the user profile under ~/.copilot/skills/, ~/.claude/skills/, or ~/.agents/skills/.
A SKILL.md file is Markdown with YAML frontmatter: the frontmatter defines the skill's metadata and the body defines its instructions and behavior.

The frontmatter 'name' field is required and must contain only lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens, must match the parent directory name, and must be at most 64 characters; invalid characters cause the skill to silently fail to load.
exception: Names containing slashes, colons, dots, or namespace prefixes are invalid and cause the skill to silently fail to load.

statement: The frontmatter 'description' field is required, must state both what the skill does and when to use it so Copilot can decide when to load it, and is limited to 1024 characters.
The optional 'argument-hint' field supplies hint text shown in the chat input when the skill is invoked as a slash command.
The optional 'user-invocable' field defaults to true; setting it to false hides the skill from the slash-command menu while still allowing the agent to auto-load it.
The optional 'disable-model-invocation' field defaults to false; setting it to true prevents automatic relevance-based loading so the skill runs only via manual slash-command invocation.
The optional experimental 'context' field defaults to inline (instructions added to the parent agent's context); setting it to 'fork' runs the skill in a dedicated subagent context.
condition: The forked-context feature is experimental and requires enabling the corresponding VS Code setting.

statement: When a skill is distributed through a plugin, the plugin name is automatically applied as a command prefix, so authors must not manually add namespace prefixes to the 'name' field.
exception: Adding namespace prefixes such as 'myorg/skillname' or 'myorg:skillname' causes the skill to silently fail to load.

statement: The skill body should describe what the skill accomplishes, when to use it, the step-by-step procedure to follow, examples of expected input and output, and references to any included scripts or resources.
Reference additional files in the skill directory using Markdown links with relative paths; a file that is not referenced in SKILL.md will not be loaded by the agent.
In a forked context the skill executes in a dedicated subagent and only its final result is returned to the parent agent, keeping the main conversation's context clean.
condition: The forked-context feature is experimental and requires enabling the corresponding VS Code setting.

statement: Use context: fork for skills that read many files or run lengthy investigations whose details need not persist, that produce a focused result the parent can act on, and that should not influence the parent beyond their final output.
Skills are exposed as slash commands in chat alongside prompt files; typing '/' lists the available skills and prompts to invoke.
Extra context can be appended after a skill's slash command, for example '/webapp-testing for the login page'.

Skill visibility is controlled by two frontmatter properties: omitting both yields a slash command that is also auto-loaded; user-invocable:false yields auto-load only; disable-model-invocation:true yields slash-command only; setting both disables the skill.

Copilot loads skills progressively in three levels — discovery from the name and description, loading the SKILL.md body, then accessing referenced resource files only when referenced — so many skills can be installed without consuming context up front.
Extensions contribute skills via the 'chatSkills' contribution point in package.json, whose 'path' must point to a directory containing a SKILL.md file.
For an extension-contributed skill, the skill directory's name must match the 'name' field in its SKILL.md or the skill is not loaded.

You can generate a skill with AI by typing '/create-skill' and describing the capability, and you can extract a reusable skill from an ongoing conversation by asking Copilot to capture the procedure you just performed.

Shared skills are available from community repositories such as github/awesome-copilot and anthropics/skills; to use one, copy its skill directory into .github/skills/ and review and customize the SKILL.md.
Always review a shared skill before using it to ensure it meets your requirements and security standards, since skills can include executable scripts.
Custom instructions are always-on context that automatically applies to every Copilot interaction within its defined scope.

Custom instructions are stored at .github/copilot-instructions.md for repo-wide scope, .github/instructions/*.instructions.md for path-specific scope, AGENTS.md for third-party agents, or in personal/org settings via the UI on GitHub.
Prompt files are reusable, standalone prompt templates that accept input variables and are stored at .github/prompts/*.prompt.md.
Custom agents are specialist personas with their own instructions, tool restrictions, and context.

Custom agents are stored at .github/agents/AGENT-NAME.md for a repository, at /agents/AGENT-NAME.md in the organization's .github or .github-private repository for org-level, at /agents/AGENT-NAME.md in a designated .github-private repository for enterprise-level, or in the user profile.
A subagent is a separate agent spawned by the main agent to handle delegated work in an isolated context, and it is a runtime process rather than a user-configured file.
Agent skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Copilot loads when they are relevant to a task.

Agent skills are stored at .github/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md, .claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md, or .agents/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md for project scope, and at ~/.copilot/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md or ~/.agents/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md for personal scope.
Hooks are custom shell commands that execute deterministically at specific points in an agent's workflow and are configured in .github/hooks/*.json.

MCP servers provide connections to external systems, APIs, and databases, and are configured via mcp.json (path varies by IDE), repository MCP settings on GitHub, or the mcp-servers property in a custom agent's configuration.
Custom instructions are triggered automatically.
Prompt files are triggered manually, by referencing them directly in chat or using the prompt file picker.
Custom agents are triggered manually, by selecting them from the agent dropdown in the IDE, on GitHub, or in Copilot CLI.
Subagents are triggered automatically, or by referencing a subagent directly in the prompt.
Agent skills are triggered automatically, chosen by Copilot when relevant to the prompt.
Hooks are triggered automatically at configured lifecycle events.
MCP servers are triggered automatically, or by asking for a specific tool by name.
Use custom instructions for standards, guidelines, or expectations that apply broadly across a context, such as enforcing coding standards, accessibility rules, or review checklists.
Use prompt files for focused single tasks that are run once with different inputs each time, such as generating unit tests or running a code review checklist.
Use custom agents for projects or processes with distinct stages that need specialized capabilities or strict handoffs, such as a React reviewer agent or a read-only auditing agent.
Use subagents for complex subtasks that should run in isolation from the main agent, such as codebase research or running test suites.
Use agent skills for multi-step workflows with bundled assets that should be loaded as needed, such as debugging GitHub Actions failures, deployment procedures, or drafting release notes.

Use hooks for tasks that must run at a specific point in the agent lifecycle with guaranteed execution, such as running a formatter after every file edit, approving or denying tool executions, or preventing credential leaks with secret scanning.

Use MCP servers for tasks that require access to external tools or real-time data, such as managing issues and PRs via the GitHub MCP server or automating browser testing via the Playwright MCP server.
GitHub recommends using the latest stable IDE, Copilot CLI, and Copilot extension versions to get the best Copilot experience.
MCP servers are supported across every listed surface: VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs, Eclipse, Xcode, GitHub.com, and Copilot CLI.
