statement: In JetBrains IDEs, the Agent Customizations editor lets you manage multiple Copilot customizations from one place, opened via the settings icon in the GitHub Copilot Chat panel and then Customizations.

The JetBrains Agent Customizations editor lets you view and edit custom agents, manage reusable skills, configure workspace or personal instructions, manage prompt files, and choose between Workspace customizations for the current project and Personal customizations that follow you across projects.
Agent skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Copilot loads when relevant to improve its performance on specialized tasks.
To create an agent skill, author a SKILL.md file, optionally accompanied by other resources such as supplementary Markdown files or scripts referenced from the SKILL.md instructions.
Project skills, specific to a single repository, are placed in a .github/skills, .claude/skills, or .agents/skills directory within that repository.
Personal skills, shared across projects, are placed in a ~/.copilot/skills or ~/.agents/skills directory in the user's home directory.
Each skill must have its own subdirectory inside the skills directory.
Skill subdirectory names must be lowercase and use hyphens in place of spaces.
A SKILL.md file is a Markdown file consisting of YAML frontmatter plus a Markdown body containing the skill's instructions, examples, and guidelines.
The SKILL.md frontmatter name field is required, must be lowercase using hyphens for spaces, and typically matches the skill's directory name.
The SKILL.md frontmatter description field is required and states what the skill does and when Copilot should use it.
The SKILL.md frontmatter license field is optional.

When a skill is invoked, Copilot automatically discovers all files in the skill's directory and makes them available alongside the instructions, so bundled scripts and resources can be referenced from SKILL.md.
Tools listed in the SKILL.md allowed-tools frontmatter field may be used by Copilot without asking for confirmation each time.
Copilot prompts the user for permission before using a tool.
condition: the tool is not listed in the SKILL.md allowed-tools frontmatter field

statement: To add a skill created by someone else, download a skill directory containing a SKILL.md (and any optional files), unzip it if it is a .zip, and move it to a valid project or personal skills location.
After adding a skill during a CLI session, run /skills reload (or start a new session) so the skill becomes available without restarting the CLI.
Running /skills info SKILL-NAME confirms that a skill has reloaded and reveals its location.
Copilot decides when to use a given skill based on the user's prompt and the skill's description.
When Copilot chooses to use a skill, that skill's SKILL.md is injected into the agent's context, giving the agent access to its instructions and any included scripts or examples.
To direct Copilot to use a specific skill, include the skill's name preceded by a forward slash in the prompt (for example, /frontend-design).
CLI skill management is available through the /skills commands: list, toggle on/off, info, add, reload, and remove SKILL-DIRECTORY.
/skills remove only removes skills that were added directly.
exception: skills added as part of a plugin, which must instead be managed through the plugin itself

statement: The list, add, and remove skill operations are also available from the terminal via the copilot skill subcommand (for example, copilot skill list or copilot skill add), which is useful for scripting or setting up skills before a session starts.
Use custom instructions for simple guidance relevant to almost every task, and use skills for more detailed instructions that Copilot should access only when relevant.
Context (assembled from the system prompt, Skills, CLAUDE.md files, memory, and other sources) is used generally across many requests, so unlike a single prompt it cannot be tuned to be as specific.
Context engineering — how you build the general prompts and guidance around an unknown user prompt — has a large impact on output quality when using Claude Code or building your own agents.
Anthropic removed over 80% of Claude Code's system prompt for newer models such as Claude Opus 5 and Claude Fable 5 with no measurable loss on their coding evaluations.
Overconstraining an agent through its system prompt, CLAUDE.md files, and skills is a real failure mode that degrades results.

Conflicting or overlapping instructions across the system prompt, skills, and user request commonly co-occur in a single request (e.g. 'leave documentation as appropriate' clashing with 'DO NOT add comments').
Overlapping and conflicting instructions cost the model reasoning effort, forcing it to reconcile them before deciding what to do.
For newer-generation models, many defensive constraints can be deleted and the model left to rely on surrounding context and its own judgement.
condition: the model is a newer-generation (Claude 5-class) model with stronger judgement
exception: older or weaker models where the constraint still prevents worst-case behaviour

statement: Claude Code now provides memory, artifacts, and skills — not just CLAUDE.md — as mechanisms for loading and sharing context across sessions.
Strong guidance that is not always true was historically added to prevent worst-case actions such as deleting files.
Blanket rules (e.g. 'default to writing no comments; never write multi-line comment blocks') are wrong for a subset of prompts.
exception: documentation, user comment preferences, or complex code that genuinely needs multi-line comment blocks

statement: Older models needed explicit guardrails (accepting incorrect output as a tradeoff), whereas newer models have better judgement and handle the same decisions well without explicit rules.
condition: choosing how much to constrain based on model generation
exception: older models still require the guardrails

statement: Replace a rigid rule with a judgement-based instruction that points at context (e.g. 'write code that matches the surrounding code's comment density, naming, and idiom') so it covers more cases correctly.
Giving newer models usage examples can constrain them to a narrower exploration space rather than help them.
Prefer designing expressive tool, script, and file interfaces — what parameters the model has and how expressive they are — over supplying usage examples.

An expressive parameter design conveys intended use without examples: e.g. a Todo tool status enum (pending / in_progress / completed) plus a rule to keep exactly one item in_progress hints at correct behaviour.
Progressive disclosure means loading the right context at the right time instead of putting everything upfront.
Move situational instructions such as verification and code review into their own skills the agent calls selectively, rather than keeping them always in the system prompt.
Deferred-loading tools, whose full definitions the agent must fetch via ToolSearch before use, let a harness expose many tools without consuming context until they are needed.
Do not make CLAUDE.md or SKILL.md a central repository of every practice you might need; instead structure a tree of files that load at the right time.
Earlier models sometimes needed repeated instructions and weighted instructions at the end of the context window more than at the start.
condition: earlier-generation models

statement: Put tool-usage instructions in the tool's description rather than duplicating them in the system prompt.
Claude now automatically saves memories relevant to the work and to the user, replacing the older practice of manually writing to CLAUDE.md via the # hotkey.
Claude can consume richer references than plain-markdown plans, including HTML artifacts.
References can be provided as code: a spec may be a detailed test suite, or a function in another codebase for the model to port.
Rubrics are a form of reference that let the agent verify subjective taste (e.g. what good API design looks like) via dynamic workflows that spin up verifier agents applying those rubrics.
A system prompt is tied to product context — it tells the model what product it operates in and what it is doing — so it warrants heavy investment when building your own agent harness.
condition: building your own agent harness (Claude Code's own system prompt is rarely modified by users)

statement: Keep CLAUDE.md lightweight: briefly state what the repo is for and spend most of the tokens on codebase gotchas.
Avoid stating in CLAUDE.md the obvious things the model can learn by looking at the file system or the repo.
Apply progressive disclosure inside CLAUDE.md — e.g. move several verification instructions into a verification skill and reference it from CLAUDE.md.
Treat skills as lightweight guides that help the model find information when needed, and avoid overconstraining them.
exception: highly important areas, where stronger constraint in the skill is warranted

statement: Split long skills into multiple files using progressive disclosure rather than one large file.
Skills are most valuable when they encode opinions, knowledge, or best practices specific to you, your team, or your product.
You can @ mention files to include them as references so the model can consult in-depth information about the current plan.

Prefer references that are code because they give clear, high-fidelity instructions in a language the model knows well — e.g. an HTML mockup of a design generally outperforms a textual description or a screenshot.
Periodically simplify across your system prompt, skills, and CLAUDE.md files; the Claude Code 'claude doctor' / /doctor command automates much of this rightsizing.

Skill creation is an iterative loop: decide the skill's intent and rough approach, write a draft, create test prompts and run Claude-with-the-skill on them, evaluate qualitatively and quantitatively, rewrite from feedback, and repeat until satisfied before expanding the test set for a larger-scale run.

Start skill creation by capturing the user's intent, and when the current conversation already contains the workflow to capture, first extract the tools used, the step sequence, the user's corrections, and observed input/output formats from the conversation history.
condition: the conversation already contains a workflow the user wants to capture

statement: Have the user confirm the captured intent before proceeding to the next step.
Capture four things up front: what the skill should enable Claude to do, when it should trigger, the expected output format, and whether to set up test cases to verify it.

Recommend test cases for skills whose outputs are objectively verifiable (file transforms, data extraction, code generation, fixed workflow steps), while skills with subjective outputs such as writing style or art often do not need them; let the user decide.
condition: the skill has objectively verifiable outputs
exception: skills with subjective outputs (writing style, art) often need no test cases

statement: During the interview, proactively ask about edge cases, input/output formats, example files, success criteria, and dependencies before writing any test prompts.

Check available MCPs and, when useful for research such as searching docs, finding similar skills, or best practices, research in parallel via subagents if available or inline otherwise, arriving with context to reduce the user's burden.
condition: research would help and MCPs/subagents are available

statement: Skill-creator users span a wide range of technical familiarity, so adapt wording to context cues about the user's expertise: 'evaluation' and 'benchmark' are borderline but acceptable, use 'JSON' and 'assertion' only given clear cues the user knows them, and briefly define terms when in doubt.
A SKILL.md requires a name and a description in its YAML frontmatter plus markdown instructions; a compatibility field for required tools or dependencies is optional and rarely needed.
The description field is the primary mechanism that determines whether Claude invokes a skill.
Write the description to state both what the skill does and the specific contexts for when to use it, and keep all 'when to use' information in the description rather than in the skill body.

Because Claude currently tends to under-trigger skills, make descriptions somewhat 'pushy' by explicitly enumerating triggering contexts, including cases where the user will not name the skill or file type.

Skills load progressively across three levels: metadata (name plus description, always in context, roughly 100 words), the SKILL.md body (loaded whenever the skill triggers, ideally under 500 lines), and bundled resources (loaded as needed and effectively unbounded, with scripts able to execute without being loaded into context).
Keep SKILL.md under about 500 lines, and when approaching that limit add another layer of hierarchy with clear pointers to where the model should read next.
exception: line and word counts are approximate; going longer is acceptable when needed

statement: Reference bundled files clearly from SKILL.md with guidance on when to read them, and give any reference file longer than about 300 lines a table of contents.
condition: a reference file exceeds ~300 lines (for the table of contents)

statement: When a skill supports multiple domains or frameworks, organize the resources by variant with one reference file per variant so Claude reads only the relevant one.
condition: the skill supports multiple domains or frameworks

statement: A skill must never contain malware, exploit code, or anything that compromises system security, must not be misleading or built to facilitate unauthorized access, data exfiltration, or other malicious activity, and its contents must not surprise the user relative to its described intent.
exception: benign roleplay skills (e.g. 'roleplay as an X') are acceptable

statement: Prefer the imperative form for skill instructions.
Pin down an output format by giving the model an exact template to follow, and include worked input/output examples where they help.
Explain why each instruction matters rather than relying on heavy-handed all-caps MUSTs, using theory of mind and keeping the skill general instead of narrowly tailored to specific examples.

After drafting, create two to three realistic test prompts in real-user language, get the user's sign-off on them, and save them to evals/evals.json without assertions, which are added later while the runs are in progress.
Run the test-and-evaluate sequence as one continuous flow without stopping partway, and do not use /skill-test or any other testing skill for it.

Spawn the with-skill run and the baseline run for every test case in the same turn, rather than launching all with-skill runs first and returning for baselines later, so they finish around the same time.
Choose the baseline by context: for a new skill run the same prompt with no skill at all, and for improving an existing skill snapshot the old skill first and run the baseline against that snapshot.
condition: creating a new skill vs improving an existing one

statement: While the runs are in progress, draft objectively verifiable, descriptively named assertions, and evaluate subjective skills qualitatively rather than forcing assertions onto them.
exception: subjective skills (writing style, design quality) are better judged qualitatively than with assertions

statement: Capture each run's total_tokens and duration_ms to timing.json the moment the task-completion notification arrives, because that is the only opportunity: the data comes through the notification and is not persisted elsewhere.
In grading.json use exactly the fields text, passed, and evidence, because the results viewer depends on those exact field names.
For assertions that can be checked programmatically, write and run a script instead of eyeballing them, because scripts are faster, more reliable, and reusable across iterations.
condition: the assertion is programmatically checkable

statement: Generate the eval viewer with generate_review.py rather than hand-written HTML, and in headless or no-display environments use its --static option to emit a standalone HTML file.
condition: a headless / no-display environment (for the --static option)

statement: Present the eval viewer to the human for review before evaluating any outputs yourself, so the human sees the examples as soon as possible.
Treat empty user feedback as approval, and focus improvements on the test cases where the user raised specific complaints.

When improving a skill, generalize from the handful of iteration examples to the skill's many future uses: avoid overfitted, fiddly changes and oppressively constrictive MUSTs, and try different metaphors or working patterns for stubborn issues.

Keep the skill prompt lean by removing instructions that are not pulling their weight, reading the run transcripts rather than only the final outputs to find where the skill wastes the model's effort.
Treat all-caps ALWAYS or NEVER and rigid structures as a yellow flag, and where possible reframe them to explain the reasoning so the model understands why the requirement matters.

When several test runs independently produce a similar helper script or the same multi-step approach, bundle that script under scripts/ and have the skill call it so future invocations do not reinvent it.
condition: multiple test runs independently reproduce the same script or approach

statement: Continue the improve-rerun-review loop until the user is satisfied, all feedback is empty, or you stop making meaningful progress.

For a rigorous judgment of whether a new skill version is better, use blind comparison: give both outputs to an independent agent without revealing which is which, then analyze why the winner won; this is optional and requires subagents.
condition: a rigorous version-versus-version quality comparison is wanted

statement: After creating or improving a skill, offer to optimize its description, and build about 20 trigger eval queries split between should-trigger and should-not-trigger cases that are realistic, concrete, and detailed (file paths, personal or job context, column names, casual speech, typos).
Make should-not-trigger queries genuine near-misses that share keywords or concepts with the skill but actually need something else, avoiding obviously irrelevant negatives that test nothing.
Run the description-optimization loop with the model ID powering the current session, so the triggering test matches what the user actually experiences.

The description optimizer splits the queries 60/40 into train and held-out test, runs each query three times for a reliable trigger rate, iterates up to five times, and selects best_description by test score rather than train score to avoid overfitting.

Claude consults a skill only for tasks it cannot easily handle itself, so simple one-step queries may not trigger a skill even with a perfectly matching description while complex, multi-step, or specialized queries trigger reliably; make eval queries substantive enough to genuinely benefit from a skill.

On Claude.ai there are no subagents, so run test cases yourself one at a time by following the SKILL.md, skip baseline runs and quantitative benchmarking, and skip description optimization, which requires the claude CLI.
condition: running on Claude.ai (no subagents available)

statement: When updating an existing skill, preserve its original name and directory and copy it to a writeable location before editing, since the installed path may be read-only.
condition: updating an existing skill rather than creating a new one

statement: Package the finished skill with package_skill.py and present the resulting .skill file to the user, doing the presentation step only when the present_files tool is available.
condition: the present_files tool is available (for the present step)

statement: Bundle instructions for specialized subagents under an agents/ directory (for example grader.md for evaluating assertions, comparator.md for blind A/B comparison, and analyzer.md for analyzing why one version beat another) and read the relevant file only when spawning that subagent.
condition: spawning the corresponding specialized subagent

statement: Document the JSON structures the skill uses, such as evals.json and grading.json, in a references/schemas.md file so their exact shape is available on demand rather than inline.

Track the skill-creation steps on a TodoList so they are not forgotten, and in Cowork specifically include a to-do to create the evals JSON and run generate_review.py so the human can review the test cases before you revise the skill.
condition: in Cowork (for the specific eval-viewer to-do)
